\section{Characters, saturation, and principal cuts (source 14)}
\label{swo:tc:sec:characters}
We use $\Ord$ as a \emph{character symbol}: it means that a uniform
ordinal-indexed cofinal or coinitial family exists, while no set-sized
one exists. It is not an ordinary cardinal. For any nonempty class
linear order with no set-sized cofinal subset, global choice permits
an increasing cofinal $\Ord$-sequence: at each set stage dominate the
earlier choices and the elements seen so far in a global enumeration.
If no such upper choice existed, the already considered set would be
cofinal. This is set-valued recursion. The dual argument handles
coinitiality. A set-sized character is the least cardinality of a
cofinal or coinitial subset; if there is a corresponding endpoint it
is $1$.

\begin{theorem}[Cut-character calculation]\label{swo:tc:thm:characters}
Write the character of a normalized cut as
$(\cf D,\ci(\Psupp(b)\setminus D))$. For the alternatives of
\Cref{swo:tc:thm:trichotomy}, the following formulas hold.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}Yl@{}}
\toprule
Cut & Character\\\midrule
$D_F$, with $F=E_\sigma$ for some core code & $(\Ord,1)$\\
$D_F$, with $F$ not represented by a core code & $(\Ord,\Ord)$\\
$D_p^-$, $\dom p=\lambda$ a nonzero limit & $(\cf\lambda,\Ord)$\\
$D_p^+$, $\dom p=\lambda$ a nonzero limit & $(\Ord,\cf\lambda)$\\
$D_p^-$ or $D_p^+$, $\dom p$ a successor & $(\Ord,\Ord)$\\
$D_{p,H}$ & $(\cf H,\ci(A_p\setminus H))$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
For the last row both characters cannot be set-sized. At every actual
point of $\Psupp(b)$, both \emph{strict} local characters are $\Ord$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a branch $F$, complete a prefix agreeing with $F$ before $\alpha$
and taking a fresh smaller entry at $\alpha$; call the result
$a_\alpha$. Similarly obtain $b_\alpha$ with a larger entry. If
$\alpha<\beta$, first difference gives
\[
 a_\alpha<a_\beta <_{\lex} F<_{\lex} b_\beta<b_\alpha.
\]
Every code below or above $F$ is surpassed on the appropriate side by
one of these approximants, once $\alpha$ exceeds its first disagreement.
A set of codes differing from $F$ has a set of first disagreements and
hence a common ordinal bound; a later approximant defeats its alleged
cofinality or coinitiality. If $F$ itself is a core point, the complement
of $D_F$ has that point as its least member. This gives $(\Ord,1)$,
not $(\Ord,\Ord)$; only the strict right side has character $\Ord$.

At the lower edge of a limit-length prefix $p$, take a cofinal sequence
of coordinates $\alpha<\lambda$ and complete a word that first differs
from $p$ there by a smaller entry. These codes are cofinal below the
cylinder. Conversely the first-disagreement coordinates of any cofinal
family must be cofinal in $\lambda$: a code which follows $p$ longer
would otherwise be above the entire family. This proves the character
$\cf\lambda$. On the other side the cylinder has no set-sized
coinitial subset by \Cref{swo:tc:prop:cylinders}, and lies below
all other points of the complement. Its character is $\Ord$. The
upper-edge calculation is dual.

For a successor-length prefix $p=q\cat(x)$, any set of points below
$C_p$ that first differ before the last coordinate can be surpassed by
one following $q$. Among those which follow $q$, their entries at the
last coordinate form a set below $x$. \Cref{swo:tc:lem:fresh} provides a
fresh entry between that set and $x$. Completion again surpasses the
whole family while remaining below $C_p$. Thus the lower side of the
lower edge has no set-sized cofinal subset. The opposite side follows
from the cylinder property. The upper edge is the dual case.

For a numerical gap, project included points in $C_p$ to their
next-coordinate labels in $H$. A cofinal set of labels, with one
completed word above each chosen label when necessary, produces a
cofinal family of codes. Conversely a cofinal family of codes must
have cofinal projected labels: otherwise a child cylinder with a
larger label in $H$ surpasses it. The absence of a greatest member of
$H$ removes any dependence on the internal character of one child.
The dual argument proves the right character. If both were sets,
cofinal labels on the left and coinitial labels on the right would
constitute a set cut of $A_p$ with no separator, contradicting
\Cref{swo:tc:lem:fresh}. Finally the branch argument at a core point
already proves the assertion about strict local characters.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Recovery of the core saturation theorem]\label{swo:tc:cor:coreeta}
Every separated pair of sets of codes $A,B\subseteq \Psupp(b)$ has a
strict separator in $\Psupp(b)$. In particular the core is an
$\eta_{\Ord}$-order: it fills all set-sized strict cuts, including
those with an empty side.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Empty-side bounds follow by choosing a first label above or below all
first labels in the specified set. Suppose both sides are nonempty
and no separator exists. If $A$ has a greatest point $a$, then $B$
would be coinitial in the strict right side of $a$, contradicting its
local character. The dual argument applies if $B$ has a least point.
Otherwise let $D=\{\sigma:(\exists a\in A)\ \sigma<a\}$. It is a
proper normalized cut with $A$ cofinal. Absence of a separator makes
$B$ coinitial in its complement: any point there below all of $B$
would be strictly above all of $A$. The character table has no
nonprincipal cut with two set-sized characters, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The known surreal order type]\label{swo:tc:cor:coreNo}
There is a class order isomorphism $\Psupp(b)\cong\No$ in $\GBC$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Both are proper class linear orders filling all set cuts. Fix set-like
global enumerations and perform back-and-forth along $\Ord$. At a set
stage the existing partial map has set domain and range; the next
point's lower and upper constraints are sets and admit a fresh image.
The union is an elementary definable class bijection preserving order.
This is the standard argument, also used by the predecessor; the
isomorphism statement itself is inherited, not claimed as a new result.
\end{proof}

The character calculation explains why the core is not Dedekind complete.
For instance the increasing core points whose first entries are natural
numbers have upper bounds but no supremum. Filling \emph{strict} set
cuts supplies another point between all those entries and any proposed
upper bound. The countable/non-set-sized numerical-gap character above
records this failure rather than contradicting saturation.

\begin{note}[\merge; which rows are new]\label{swo:viii:note:characters}
The branch rows of \cref{swo:tc:thm:characters} are source~11's
\cref{swo:gl:local} and source~09's \cref{swo:ec:thm:class-gap}
($(\Ord,\Ord)$ at a non-core branch); \cref{swo:tc:cor:coreeta} is
\cref{swo:gl:interpolation} for sets of codes and \cref{swo:tc:cor:coreNo} is
\cref{swo:gl:pbd-no}, both stated by source~14 as recoveries. New are the
characters of the edge and numerical-gap cuts and the statement that no
nonprincipal cut has two set-sized characters. The same table is proved,
case by case, by source~13 (\cref{swo:fs:prop:characters}), source~15
(\cref{swo:cb:prop:cutcharacters}), source~16 (the paragraph after its
table) and source~17 for non-core branches (\cref{swo:gs:prop:class-characters});
those statements are printed with their sources' recognition theorems in
\cref{swo:viii:sec:routes}.
\end{note}

\section{Recognizing exhaustive cuts and preserving old cuts (source 14)}
\label{swo:tc:sec:recognition}
\begin{theorem}[Exhaustive-cut recognition]\label{swo:tc:thm:recognition}
Let $D$ be a proper normalized class cut of $\Psupp(b)$. There exists
$E\in \Hsl$ with $D=D_E$ if and only if both conditions hold:
\begin{align}
 &\forall\alpha\in\Ord\ \exists p\,
   [\dom p=\alpha\ \wedge\ \operatorname{Cross}_D(p)],
       \tag{C}\label{swo:tc:eq:coherence}\\
 &\forall x\in\No\ \exists p\,
   [\operatorname{Cross}_D(p)\ \wedge\ x\in\ran p].
       \tag{X}\label{swo:tc:eq:coverage}
\end{align}
Such an enumeration is unique, and its graph is given by
\[
 E(\alpha)=x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists p\,[\operatorname{Cross}_D(p)\ \wedge\ \alpha\in\dom p
                         \ \wedge\ p(\alpha)=x].
\]
All quantifiers in the criterion and reconstruction range over sets;
only $D$ and $b$ are class parameters.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For an exhaustive $E$, every restriction $E\res\alpha$ crosses its
trace by the smaller and larger completions in
\Cref{swo:tc:lem:branchdensity}. Every surreal occurs in one of these
restrictions, giving (C) and (X). Conversely (C) and
\Cref{swo:tc:lem:crosschain} produce an injective union $F$ on all of
$\Ord$. Condition (X) makes it surjective. The unbounded case of
\Cref{swo:tc:thm:trichotomy} gives $D=D_F$. The displayed graph formula
is exactly the union of the crossing chain; its functionality and
uniqueness follow from the chain lemma.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{A logical simplification.}
For this proper-class alphabet, (X) by itself already implies (C).
Indeed, the union of the crossing chain then has range all of $\No$;
if its domain were a set ordinal, class Replacement would make that
range a set. Its domain is therefore $\Ord$, and prefix closure gives
(C). We retain the two conditions in the theorem to distinguish
coherent nonexhaustive branches from failures that stop at a set stage;
we do not claim that the conditions are logically independent.

This answers the predecessor's question ``Which cuts of the core
represent exhaustive branches?'' (\cref{swo:n16.1}; source~09's third direction in \cref{swo:ec:sec:research})
\emph{in the prefix-enriched structure}. A bare linear-order isomorphism
of the core does not come equipped with its prefix cylinders or the
label evaluation. The theorem does not show that those enrichments are
definable from the order relation alone. \Cref{swo:tc:cor:nonintrinsic} below proves that an automorphism-invariant
bare-order criterion cannot recognize exhaustiveness: some core
automorphisms carry exhaustive traces to nonbranch cylinder edges.

The criterion also separates two notions of completion. An injective
branch always gives a cut coherent through every set stage. It gives
a global enumeration only if it eventually visits every label. No
condition at a single bounded stage can enforce the latter assertion.
For the branch $F(\alpha)=\alpha$, (C) holds and (X) fails at $x=-1$.
The two cylinder-edge alternatives fail (C) at a bounded length; a
numerical-gap alternative also fails (C), because there is no crossing
child after its last crossing prefix.

\merge\ The second half of source~14's Section~7, on preserving old cuts
under class extensions (its \cref{swo:tc:thm:absolute}, the corollary and
the remark after it), is printed in \cref{swo:viii:sec:extensions}.

\section{Five further proofs of the represented-cut theorem (sources 16, 15, 13, 17 and 18)}\label{swo:viii:sec:routes}

\begin{note}[\merge; one theorem, six proofs]\label{swo:viii:note:sixfold}
The theorem that a normalized class cut of the core is the cut of an
injective class word exactly when a crossing (straddling) prefix exists at
every set length, that the word is then unique and elementary in the cut,
and that it is exhaustive exactly when the ranges of these prefixes cover
$\No$, is proved independently in all six batch-81 sources:
source~14's \cref{swo:tc:thm:trichotomy}(iii) and \cref{swo:tc:thm:recognition},
source~16's \cref{swo:ds:thm:cutrecognition}, source~15's
\cref{swo:cb:thm:cutcriterion} with \cref{swo:cb:cor:kernel}, source~13's
\cref{swo:fs:thm:reconstruction}, source~17's \cref{swo:gs:thm:recognition}
and source~18's \cref{swo:sh:thm:represented-class-cut} with
\cref{swo:sh:cor:elementary-cut-recognition}. Each source presents it as its
own answer to source~11's \cref{swo:n16.1}; it answers that question
(\cref{swo:viii:sec:status}), and no source has priority over another. The
six proofs are the same argument: uniqueness of a crossing prefix at each
length, coherence under restriction, the elementary union, and the first
disagreement with a code. They are printed as routes because each source
builds different examples and corollaries on its own proof.

The analysis of a failing cut is likewise proved five times. Source~14
partitions the proper cuts by their form (edge, numerical gap, branch:
\cref{swo:tc:thm:trichotomy}); sources~13, 15, 16 and~18 partition the
failing cuts by their first failed length (successor or limit:
\cref{swo:fs:thm:failure,swo:cb:thm:terminal,swo:ds:thm:firstfailure,swo:sh:thm:cut-first-failure}).
The two partitions are equivalent: a limit failure is an edge of a
limit-length cylinder, and a successor failure is an edge of a child cylinder
or a numerical gap. Source~15's successor case is the finest, separating a
\emph{forbidden repeated label} (the unused alphabet split at a label already
used by the prefix, \cref{swo:cb:n7.7}, source~16's second table row and
source~18's \cref{swo:sh:ex:repeated-label-cut}) from a numerical gap with no
surreal separator; in source~14's terms both are numerical-gap cuts
$D_{p,H}$, the first with $A_p\setminus H$ and $H$ separated by a point of
$\ran p$.

Source~18 states its theorem ``in $\GB$ with the fixed baseline''. A baseline
$b:\Ord\to\No$ already yields global choice over $\GB$
(\cref{swo:cf:choice}), so the hypothesis is not weaker than $\GBC$; the
theorem's own content is that no class choice and no $\ETR$ are used beyond
the baseline. Sources~13, 14, 15, 16 and~17 say $\GBC$.
\end{note}

% ---- source 16 (batch-81 manuscript 04), lines 1438-1611
\subsection{Source 16: exact recognition of cuts represented by branches}\label{swo:ds:sec:cutrecognition}

Fix the core $\Pbd(b)$ and its evaluation. For an injective set prefix
$p:\alpha\to\No$ write
\[
 C_p=\{q\in \Pbd(b):E_q\res\alpha=p\}.
\]
These cylinders are nonempty and convex, and at each fixed length they
form an ordered partition. Each cylinder has no endpoint: change the
next coordinate of one completion to a fresh smaller or larger surreal
and apply \Cref{swo:ds:lem:completion}.

A \emph{lower cut} here means an available class
$\varnothing\ne L\subsetneq \Pbd(b)$ that is initial and has no greatest
member. Put $U=\Pbd(b)\setminus L$. A prefix \emph{straddles} the cut if
$C_p\cap L$ and $C_p\cap U$ are both nonempty. This is a property with
only set quantifiers and the class parameters $L,b$.

\begin{theorem}[Prefix-cylinder recognition]\label{swo:ds:thm:cutrecognition}
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item There is an injective class function $F:\Ord\to\No$ such that
\[
 L=\{q\in \Pbd(b):E_q<_{\lex}F\}=:L_F.
\]
\item At every ordinal length $\alpha$ some injective prefix straddles
the cut.
\end{enumerate}
When these conditions hold, the prefix at each length is unique and is
exactly $F\res\alpha$. The branch is exhaustive if and only if every
surreal occurs in the range of some straddling prefix.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a given $F$, choose fresh values below and above $F(\alpha)$ and
complete the corresponding one-letter extensions of $F\res\alpha$.
They lie on opposite sides of $F$, so its prefix straddles.

Two different prefixes at the same length cannot both straddle an
initial cut. Their cylinders are entirely ordered one before the
other, and an upper witness in the earlier cylinder would be below a
lower witness in the later one. This contradicts initiality.
Restrictions of straddling prefixes still straddle. Hence the prefixes
$p_\alpha$ supplied by condition 2 are unique and coherent.

Define the branch directly, by elementary comprehension:
\[
 F(\alpha)=x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists p\,[p\text{ straddles},\ \dom(p)=\alpha+1,\ p(\alpha)=x].
\tag{S16.14}\label{swo:ds:eq:recognitionformula}
\]
Here the prefix and the witnesses from both sides are sets. Coherence
proves that this is a total injective class function and that
$F\res\alpha=p_\alpha$. This is not a class-valued recursion.

If $E_q<F$ first differ at $\delta$, every point of
$C_{p_{\delta+1}}$ is above $q$. One such point is in $L$, so $q\in L$.
If $F<E_q$, an upper witness in the same cylinder lies below $q$, so
$q\in U$. Finally, if $E_q=F$, placing $q$ in $L$ would make it the
greatest member of $L$ by the preceding two implications. Thus it is
in $U$, and $L=L_F$. The prefixes determine $F$ uniquely, and their
range union gives exactly the stated exhaustion criterion.
\end{proof}

The no-greatest convention matters only at a represented core point:
without it, both $\{q:E_q<F\}$ and $\{q:E_q\le F\}$ would straddle
every level when $F=E_q$ for a code. The two improper cuts fail already
at the empty prefix and represent no injection.

\begin{theorem}[Complete classification of the first failure]
\label{swo:ds:thm:firstfailure}
If a lower cut is not represented, let $\lambda$ be the least length
with no straddling prefix. Then $\lambda>0$, and exactly one of the
following occurs.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Successor failure.} If $\lambda=\alpha+1$, let $p$ be
the unique straddling prefix of length $\alpha$. The unused labels
$\No\setminus\ran(p)$ split into nonempty initial and final classes
$A+B$, with
\[
 C_{p\cat(x)}\subseteq L\ (x\in A),\qquad
 C_{p\cat(x)}\subseteq U\ (x\in B).
\]
All codes below $C_p$ are in $L$ and all codes above it in $U$.
\item \textbf{Limit failure.} If $\lambda$ is a nonzero limit, the
coherent earlier prefixes have an injective set union $p$ of length
$\lambda$. The cut is exactly the lower or upper edge of its cylinder:
\[
 L=C_p^-\quad\text{or}\quad L=C_p^-\cup C_p,
 \qquad C_p^-:=\{q:\forall c\in C_p\ (q<c)\}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Minimize below any ordinal witnessing failure; this uses no ordering of
classes. The empty prefix straddles. At a successor, every nonempty
child cylinder is wholly on one side, and the children partition the
parent cylinder, which straddles. Both parts of the label split are
therefore nonempty, and their order follows from that of the children.
The outside-code assertion follows by comparison with a lower and an
upper witness in the parent.

At a limit, Class Replacement applied to the unique prefixes indexed
by the set $\lambda$ makes their union a set. Coherence ensures
injectivity, and completion ensures a nonempty cylinder. Since the
length fails, that cylinder is wholly on one side. Any code outside it
first differs from $p$ at $\delta<\lambda$; the shorter prefix of
length $\delta+1$ still straddles. Its witnesses force the code to the
lower side if it differs downward and to the upper side if upward.
Including or excluding the entire limit cylinder gives exactly its
two edges.
\end{proof}

A successor failure need not be a numerical gap with both sides lacking
endpoints. It can be an edge of a whole child cylinder, or a cut for which
the numerically suitable next label has already been used. The theorem
distinguishes these from a failure of coherence at a limit length.

\subsubsection{Explicit cuts and their meaning}

The following table gives concrete, fully defined examples.

\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.49\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.12\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.32\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Lower side & First failure & Interpretation\\
\midrule\endhead
$\{q:E_q(0)\le0\}$ & $1$ & Upper edge of the entire zero-first
cylinder.\\[5pt]
$\{q:E_q(0)<0\}\cup\{q:E_q(0)=0,\ E_q(1)<0\}$ & $2$ & The apparent
second separator would repeat the already used zero.\\[5pt]
$C_p^-$ or $C_p^-\cup C_p$, with $p(n)=n$ for $n<\omega$ & $\omega$ &
Every finite prefix straddles, but the whole countable-prefix cylinder
lies on one side.\\[5pt]
$L_F$ for $F:\Ord\overset{\sim}{\to}\No\setminus\{r\}$ & None &
A genuine injective branch, failing only the exhaustion test.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

All displayed lower sides have no greatest member. For a nonzero limit
prefix length $\lambda$, its lower cylinder edge has lower cofinality
exactly $\cf(\lambda)$ and no set coinitial family on its upper side.
To see this, make a fresh downward deviation at cofinally many positions
of $p$. The completions increase cofinally below $C_p$; any cofinal
family must have unbounded deviation coordinates. On the upper side,
the initial portion $C_p$ has no set coinitial family, since one can
choose a fresh next value below any set of next values. The upper
edge has the dual characters.

\begin{corollary}[Exactly what raw tails add]\label{swo:ds:cor:rawcutimage}
For a raw order $R\in \Hall$, its strict lower cut in $\Pbd(b)$ is
$L_{F_R}$. Thus the cut image of all raw orders consists exactly of
the cuts passing the straddling test. Over the cut of $F$, the fiber
is the convex order $\WO(\No\setminus\ran F)$.
Neither successor nor limit first-failure cuts are filled by any raw
class well-order.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A bounded-support enumeration unequal to $F_R$ first disagrees at a
set ordinal, before any non-set-like tail begins. Its comparison with
$R$ is therefore its comparison with $F_R$. Equality is possible
only when $F_R$ is exhaustive, in which case it determines $R$.
Conversely every injection occurs as a first core, by
\eqref{swo:ds:eq:fiber}. Distinct cores give different cuts by
\Cref{swo:ds:thm:cutrecognition}, proving exactly the asserted image
and fibers.
\end{proof}

This resolves the earlier report's represented-cut question using the
prefix tree with its numerical labels. It does not claim that the tree
is recoverable from the bare order on $\Pbd(b)$. Since $\Pbd(b)\cong\No$,
forgetting those additional predicates can lose precisely the information
used by the recognition test.

\begin{note}[\merge; on source~16's last paragraph]\label{swo:viii:note:ds-resolves}
Source~16's sentence that this ``resolves the earlier report's
represented-cut question'' is true of the theorem, which all six batch-81
sources prove (\cref{swo:viii:note:sixfold}). Its \cref{swo:ds:cor:rawcutimage}
is the statement about raw orders that sources~13, 15, 17 and~18 make in
\cref{swo:fs:cor:rawtraces}, \cref{swo:cb:cor:kernel},
\cref{swo:gs:prop:raw-lifts} and \cref{swo:sh:cor:cut-representation-levels};
the fibre description in it is source~12's \cref{swo:cf:fibers}, and the
image of all raw orders, exactly the cuts passing the straddling test, is the
new part. Part~IX prints source~14's trace-fibre theorem
(\cref{swo:tc:thm:tracefibers}).
\end{note}

\subsection{Source 15: a prefix criterion for all represented core cuts}\label{swo:cb:sec:cuts}
\merge\ Source~15's Section~7, from its Subsection~7.2 (Subsection~7.1, the
class of codes, is printed in \cref{swo:viii:sub:cb-core}; Subsection~7.5,
the automorphism theorem, in \cref{swo:viii:sec:automorphisms}).

% ---- source 15 (batch-81 manuscript 03), lines 938-1147
\subsubsection{The persistent-cylinder theorem}

A normalized class cut of $\Pbd(b)$ is a nonempty proper initial subclass
$L$ with no greatest member; write $R=\Pbd(b)\setminus L$. The upper side
may have a least element. A cylinder \emph{crosses} the cut if it meets
both sides. For an injective class word $F:\Ord\to\No$, put
\[
 L_F=\{d\in \Pbd(b):E_d<_{\lex}F\}.
\]
The comparison is defined at the first ordinal difference, unless the
functions agree, in which case the strict inequality is false.

\begin{theorem}[Exact criterion for representation]\label{swo:cb:thm:cutcriterion}
\textit{Extension proved in source~15.}\ In GBC, for a normalized class cut $L$ the following are
equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $L=L_F$ for an injective class word $F:\Ord\to\No$;
\item for every ordinal $\alpha$, some cylinder $C_p$ with
      $\dom(p)=\alpha$ crosses the cut.
\end{enumerate}
The representing word is unique. Its restrictions are exactly the unique
crossing prefixes. Its construction uses elementary comprehension, not ETR.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At most one cylinder at a given level crosses. If $C_p<C_q$ both crossed,
a point of $R$ in $C_p$ would precede a point of $L$ in $C_q$,
contradicting initiality. A restriction of a crossing prefix also
crosses. Thus the unique prefixes $p_\alpha$ in (2) are coherent.

Define $F(\alpha)=x$ when the crossing prefix of length $\alpha+1$
has last value $x$. This is an elementary formula: prefixes and codes
are sets, and crossing is expressed by two existential set quantifiers
with the cut and evaluation as class parameters. Coherence shows that
$F\res\alpha=p_\alpha$; injectivity holds on every such restriction
and hence globally.

If $E_d\ne F$, let $\delta$ be the first difference. The cylinder
$C_{p_{\delta+1}}$ crosses the cut. If $E_d(\delta)<F(\delta)$,
the whole cylinder is above $d$, and its lower-side member forces
$d\in L$. If $E_d(\delta)>F(\delta)$, its upper-side member lies
below $d$, forcing $d\in R$. If $E_d=F$, the code $d$ cannot lie
in $L$, since it would then be its greatest member. This proves (1).

Conversely, at every $\alpha$ choose fresh labels
$a<F(\alpha)<c$, neither in $\ran(F\res\alpha)$. Completions of
$(F\res\alpha)\concat a$ and $(F\res\alpha)\concat c$ lie on
opposite sides of $F$. Thus $C_{F\res\alpha}$ crosses. These same
perturbations show that $L_F$ is nonempty, proper, and has no greatest
member. Uniqueness follows from recovery of every prefix.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The normalization is necessary]\label{swo:cb:n7.3}
Without the no-greatest condition, persistence determines a unique $F$
but allows either side of a principal point:
\[
 L_F\subseteq L\subseteq L_F\cup\{d:E_d=F\}.
\]
Only a word already represented by a core code permits the two choices.
Both $\{d:E_d<F\}$ and $\{d:E_d\leq F\}$ cross every level, but
the second has a greatest member. Terminal cuts below have neither endpoint.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Exhaustiveness and the kernel of the raw cut map]\label{swo:cb:cor:kernel}
A persistent cut is represented by a set-like global well-order exactly when
\[
 \forall x\in\No\ \exists\alpha\quad x\in\ran(p_\alpha).
\]
Every persistent cut is represented by an arbitrary raw class well-order.
Two raw orders determine the same strict lower cut on $\Pbd(b)$ exactly when
their initial words $F_R$ agree. The common fibre is precisely
$\WO(\No\setminus\ran(F_R))$, interpreted at the appropriate size level.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The displayed condition says exactly that the recovered word is onto.
Every injective word has a raw completion by source~15's Proposition~4.2
(prefix convexity and initial-word fibres; \merge\ \cref{swo:cb:prop:fibres}; it is
\cref{swo:cf:fibers}).
A raw order and its initial word compare with a core evaluation at the
same first ordinal disagreement. If a core evaluation equals that word,
its exhaustiveness forces the raw order to have no residual tail.
Thus its lower cut is $L_{F_R}$. Apply uniqueness in the theorem and the
fibre description of the same proposition.
\end{proof}

This answers the prior report's represented-cut question by a necessary
and sufficient condition on all set-length prefix levels. Missing labels
are not a failure of persistence. They distinguish the exhaustive words
inside the persistent branches. Any ordering information after the first
proper block is invisible to comparisons with the bounded-support core.

\subsubsection{An exhaustive description of first failure}

\begin{theorem}[Terminal-cut classification]\label{swo:cb:thm:terminal}
\textit{Extension proved in source~15.}\ If a normalized class cut fails the criterion, let
$\theta>0$ be the least length without a crossing cylinder.
Exactly one of the following descriptions applies.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Successor failure.} If $\theta=\alpha+1$, there is a unique
crossing prefix $p:\alpha\to\No$ and a nonempty initial/final partition
\[
 A+B=\No\setminus\ran(p),\qquad A<B,
\]
such that each child $C_{p\concat x}$ lies wholly in $L$ for $x\in A$
and wholly in $R$ for $x\in B$. The four mutually exclusive forms are:
an upper boundary of a child cylinder when $A$ has a greatest element;
a lower boundary when $B$ has a least element;
a unique forbidden repeated label separating $A$ and $B$ when neither
endpoint exists but a surreal separator exists;
or a numerical class gap with no surreal separator.
\item \textbf{Limit failure.} If $\theta$ is limit, the coherent union
$p=\bigcup_{\alpha<\theta}p_\alpha$ is an injective set word. The cut
is exactly the lower or upper boundary of its nonempty cylinder:
\[
 L=\{d:E_d\res\theta<p\}
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 L=\{d:E_d\res\theta\leq p\}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The empty cylinder crosses, so $\theta\ne0$. At a successor, child
cylinders partition the crossing parent and none crosses. Each is
nonempty, giving the asserted partition of allowed labels. Both parts
are nonempty because the parent crosses. Their order follows from the
order of the cylinders and initiality of $L$. All codes below the
parent lie in $L$, and all those above it lie in $R$.

The numerical residual alphabet is dense by the fresh-separator lemma
(source~15's Lemma~3.1, \cref{swo:cb:lem:fresh}; \cref{swo:lem:delete}),
so $A$ cannot have a greatest element while $B$ has a least one.
If neither endpoint exists and $s$ strictly separates them, $s$ cannot
be an allowed label: membership in $A$ or $B$ would contradict strict
separation. Hence $s\in\ran(p)$. Two different separators would enclose
a fresh allowed label, which is impossible. This proves all four subcases.

At a limit, replacement over the set ordinal $\theta$ collects the
coherent prefixes, and their union is an injective set word. Its
cylinder is nonempty by prefix completion but does not cross. A code
outside it differs from $p$ at a coordinate $\delta<\theta$; the
crossing cylinder of length $\delta+1$ then fixes its side. The only
remaining choice is which side contains all of $C_p$, giving precisely
the two formulas. There is no incoherent-branch case: uniqueness at the
earlier levels already ruled it out.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[A cut not filled even by arbitrary class well-orders]\label{swo:cb:ex:firstlabelcut}
The initial class $L=\{d:E_d(0)<0\}$ has no greatest member. Its
empty cylinder crosses, but each length-one cylinder lies on one side.
It is the lower boundary of $C_{(0)}$. Therefore no injective
$\Ord$-word and no raw class well-order represents this cut.
The upper boundary $\{d:E_d(0)\leq0\}$ is likewise unrepresented.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Repeated label, numerical gap, and limit boundary]\label{swo:cb:n7.7}
The cut defined by
\[
 E_d(0)<0\quad\text{or}\quad(E_d(0)=0\ \land\ E_d(1)<0)
\]
first fails at length two: the putative continuation of $(0)$ would
repeat $0$. For a numerical-gap example, use
$A=\{x:\exists n\in\omega\ x<n\}$ and its complementary final class
of positive infinite surreals, and put $d\in L$ when $E_d(0)\in A$.
No surreal strictly separates these label classes; neither relevant
endpoint exists. Finally, if $p(n)=n$ for $n<\omega$, the lower and
upper boundaries of $C_p$ first fail at length $\omega$ even though
every finite prefix still crosses.
\end{example}

For a persistent but nonexhaustive example, take $F(\alpha)=\alpha$.
Every prefix level crosses, but the range omits the negative surreals.
Appending a well-order of the omitted range gives many raw completions
with exactly the same lower core cut. If $F$ instead omits just one
label, it has one raw completion of type $\Ord+1$. These are sharply
different from the terminal cuts in \Cref{swo:cb:ex:firstlabelcut}.

\subsubsection{Local characters of terminal cuts}

Here a ``set cofinal family'' is an actual set of codes cofinal in an
ordinary class side of a cut. We say explicitly when none exists;
$\Ord$ is not being used as a set cardinal.

\begin{proposition}[Cofinality read from first failure]\label{swo:cb:prop:cutcharacters}
At a first limit failure $\theta$, the lower-boundary case has
$\cf(L)=\cf(\theta)$, while $R$ has no set coinitial family.
The upper-boundary case has the dual properties.
At a successor failure with label partition $A+B$, if $A$ has no
greatest label, $L$ has exactly the same least set cofinality as $A$,
or no set cofinality if $A$ has none. If $A$ has a greatest label,
$L$ has no set cofinal family. The dual statements hold for $B$ and $R$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
At a limit, choose cofinally many coordinates $\beta<\theta$ and
complete prefixes agreeing with $p$ before $\beta$ but smaller at
$\beta$. These form an increasing cofinal family on the lower side.
Any cofinal family must have first-divergence coordinates unbounded
in $\theta$, since a later lower perturbation dominates every family
with bounded divergence coordinates. This proves equality. The upper
side begins with the whole cylinder $C_p$, which has no set coinitial
family; all remaining upper-side points are above it.

At a successor with no greatest label in $A$, a cofinal set of labels
can be lifted to completions, and conversely the next labels of any
cofinal family eventually inside the parent cylinder must be cofinal
in $A$. If $A$ has a greatest label, its final child cylinder has no
set cofinal family and is final on the lower side. The dual argument
proves the remaining assertions.
\end{proof}

No gap of $\Pbd(b)$ can have both a set cofinal lower side and a set coinitial
upper side: the core's set-cut filling theorem would put a point between
such two sets. The character calculation is compatible with this
restriction, while identifying many genuinely different class cuts.

% ---- source 15 (batch-81 manuscript 03), lines 1190-1208
\subsubsection{What a completion would have to mean}

The normalized class cuts of $\Pbd(b)$, ordered by inclusion, give the natural
Dedekind-cut interpretation at the next size level. For a uniform family
of such cuts whose union is nonempty and proper, the union is again a
normalized class cut: its defining membership formula quantifies over
set indices. This is a precise available-family completeness statement,
not a same-level class containing all its subclasses.

The map from raw orders to these cuts collapses exactly the residual
fibres of \Cref{swo:cb:cor:kernel}. Therefore adjoining all raw orders
is neither a faithful Dedekind completion of the core nor a realization
of every core cut. It both retains multiplicity over persistent cuts
and omits all terminal cuts. Any order embedding into a dense completion
that fixes the core would have to identify distinct raw orders lying in
one fibre, which is impossible. Arbitrary embeddings that move the core
are a different question.

% ---- source 13 (batch-81 manuscript 01), lines 808-1102
\subsection{Source 13: exact reconstruction of cuts from prefix cylinders}\label{swo:fs:sec:cuts}

We now address the earlier report's question asking for a necessary
and sufficient cylinder criterion for represented cuts
(\cref{swo:n16.1}). The criterion is relative
to the chosen core and prefix system; \Cref{swo:fs:sec:automorphisms}
will show why it is not a statement about the pure linear order alone.

\subsubsection{Normalization and crossing}

\begin{definition}\label{swo:fs:def:cut}
A \emph{normalized proper cut} of $\Psupp(b)$ is a pair of ordinary classes
$(L,U)$ such that $L\sqcup U=\Psupp(b)$, both sides are nonempty, every
member of $L$ precedes every member of $U$, and $L$ has no greatest
member. The upper side may have a least member.

An injective set prefix $p$ \emph{crosses} this cut when
\[
                         \Psupp(b)_p\cap L\ne\varnothing,
             \qquad      \Psupp(b)_p\cap U\ne\varnothing.
\]
\end{definition}

The normalization is essential. Immediately below and immediately above
a code $d$, two different cuts would otherwise reconstruct the same
branch $E_d$. We choose the lower trace convention, so the cut at $d$
puts $d$ in the upper side.

\begin{lemma}[Uniqueness and coherence of crossing prefixes]\label{swo:fs:lem:crossing}
At a fixed ordinal length there is at most one crossing prefix.
Restrictions of a crossing prefix cross the same cut. Consequently
crossing prefixes of different lengths are coherent.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Distinct same-length prefixes first differ at a coordinate, placing
one entire cylinder below the other. If both cylinders crossed, an
upper-side point in the first would precede a lower-side point in the
second, impossible. Restriction enlarges a cylinder, so preserves
crossing. Apply same-length uniqueness to the restriction of a longer
crossing prefix.
\end{proof}

For $F\in \Jinj$, its lower trace is the class
\[
                       \operatorname{tr}(F)=\{d\in \Psupp(b):E_d<F\}.
\]
All comparisons use a least set-ordinal disagreement, except equality,
which simply excludes a code from the lower trace.

\begin{theorem}[Exact branch representation]\label{swo:fs:thm:reconstruction}
In $\GBC$, a normalized proper cut $(L,U)$ of $\Psupp(b)$ is the lower trace
of a unique $F\in \Jinj$ if and only if
\[\tag{S13.1}\label{swo:fs:eq:crossall}
 \text{for every ordinal }\alpha\text{ there exists a crossing prefix
 of length }\alpha.
\]
The represented word is exhaustive, hence belongs to $\Hsl$, if and
only if it also satisfies
\[\tag{S13.2}\label{swo:fs:eq:coverage}
 \text{for every }x\in\No\text{ some crossing prefix has }x
 \text{ in its range}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose first that $L=\operatorname{tr}(F)$. For each ordinal $\alpha$, the prefix
$F\restr\alpha$ has code completions below and above $F$, by choosing
a fresh next value on the desired side. Thus it crosses. It is the
unique crossing prefix of that length. Equation~\eqref{swo:fs:eq:coverage}
is then precisely surjectivity of $F$.

Conversely, let $p_\alpha$ be the unique crossing prefix of length
$\alpha$. Coherence gives $p_\alpha=p_\beta\restr\alpha$ whenever
$\alpha<\beta$. Define
\[
                            F(\alpha)=p_{\alpha+1}(\alpha).
\]
This is an elementary class definition quantifying over the set code
$p_{\alpha+1}$. It does not ask for a class-valued choice or a
class-valued recursive sequence of prefixes. Every two coordinates
belong to one longer injective prefix, so $F$ is injective.

We check the trace equality. If $E_d<F$, let $\xi$ be the first
disagreement and choose a crossing prefix of length greater than
$\xi$. Every code in its cylinder is above $d$. One of those codes is
in $L$, so downward closure gives $d\in L$. If $E_d>F$, the symmetric
argument with an upper-side code gives $d\in U$.

The only possible remaining case is $E_d=F$. Every other lower-side
code has smaller evaluation, by the two arguments just given. If $d$
were in $L$, it would therefore be its greatest member, contradicting
normalization. Thus $L=\operatorname{tr}(F)$. Distinct words have a code strictly
between them by \Cref{swo:fs:cor:core}, so their traces are
distinct. Finally, the union of the prefix ranges is exactly $\ran(F)$,
which proves the exhaustion criterion.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{What raw well-orders add, and what they cannot add}

\begin{corollary}[Trace image and fibers of raw orders]\label{swo:fs:cor:rawtraces}
For $R\in\Hall$, define $L_R=\{d\in \Psupp(b):E_d<R\}$. The normalized
proper cuts represented in this way are exactly those satisfying
\eqref{swo:fs:eq:crossall}. For such a cut the unique reconstructed word
is $F_R$. Its raw realization fiber is precisely the order of all
well-orders of $\No\setminus\ran(F_R)$. The fiber contains a set-like
realization exactly when the coverage condition holds, and then it is
a singleton.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Every comparison with a code is decided inside the ordinal head unless
the code equals the entire raw order; equality can occur only when the
head is exhaustive. Hence $L_R=\operatorname{tr}(F_R)$. Conversely, append a
well-order of the omitted range to the branch reconstructed by
\Cref{swo:fs:thm:reconstruction}. Source~13's Proposition~6.2 (``Canonical
head; prior structural lemma'', \merge\ \cref{swo:fs:prop:head}; it is
\cref{swo:cf:core,swo:cf:fibers})
gives every realization and proves the fiber statement.
\end{proof}

If the omitted range has $n$ elements, there are exactly $n!$ raw
realizations. A single omitted label gives one additional point of type
$\Ord+1$; two omitted labels give two adjacent realizations of type
$\Ord+2$. These examples were already constructed in the earlier
report. The new criterion determines the complete trace image: adding
arbitrary non-set-like tails still does not fill a cut that fails the
all-level crossing test.

\begin{example}[A branch that fails only exhaustion]\label{swo:fs:n8.5}
Let $F(\alpha)=\alpha$, viewed as the all-plus surreal of length
$\alpha$. Its lower trace crosses every prefix length, but its prefixes
never contain $-1$. It has raw realizations obtained by well-ordering
the nonordinal surreals after its head, and no realization in $\Hsl$.
This recovers the earlier omitted-range example through the exact
criterion rather than through a single selected gap.
\end{example}

\subsection{Source 13: a complete first-failure classification}\label{swo:fs:sec:failure}

The representation theorem reduces the problem to a question about
crossing prefixes. The next theorem describes every way the test can
fail. In particular, failure at a limit is not an unexplained
compactness assumption: it has an exact geometric form.

\begin{theorem}[Branch, horizontal cut, or limit boundary]\label{swo:fs:thm:failure}
Let $(L,U)$ be a normalized proper cut of $\Psupp(b)$. Exactly one of the
following descriptions applies.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item There is a crossing prefix at every ordinal length. The cut is
the trace of a unique injective class word.
\item There is a least failed length $\lambda=\beta+1$. Let $p$ be
the crossing prefix of length $\beta$. There is a nonempty cut
$A<B$ partitioning $Y=\No\setminus\ran(p)$ such that, within $\Psupp(b)_p$,
\[
 L\cap \Psupp(b)_p=\bigcup_{x\in A}\Psupp(b)_{p\cat x},\qquad
 U\cap \Psupp(b)_p=\bigcup_{x\in B}\Psupp(b)_{p\cat x}.
\]
Thus the cut separates whole next-letter cylinders. We call it
\emph{horizontal at $p$}.
\item There is a least failed length $\lambda$ that is a nonzero
limit. The union $p$ of the shorter crossing prefixes has length
$\lambda$, and the cut is exactly the lower or upper boundary of
$\Psupp(b)_p$.
\end{enumerate}
All descriptions are expressible with ordinary class parameters in
$\GBC$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The empty prefix crosses every proper cut. If some length fails, the
class of failed ordinals has a least member $\lambda>0$.

For $\lambda=\beta+1$, uniqueness gives the crossing $p$ of length
$\beta$. Every child cylinder is nonempty by prefix completion, but
none crosses the cut. Each is therefore entirely on one side. Put
$x\in A$ or $x\in B$ according to that side. These are ordinary
classes: the predicate ``every code in this child is in $L$'' quantifies
only over set codes. Their union is $Y$, they are disjoint, and the
label order of the children shows $A<B$. Both sides are nonempty
because the parent crosses. Every code outside the parent lies below
all of it or above all of it, so its placement in the cut is forced.

For limit $\lambda$, coherence gives an injective set word
$p=\bigcup_{\alpha<\lambda}p_\alpha$. Its cylinder is nonempty but
cannot cross. If a code does not extend $p$, it first disagrees at
some $\xi<\lambda$. A shorter crossing prefix of length greater than
$\xi$ forces its side: a lower disagreement puts it in $L$, and an
upper disagreement puts it in $U$. Thus every code below $\Psupp(b)_p$ is
in $L$, and every code above it is in $U$. The entire $\Psupp(b)_p$ lies on
one side, giving precisely one of its two boundaries.

If there is no failed set ordinal, \Cref{swo:fs:thm:reconstruction}
applies. The three cases are disjoint by their first failed length.
\end{proof}

There is no fourth case called ``failure at $\Ord$''. An injective
branch that omits labels still crosses every set level; its failure
is exhaustion, not prefix existence. Treating $\Ord$ as one more set
stage would conflate the two tests.

\subsubsection{One-sided characters of the three cases}

For a class order, say that a side has character $\Ord$ when it has
no set-sized cofinal (respectively coinitial) family but does have a
uniform increasing (respectively decreasing) $\Ord$-indexed family.
This is a notation for a pair of properties, not a set cardinal.
When a set-sized family suffices, use the usual least cofinal cardinal;
an endpoint has character $1$.

Every ordinary class order without a set-cofinal subset has an
$\Ord$-indexed increasing cofinal sequence in $\GBC$: enumerate its
points by the global well-order and at each stage choose a point above
both the earlier set of choices and the next enumerated point. Absence
of a set-cofinal subset guarantees this choice. The dual construction
handles coinitiality.

\begin{proposition}[Characters at first failure]\label{swo:fs:prop:characters}
The cut descriptions have the following character consequences.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item A branch trace has character $(\Ord,\Ord)$ when its word is
not a code evaluation. If $F=E_d$, its normalized trace has character
$(\Ord,1)$; the punctured upper side again has character $\Ord$.
\item A lower boundary of a limit-length cylinder $\Psupp(b)_p$, of length
$\lambda$, has character $(\cf\lambda,\Ord)$. Its upper boundary
has character $(\Ord,\cf\lambda)$.
\item For a horizontal cut associated with $A<B$, the lower
character is $\cf(A)$ if $A$ has no greatest label, and is $\Ord$
if $A$ has a greatest label. The upper character is $\ci(B)$ if
$B$ has no least label, and is $\Ord$ if it has a least label.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The branch statement is \Cref{swo:fs:lem:approximants}, with the
possible equal code placed in the upper side.

At a lower limit boundary, choose prefixes agreeing with $p$ up to
$\xi$ and then taking a fresh lower letter. Completions at lengths
$\xi$ cofinal in $\lambda$ are cofinal below the whole cylinder.
Conversely, fewer than $\cf\lambda$ many codes below it have their
first-disagreement coordinates bounded below $\lambda$, so a later
such completion lies above them all. The right side has $\Psupp(b)_p$ as a
coinitial subclass, and that cylinder has no set-coinitial family by
\Cref{swo:fs:cor:core}. The upper-boundary proof is dual.

For a horizontal cut whose lower label side has no greatest member,
choose one code in each child along a cofinal family of labels. This
family is cofinal among all lower codes. Conversely, projecting a
cofinal family of lower codes in the parent onto its next labels is
cofinal in $A$. Codes below the parent cannot improve this bound. If
$A$ has a greatest label $a$, the whole terminal child $\Psupp(b)_{p\cat a}$
is cofinal on the lower side. Its character is $\Ord$, not $1$.
The upper assertion is the reversed argument.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Equal characters do not imply representability}

\begin{example}[A horizontal $(\Ord,\Ord)$ cut]\label{swo:fs:ex:horizontalgap}
Let $s:\Ord\to\{-,+\}$ be the proper-class sign string whose sign is
$+$ when the finite remainder of its ordinal index is even and $-$
when it is odd. Both signs occur cofinally. This is \emph{not} a
surreal number.

Compare each set-length surreal sign sequence with $s$ at its first
difference, regarding its termination as $0$. Every surreal differs
from $s$ by the time of its termination. Define
\[
       A=\{x\in\No:x<s\},\qquad B=\{x\in\No:s<x\}.
\]
These are nonempty classes partitioning the label order. Neither
side has an endpoint or a set-sized cofinal or coinitial family.
Indeed, the birthdays of any proposed set family are bounded by some
$\gamma$. Truncating $s$ at a later $+$ position gives a larger lower
label than all lower members of the family; truncating at a later
$-$ position gives a smaller upper label. The corresponding ordinal
sequences of truncations supply cofinal and coinitial class families.

Now partition the core by its first label:
\[
           L=\{d:E_d(0)\in A\},\qquad U=\{d:E_d(0)\in B\}.
\]
This cut has character $(\Ord,\Ord)$ but no crossing prefix of
length $1$. It is horizontal at the root, and is not the trace of
any injective class word or of any raw class well-order.
\end{example}

Thus neither saturation below set size nor the ordered pair of local
characters identifies the represented cuts. The labeled prefix
criterion contains strictly more information.

\subsubsection{An explicit limit-boundary example}

Let $p(n)=n$ for $n<\omega$. The cut just below $\Psupp(b)_p$ is crossed by
every finite initial prefix of $p$, but not by any prefix of length
$\omega$. At each finite level, some lower code leaves the ordinal
prefix later, while an upper code extends all of $p$. The cut has
character $(\omega,\Ord)$ and is not represented by a raw global
well-order. Its obstruction is a set-length limit boundary rather than
an omitted proper-class range. This is the distinction that an informal
``keep taking longer prefixes'' argument would overlook.

% ---- source 17 (batch-81 manuscript 05), lines 1144-1313
\subsection{Source 17: recognizing exactly which core cuts are global enumerations}
\label{swo:gs:sec:recognition}

The preceding source results place $\Hsl$ in a larger collection of cuts
of $\Psupp(b)$, but do not by themselves identify its image. We now give a
necessary-and-sufficient test in terms of the displayed prefix cylinders.
This addresses source question \code{swo:n16.1} (\cref{swo:n16.1}) and its parallel in
source 09 (its third direction in \cref{swo:ec:sec:research}). It is a \emph{labelled-tree} recognition theorem; a pure-order
recognition theorem would be stronger and, as shown below, cannot hold in
the naive invariant form.

\subsubsection{The straddling test}
For an injective set prefix $p:\alpha\to\No$, define the ordinary class
\[
 C_p=\{c\in \Psupp(b):E_c\res\alpha=p\}.
\]
Let $L$ be a proper nonempty lower subclass of $\Psupp(b)$ with no greatest
element, and put $U=\Psupp(b)\setminus L$. We allow $U$ to have a least
element. Thus the convention is the \emph{open lower cut}, including the
one immediately before an actual core point. Say that $p$ straddles $L$
when $C_p$ meets both $L$ and $U$.

\begin{theorem}[Recognition of injective branches]\label{swo:gs:thm:recognition}
The following conditions are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item There is an injective class word $f:\Ord\to\No$ such that
\[
 L=L_f:=\{c\in \Psupp(b):E_c<_{\lex} f\}.
\]
\item For every set ordinal $\alpha$, there is a straddling injective
prefix of length $\alpha$.
\end{enumerate}
When these conditions hold, both the straddling prefix at each length
and the word $f$ are unique. Moreover $f$ is surjective if and only if
\[\tag{S17.8}\label{swo:gs:eq:coverage}
 \forall x\in\No\ \exists p\,
 \bigl(p\text{ straddles }L\ \wedge\ x\in\ran p\bigr).
\]
The reconstruction uses elementary class comprehension over $\GBC$,
not $\ETR$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Distinct cylinders of the same length are disjoint convex blocks in
lexicographic order. At most one can meet both sides of a cut: if an
earlier block met $U$, every later block would be in $U$.

Suppose first that $f$ is given. For any $\alpha$, take its prefix
$p=f\res\alpha$. A fresh smaller next label than $f(\alpha)$, and a
fresh larger one, yield core completions respectively below and above
$f$. Thus $p$ straddles. These completions also show that $L_f$ has no
greatest element and is proper and nonempty.

Conversely, let $p_\alpha$ denote the unique straddling prefix at length
$\alpha$. Restrictions of straddling prefixes straddle, so uniqueness
implies $p_\beta\res\alpha=p_\alpha$ for $\alpha<\beta$. Define a
class graph by
\[
 f(\alpha)=x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists p\bigl(p\text{ is a straddling prefix of length }\alpha+1
                  \ \wedge\ p(\alpha)=x\bigr).
\]
The quantifier over $p$ ranges over sets. Straddling itself quantifies over
the set codes in $\Psupp(b)$, with $L$ and $b$ as class parameters. Thus this
is elementary comprehension. Coherence makes $f$ a total function; its
set restrictions are injective, so it is injective.

If $E_c\ne f$, let $\delta$ be their first disagreement. The cylinder
of $p_{\delta+1}$ straddles. If $E_c(\delta)<f(\delta)$, then $c$ is
below every code in that cylinder, including a code in $L$, so $c\in L$.
The reversed inequality places $c$ in $U$. If $E_c=f$, putting $c$ in
$L$ would make it the greatest member of $L$, already excluded. Hence
$L=L_f$ exactly, including the principal-cut case. Two different words
would be separated by a core code, so the representing word is unique.
Finally $\ran f$ is the union of the ranges of its straddling prefixes;
this proves the coverage criterion.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why every ordinal length and the endpoint convention matter]\label{swo:gs:n9.2}
Checking only successor extensions along finite histories is inadequate.
A cut can track a coherent prefix through all finite levels and then lie
at the boundary of its length-$\omega$ cylinder. There is then no
straddling cylinder at that limit. In contrast,
\Cref{swo:gs:thm:recognition} requires a straddler at \emph{every} set
ordinal. Also, a closed principal lower cut would have the same
straddling prefixes as the corresponding open one. The hypothesis that
$L$ has no greatest element removes that ambiguity.
\end{remark}

\subsubsection{Three independent failures}
\begin{example}[A coordinate cut that does not follow a branch]\label{swo:gs:n9.3}
Let $A\subseteq\No$ consist of those $x$ with $x<n$ for some natural
number $n$, and let $B=\No\setminus A$. Both are nonempty, $A$ has no
largest element, and $B$ has no least element: a positive infinite member
of $B$ has a smaller positive infinite half. Partition core codes by
whether their first label lies in $A$ or $B$. The root cylinder straddles,
but no length-one cylinder does. This is a genuine cut of the core, but
not comparison with an injective $\Ord$-word.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[A limit boundary that defeats finite-depth testing]\label{swo:gs:n9.4}
Fix an injective prefix $p:\omega\to\No$. Take the cut immediately
before $C_p$. At every finite length $n$, the cylinder for
$p\res n$ meets both cut sides, because a fresh lower label at a later
finite coordinate gives a code strictly below $C_p$. At length
$\omega$, the entire cylinder lies on the upper side and no cylinder
straddles. This is precisely the limit obstruction in the set-sized cut
trichotomy, now at an ordinary class of set codes.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[A coherent branch which is not exhaustive]\label{swo:gs:n9.5}
Fix $r_0\in\No$ and a bijection $f:\Ord\to\No\setminus\{r_0\}$.
The cut $L_f$ passes the straddling test at every ordinal length, but fails
\eqref{swo:gs:eq:coverage} for $r_0$. It is not represented by any member of
$\Hsl$, since the representing injective word is unique.
\end{example}

These examples separate numerical-cut failure, limit coherence, and
exhaustiveness. The test is not merely the assertion that a representation
exists restated in different notation: its quantifiers over prefixes and
core witnesses are over \emph{sets}, and the representing proper-class
function is recovered by one elementary formula.

\begin{proposition}[Characters of branch cuts outside the core]
\label{swo:gs:prop:class-characters}
If $f\in \Jinj$ has no code in $\Psupp(b)$, both sides of its core cut have no
set-sized cofinal or coinitial subset, respectively. Both admit uniform
$\Ord$-indexed approximation families. This is often abbreviated by
saying that the cut has character $(\Ord,\Ord)$; that notation does not
make $\Ord$ into a cardinal or set.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For each $\alpha$, extend $f\res\alpha$ by a smaller or larger fresh
label and complete in the core, making the choices uniformly using global
choice. As $\alpha$ increases, these codes approach the cut from their
respective sides. For any set of codes below $f$, Class Replacement bounds
all their first disagreements with $f$ by a set ordinal. A later lower
approximation lies above them all. The upper argument is identical.
There is no equality case because $f$ has no core code.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{What the same cut remembers about unrestricted orders}
For $f\in \Jinj$, put $D_f=\No\setminus\ran f$. Append to the well-order
listed by $f$ any class well-order of $D_f$, choosing one using global
choice when necessary. The result is a raw class well-order of $\No$.
Every appended label has a proper class of predecessors; the initial
set-like part is exactly $f$.

\begin{proposition}[Raw lifts and loss of residual information]
\label{swo:gs:prop:raw-lifts}
All raw well-orders with canonical initial enumeration $f$ induce the
same comparison cut $L_f$ on $\Psupp(b)$. Their convex fibre is the
lexicographic order of all well-orders of $D_f$. Consequently the fibre
is a singleton when $|D_f|=0$ or $1$, and has $n!$ members when
$|D_f|=n<\omega$. For larger complements it retains the full residual
well-order problem.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Unless a core enumeration equals $f$, its comparison is decided at a set
ordinal before any appended label. Equality is possible only when $f$ is
exhaustive, in which case no tail remains. Restriction to $D_f$ and
concatenation with the fixed initial order are inverse order-preserving
operations. The source proves this convex-fibre description for all
raw orders (\cref{swo:cf:fibers}); the argument here identifies
its interaction with the reconstructed cut.
\end{proof}

Thus recognition of an injective branch determines the raw order's first
$\Ord$-part but not its residual order. The core is dense in $\Hsl$ and
$\Jinj$, not in the interiors of these nontrivial raw fibres.

% ---- source 18 (batch-81 manuscript 06), lines 2753-3058
\subsection{Source 18: exactly which class cuts of a core are represented}
\label{swo:sh:sec:represented-class-cuts}

Fix a baseline bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$ and let
$\Psupp(b)$ be its ordinary class of normalized bounded-support
permutation codes.  Write $E_c$ for the enumeration evaluated from a
code $c\in\Psupp(b)$.  All such evaluations are supplied by one
class relation.  For an injective set prefix $p:\delta\to\No$,
put
\[
 C_{p}=\{c\in\Psupp(b):E_c\restriction\delta=p\}.
\]
The core-completion lemma ensures that every such cylinder is
nonempty.  It is convex.  At a fixed length $\delta$, these cylinders
partition $\Psupp(b)$ and are linearly ordered without overlap.

Throughout this section, a cut is an ordinary class
$L\subseteq\Psupp(b)$ that is nonempty, proper, initial, and has
no greatest element.  This convention uses the strict lower side of
a represented point.  In particular, it excludes the closed principal
cut at a code.  Say that $p$ \emph{straddles} $L$ if
\[
 C_{p}\cap L\ne\varnothing,
 \qquad
 C_{p}\setminus L\ne\varnothing.
\]
This is an elementary predicate of the set $p$, with class parameters
$b,L$.  Its witnesses are set codes, not arbitrary classes.

\begin{theorem}[The prefix criterion for represented class cuts]
\label{swo:sh:thm:represented-class-cut}
In GB with the fixed baseline above, the following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item There is an injective class function
$f:\Ord\to\No$ such that
\[
 L=\{c\in\Psupp(b):E_c<_{\rm lex}f\}.
\]
\item For every ordinal $\delta$ there is an injective prefix
$p:\delta\to\No$ that straddles $L$.
\end{enumerate}
When they hold, $f$ is unique.  At every length $\delta$, the unique
straddling prefix is $f\restriction\delta$.  The function $f$ is
defined by an elementary formula from $b,L$; no class choice or ETR
is needed to assemble it.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At most one prefix of a given length can straddle.  Indeed, if the
cylinder of $p$ lies below that of $q$, an element outside $L$ in
the first cylinder lies below an element of $L$ in the second,
contradicting initiality.

Assume the second condition and denote the unique prefix at length
$\delta$ by $p_\delta$.  If $\gamma<\delta$, the restriction
$p_\delta\restriction\gamma$ also straddles, since its cylinder
contains the straddling cylinder of $p_\delta$.  Uniqueness gives
\[
 p_\delta\restriction\gamma=p_\gamma.
\]
Define
\[
 f(\alpha)=p_{\alpha+1}(\alpha).
\]
The graph is elementary because each $p_\delta$ is a uniquely
specified set.  Coherence proves that this is an injective class
function and that $f\restriction\delta=p_\delta$.

Take a core code $c$ with $E_c\ne f$, and let $\alpha$ be the first
coordinate of disagreement.  If $E_c(\alpha)<f(\alpha)$, then
$c$ lies below every code in $C_{p_{\alpha+1}}$.
That cylinder meets $L$, so $c\in L$ by initiality.  If
$E_c(\alpha)>f(\alpha)$, then $c$ lies above every code in the
same cylinder.  Its member outside $L$ shows that $c\notin L$.
Finally, if $E_c=f$ and $c\in L$, the absence of a greatest element
of $L$ supplies $d\in L$ with $E_d>f$, contradicting the previous
case.  Hence the displayed cut identity holds in every case.

Conversely, let $L$ be the strict lower cut of an injective class
word $f$.  For any ordinal $\delta$, its prefix
$p=f\restriction\delta$ is a set.  Choose fresh surreal labels
\[
 u<f(\delta)<v,
 \qquad u,v\notin\operatorname{ran}(p).
\]
Such labels exist because a set cannot exhaust either numerical
interval next to a given surreal.  Complete $p$ followed by $u$,
and $p$ followed by $v$, to core enumerations.  Both completions
belong to $C_{p}$, and they lie respectively below and
above $f$.  Thus every prefix straddles.  Its uniqueness at each
length also proves the uniqueness of $f$.
\end{proof}

For completeness, the strict lower cut of every injective class word
is indeed nonempty, proper, and without a greatest element.  The
first two assertions follow by choosing a smaller or larger first
label.  If $E_c<f$ first differs at $\alpha$, complete
$f\restriction(\alpha+1)$ with a fresh next label smaller than
$f(\alpha+1)$.  The resulting core row lies strictly between
$E_c$ and $f$.

\begin{remark}[Why the strict-cut convention matters]\label{swo:sh:n15.2}
If $f=E_c$ is itself a core row, both its strict lower cut and its
closed lower cut have a straddling cylinder at every length.  The
closed cut has greatest element $c$.  The no-greatest-element
hypothesis is therefore necessary for the stated strict-cut
criterion; it is not an incidental regularity assumption.
\end{remark}

\subsubsection{Set-like representation and all raw representations}

For a raw class well-order $R$ of $\No$, let
$F_R:\Ord\to\No$ be the unique enumeration of
its canonical initial set-like part.  It is injective, and the
remaining labels, if any, occur after its entire ordinal-class prefix.
The earlier common-prefix theorem shows that a core row and $R$
are compared at their first ordinal disagreement with $F_R$,
unless they are identical.

\begin{corollary}[Surjectivity is the exact remaining obstruction]
\label{swo:sh:cor:cut-representation-levels}
A cut $L$ is represented by a raw class well-order of
$\No$ if and only if it satisfies the prefix criterion
of \Cref{swo:sh:thm:represented-class-cut}.  Let $f$ be the unique
class word recovered from such a cut.  Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $L$ is represented by a set-like global well-order if and
only if $f$ is surjective onto $\No$.
\item All its raw representatives are exactly the well-orders
obtained by putting the sequence $f$ first and then well-ordering
$Y_f=\No\setminus\operatorname{ran}(f)$.
\item These representatives form the previously described convex
fiber isomorphic, in the typed uniform sense, to
$\WO(Y_f)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For any raw representative $R$, its cut on the core is the strict
lower cut of $F_R$.  \Cref{swo:sh:thm:represented-class-cut} therefore
applies and gives $f=F_R$.  Conversely, append the restriction of the
baseline well-order to $Y_f$ after $f$.  The range
of $f$ is proper, and its points have precisely set-many earlier
$f$-values; every appended point has the whole proper range before
it.  Thus the canonical initial function is exactly $f$, and the
resulting raw order has cut $L$.

A set-like representative has no residual labels, so its canonical
function is a bijection.  Conversely a bijective $f$ directly defines
a set-like representative.  Uniqueness of the recovered class word
excludes a different surjective word representing the same cut.
The last two statements are the canonical-fiber description.
\end{proof}

Thus allowing arbitrary raw well-orders fills the omitted-range
branch cuts, but it still does not fill every class cut of the core.
The first-failure theorem below identifies exactly where an
unsuccessful prefix criterion breaks down.

\begin{corollary}[Elementary recognition in uniform families]
\label{swo:sh:cor:elementary-cut-recognition}
Relative to the baseline, raw representability of a cut is an
elementary property of its class parameter.  Set-like representability
is also elementary: in addition to a straddling prefix at every length,
require
\[
 \forall x\in\No\ \exists\delta\in\Ord\ \exists p
 \bigl[p:\delta\to\No\text{ straddles }L
       \ \wedge\ x\in\operatorname{ran}(p)\bigr].
\]
Consequently a uniformly class-indexed family of cuts has an
elementary class of raw-represented indices, an elementary class of
set-like-represented indices, and a uniform relation recovering the
injective words of all raw-represented members.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
All displayed variables are sets.  The coverage condition is
equivalent to surjectivity of the uniquely recovered word.
Insert the family index into the same formulas and apply elementary
class comprehension.  The input cut remains a class parameter;
this does not provide set codes for all cuts or all class words.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{The first failure: a numerical split or a limit boundary}

\begin{theorem}[First-failure classification]
\label{swo:sh:thm:cut-first-failure}
Suppose $L$ fails the prefix criterion, and let $\delta$ be the
least length with no straddling prefix.  Then $\delta>0$ and
exactly one of the following descriptions applies.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Successor failure.} If $\delta=\eta+1$, let $p$ be
the unique straddling prefix of length $\eta$.  The unused alphabet
$Y=\No\setminus\operatorname{ran}(p)$ has a nontrivial
class cut $Y=A\sqcup B$, with $A<B$, such that
\[
 C_{p\mathbin{{}^\frown}\langle x\rangle}
 \subseteq
 \begin{cases}
 L,&x\in A,\\
 \Psupp(b)\setminus L,&x\in B.
 \end{cases}
\]
Outside $C_{p}$, the codes below that cylinder lie in
$L$ and those above it do not.
\item \textbf{Limit failure.} If $\delta$ is a limit ordinal,
the shorter unique straddling prefixes have a coherent union
$p:\delta\to\No$, which is an injective \emph{set}
prefix.  Its nonempty cylinder lies wholly in $L$ or wholly outside
$L$.  The cut is respectively the upper or lower boundary of
that cylinder: codes strictly below the cylinder belong to $L$,
and codes strictly above it do not.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The empty prefix straddles because $L$ and its complement are
nonempty, so $\delta>0$.  Unique shorter straddling prefixes are
coherent by the proof of \Cref{swo:sh:thm:represented-class-cut}.

In the successor case, every next-letter cylinder is nonempty
and fails to straddle, so it lies wholly on one side.  The two
sides of the parent cylinder supply a letter of each kind.
Initiality orders the resulting classes $A<B$.  The straddling
parent also forces every code below it into $L$ and every code
above it outside $L$.

In the limit case, Class Replacement on the set ordinal $\delta$
collects the uniquely defined shorter prefixes into a set, so their
union $p$ is a set.  Its cylinder is nonempty by core completion,
and does not straddle by the defining failure at $\delta$.
A code outside it first differs from $p$ at some $\alpha<\delta$.
The straddling cylinder at length $\alpha+1<\delta$ then decides
its side exactly as in the main proof.  All codes below the
length-$\delta$ cylinder lie in $L$, all those above it lie
outside, and the entire cylinder itself lies on one side.
\end{proof}

The successor split is a class cut in the \emph{unused} numerical
alphabet.  It can be principal at a remaining label, can occur at
a label deleted by the prefix, or can be an unfilled class cut of
the surreal numerical order.  Surreal set-cut interpolation does
not imply that an arbitrary class cut has a surreal boundary.
The limit case records the independent possibility of reaching an
entire set prefix while the cut lies at one of its cylinder's
boundaries.  Neither failure type is represented even by a raw
class well-order, by \Cref{swo:sh:cor:cut-representation-levels}.

\begin{example}[A deleted-label cut caused by repetition]
\label{swo:sh:ex:repeated-label-cut}
Fix $x\in\No$ and put
\[
 L_x=\{c\in\Psupp(b):
 E_c(0)<x\ \text{or}\
 (E_c(0)=x\ \text{and}\ E_c(1)<x)\}.
\]
This is a nonempty proper initial class without a greatest element.
The unique straddling prefix of length $1$ is $\langle x\rangle$.
There is no straddling prefix of length $2$: its first entry other
than $x$ already decides the side, and when its first entry is
$x$, its second entry must be different from $x$ by injectivity.
The first failure is therefore at length $2$, where the unused
alphabet is split at the deleted label $x$.

The cut is not represented by any injective ordinal-class word,
and hence by no raw class well-order of $\No$.  A would-be
word would have to begin with $x,x$.  This is an explicit omitted
class cut distinct from the omitted-range branch cuts: enlarging
the order from set-like to unrestricted raw well-orders does not
repair it.  If repeated labels are allowed in class words, however,
the constant word $x,x,x,\ldots$ represents this cut.  Every injective
core row differs from that word by coordinate $1$ at the latest.
\end{example}

\begin{remark}[Class character does not decide representability]\label{swo:sh:n15.7}
Both sides of $L_x$ have no set-sized cofinal or coinitial witness,
respectively, although they have uniform witnesses indexed by
$\Ord$. To see this, complete the prefixes
\[
 \left\langle x,x-\frac{1}{\alpha+1}\right\rangle,
 \qquad
 \left\langle x,x+\frac{1}{\alpha+1}\right\rangle
 \quad(\alpha\in\Ord)
\]
uniformly to core rows. Since ordinals are cofinal in the numerical
surreal order, the first family is cofinal in $L_x$ and the second
is coinitial in its complement. Any proposed set-sized witness can
be improved at its second coordinate by surreal set interpolation.
Thus this unrepresented cut has the same $(\Ord,\Ord)$
class character as omitted-range branch cuts that do have raw
representatives. This notation records the stated existence and
nonexistence of uniform witnesses; it does not assign a set cardinal
to a proper class.
\end{remark}

\subsubsection{Foundational accounting}

All cylinders, cuts, and recovered graphs in this section are
ordinary classes of sets.  Prefixes are set functions; core rows
are accessed through set codes.  Uniqueness assembles coherent
prefixes without a class-choice principle.  Replacement is used
only on set-sized domains, including the union at a limit failure.
The argument never constructs a class containing all class words,
never invokes a truth predicate for arbitrary formulas, and never
uses ETR.  The fixed baseline already supplies the choice strength
needed for the previously proved completion and extension lemmas.

\merge\ Four sources show that the bare order of the core, or of the full
order of global enumerations, does not remember what the recognition theorem
uses. Source~14 classifies the automorphism orbits of class cuts by their
characters (complete invariant) and derives that exhaustiveness is not
invariant; source~17 gives an exact criterion for an automorphism of the
core to extend to the global enumerations, the non-extension theorem and the
positive family of numerical relabellings; source~15 gives a weaker form of
