% ---- source 14 (batch-81 manuscript 02), lines 961-1062
\subsection{Source 14: automorphism orbits and the limits of bare-order recognition}
\label{swo:tc:sec:orbits}
The prefix classification has a complementary classification in the
language of order alone. It is coarser: different prefix-boundary types
can belong to the same orbit under class order automorphisms.

\begin{lemma}[Set homogeneity of the core]\label{swo:tc:lem:sethomogeneous}
Every increasing bijection between two set-sized suborders of $\Psupp(b)$
extends to a class order automorphism of $\Psupp(b)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Begin with the given partial map and carry out the back-and-forth
construction used in \Cref{swo:tc:cor:coreNo}. At any set stage its
domain and range are sets, even though they may already contain the
entire initial partial map. The lower and upper images of a new point
form a set cut. A strict separator automatically avoids all previously
used image points, since each of those is on one of the two sides.
The inverse step is symmetric. Taking the coherent union gives a
surjective class order embedding extending the original map.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Complete character invariant for cut orbits]
\label{swo:tc:thm:orbits}
Two proper normalized class cuts of $\Psupp(b)$ lie in the same orbit
under class order automorphisms if and only if they have the same
character pair. The possible pairs are exactly
\[
 (\rho,\Ord),\quad (\Ord,\rho),\quad
 (\Ord,1),\quad (\Ord,\Ord),
\]
where $\rho$ ranges over the infinite regular set cardinals.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A class automorphism and its inverse carry sets to sets and preserve
cofinality and coinitiality, so equality of characters is necessary.
A normalized lower cut has no maximum, so any set-sized cofinality is
an infinite regular cardinal. The upper complement either has a least
point, with character $1$, has infinite regular set coinitiality, or
has character $\Ord$. Both characters cannot be set-sized by the core
set-cut property. These observations exhaust the displayed possibilities.
They all occur: lower and upper edges of a prefix of length $\rho$
realize the first two, a core point realizes the third, and a
successor-prefix cylinder edge realizes the fourth.

Suppose first that $D,D'$ have the same set-sized left cofinality
$\rho$. Choose strictly increasing cofinal sequences of type $\rho$
in them. Matching the sequences gives a set partial isomorphism.
\Cref{swo:tc:lem:sethomogeneous} extends it to an automorphism. Since a
normalized lower set is the strict downward closure of any cofinal
sequence with no last member, that automorphism carries $D$ onto $D'$.
For equal right coinitialities use coinitial sequences in their
complements and the same argument with upward closures. This includes
right character $1$, where one simply matches the two least points
of the complements.

It remains to consider two cuts with character $(\Ord,\Ord)$.
Each of their four sides is itself a proper class
$\eta_{\Ord}$-order. For example a set cut inside $D$ with a nonempty
upper side is filled by core saturation, with the interpolant still
below an element of $D$; a set with no upper constraints has an upper
bound inside $D$ because $D$ has no set-sized cofinal subset. Lower
bounds remain available from the ambient core. The corresponding
argument for the complement uses its absence of a set-sized coinitial
subset. None of these sides has an endpoint. Back-and-forth therefore
gives one class isomorphism $D\to D'$ and another between their
complements. Their union is an order automorphism of the core, since
all points on a lower side precede all points on its upper side.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exhaustiveness is not a bare-order invariant]
\label{swo:tc:cor:nonintrinsic}
There are a global exhaustive enumeration $E$ and a class order
automorphism $g$ of $\Psupp(b)$ such that $g[D_E]$ is not the trace of
\emph{any} unrestricted class well-order on $\No$. In particular,
exhaustive representability and even branch representability cannot
be recognized by a criterion invariant under all class automorphisms
of the bare core order.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Let $E$ swap every consecutive ordinal pair of the baseline:
\[
 E(2\cdot\alpha)=b(2\cdot\alpha+1),\qquad
 E(2\cdot\alpha+1)=b(2\cdot\alpha).
\]
It is exhaustive, but it is not represented by a core code, because
it moves a proper class of coordinates. Hence $D_E$ has character
$(\Ord,\Ord)$. The lower edge of the one-letter cylinder
$C_{(b(0))}$ has the same character. The orbit theorem supplies $g$
carrying the former cut to the latter. A cylinder edge is not a branch
trace by \Cref{swo:tc:thm:trichotomy}, and is not a raw-order trace by
source~14's Theorem~10.2 (trace fibres; \merge\ \cref{swo:tc:thm:tracefibers}, and
\cref{swo:cf:fibers} for the fibre description). This proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

Thus the reference to named cylinders in the recognition theorem is
not merely a technical limitation of its proof. A genuine symmetry of
the bare linear order can destroy the property being recognized.
Principal exhaustive cuts are distinguished by their right character
$1$, but non-core exhaustive cuts are not distinguished from other
$(\Ord,\Ord)$ boundaries. The stabilizer of the exhaustive-cut
collection inside the full automorphism group is therefore a proper
subgroup, deserving its own study.

\begin{note}[\merge; overlaps]\label{swo:viii:note:orbits}
\Cref{swo:tc:lem:sethomogeneous} is the set-homogeneity of an order filling
all set cuts (\cref{swo:ec:thm:backforth}, source~09's remark on set-sized
partial isomorphisms in its direction~4). \Cref{swo:tc:cor:nonintrinsic} and
source~17's \cref{swo:gs:thm:nonextension} use the same exhaustive
enumeration (the baseline with every consecutive pair swapped); source~14
sends its cut to a cylinder edge, source~17 to the cut of a nonexhaustive
injective word, and source~15's \cref{swo:cb:thm:automorphism} to a
first-label cut, so all three show that neither represented cuts nor
exhaustive cuts are invariant under automorphisms of the bare core.
Source~15's proof that each side of such a cut is a copy of $\No$ is the
argument of source~17's \cref{swo:gs:lem:gap-homogeneity} and of the last
paragraph of the proof of \cref{swo:tc:thm:orbits}.
\end{note}

% ---- source 17 (batch-81 manuscript 05), lines 1314-1449
\subsection{Source 17: automorphisms, an exact extension test and a negative result}
\label{swo:gs:sec:automorphisms}

Let $\mathscr R_b(L)$ be the predicate saying that $L$ is a proper nonempty
open lower cut of $\Psupp(b)$ which satisfies both the straddling and coverage
conditions of \Cref{swo:gs:thm:recognition}. Thus $\mathscr R_b$ describes
exactly the cuts $L_E$ with $E\in \Hsl$. It is a predicate on individual
class parameters, not an ordinary class of cuts.

For a class order-automorphism $h:\Psupp(b)\to \Psupp(b)$, its action on cuts is
$h_*L=h[L]$. An extension of $h$ to $\Hsl$ means a uniform operator sending
each global enumeration to a global enumeration, preserving comparisons
and having a uniform inverse, whose action on core enumerations is $h$.
This convention states the higher-order typing of the assertion.

\begin{theorem}[Extension criterion]\label{swo:gs:thm:extension-criterion}
A class order-automorphism $h$ of $\Psupp(b)$ extends to an automorphism of
$\Hsl$ if and only if
\[\tag{S17.9}\label{swo:gs:eq:automorphism-criterion}
 \mathscr R_b(L)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathscr R_b(h_*L)
 \qquad\text{for every admissible lower class cut }L.
\]
When it exists, the extension is unique and is reconstructed uniformly by
\Cref{swo:gs:thm:recognition}. No new class-valued recursion is required.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $H$ extends $h$, order preservation gives
\[
 L_{H(E)}=h_*L_E.
\]
Applying the same fact to $H^{-1}$ proves preservation of the represented
cut predicate in both directions.

Conversely assume \eqref{swo:gs:eq:automorphism-criterion}. For each $E$, form
$L_E$, take its image under $h$, and reconstruct its unique exhaustive
word by \Cref{swo:gs:thm:recognition}. Call this word $H(E)$. The entire
construction is elementary from $E,h,b$. Distinct rows have distinct cuts,
and $E<F$ if and only if $L_E\subsetneq L_F$, because the core is dense
between them. Hence $H$ preserves and reflects order. The same recipe
using $h^{-1}$ is its inverse. For a code $c$, the image of the strict
lower segment below $c$ is the strict lower segment below $h(c)$, so $H$
agrees with $h$ on the core. Finally an extension's value is determined
by its comparisons with every core code, proving uniqueness.
\end{proof}

The criterion gives a precise role to the represented-cut predicate. It
is not automatic that an abstract automorphism of the dense core preserves
it. In fact it can fail in a strong way.

\begin{lemma}[Homogeneity of large two-sided core gaps]
\label{swo:gs:lem:gap-homogeneity}
Let $(L,U)$ be a gap of $\Psupp(b)$ such that $L$ has no set-sized cofinal
subset and $U$ no set-sized coinitial subset. Each of the class orders
$L$ and $U$ is isomorphic to $\No$. Any two such gaps are conjugate by a
class order-automorphism of $\Psupp(b)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Consider a separated pair of sets $A<B$ in $L$. If $B$ is nonempty,
\Cref{swo:gs:thm:core-interpolation} gives a core interpolant below every
member of $B$, hence lying in $L$. If $B$ is empty, the absence of a
set-sized cofinal subset of $L$ supplies a member of $L$ strictly above
all of $A$; this includes the case $A=\varnothing$ after choosing any
member. Therefore $L$ has the full set-cut interpolation property.
It is proper: a set $L$ would be a set-sized cofinal subset of itself.
The dual proof gives the same property and properness for $U$.

The class back-and-forth proof of \Cref{swo:gs:cor:core-isomorphism}
now yields $L\cong\No\cong U$. Given two gaps, choose order-isomorphisms
between their lower sides and between their upper sides. The union of
these two class maps is an order-automorphism of the core carrying the
first gap to the second. This uses only two class maps at a time, not an
exhaustive choice of maps for a higher collection of gaps.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Some core automorphisms do not extend]
\label{swo:gs:thm:nonextension}
In $\GBC$ there is a class order-automorphism of $\Psupp(b)$ which does not
extend to an automorphism of $\Hsl$. More precisely, there is one taking
the cut of an exhaustive enumeration to the cut of a nonexhaustive
injective word.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Construct an exhaustive enumeration $E$ by transposing the two entries
in every successive pair of positions of $b$. It differs from $b$ on a
proper class of positions, so it has no core code. Choose also a bijection
$F:\Ord\to\No\setminus\{r_0\}$ for one fixed label $r_0$. It cannot
have a core code because it is not exhaustive.

By \Cref{swo:gs:prop:class-characters}, both $L_E$ and $L_F$ are
genuine two-sided core gaps with no small cofinal or coinitial side.
\Cref{swo:gs:lem:gap-homogeneity} supplies an automorphism $h$ with
$h_*L_E=L_F$. The first cut satisfies $\mathscr R_b$, whereas the second
fails coverage. \Cref{swo:gs:thm:extension-criterion} rules out an
extension. Alternatively, any proposed image $H(E)\in \Hsl$ would have
cut $L_F$, whose unique representing injection is the nonexhaustive
word $F$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A limit to pure-order recognition]\label{swo:gs:n10.4}
Exhaustiveness of a branch cut is not invariant under all automorphisms
of the bare class order $\Psupp(b)$. In particular it cannot be characterized
by a parameter-free, automorphism-invariant property of that order and
its cuts alone. The two-sided character $(\Ord,\Ord)$ does not suffice.
\end{corollary}

This does not preclude recognition using the baseline, labelled prefix
tree, or suitable additional predicates. \Cref{swo:gs:thm:recognition}
provides exactly such a positive result. Nor does it rule out more subtle
reconstruction after adding a distinguished represented-cut predicate.
It shows why order-isomorphism of dense cores, by itself, cannot be used
to extend maps of the entire higher-order comparison.

\subsubsection{A natural positive family}
\begin{proposition}[Relabelling by numerical automorphisms]
\label{swo:gs:prop:relabelling}
If $\varphi:\No\to\No$ is an increasing class bijection, then
$E\mapsto\varphi\circ E$ is an automorphism of $\Hsl$, and transporting
relations by $\varphi$ is an automorphism of the unrestricted comparison
$\Hall$. It carries the core associated with $b$ onto the core associated
with $\varphi\circ b$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The first differing labels are transformed by an increasing bijection,
so their comparison is unchanged. Surjectivity, injectivity, and the
class well-order property are preserved under relabelling. Finally
$\varphi\circ(b\circ\widehat\sigma)
=(\varphi\circ b)\circ\widehat\sigma$, with the same set support code.
\end{proof}

This is a sufficient family of extendible maps, not a classification of
all of them. Arbitrary permutations of the label class need not preserve
lexicographic order. A general isomorphism between two cores whose
baselines differ on a proper class of positions need not extend either;
\Cref{swo:gs:thm:extension-criterion} identifies the additional condition
that must be checked.

\subsection{Source 15: the bare order does not determine represented cuts}

\begin{theorem}[An automorphism destroys prefix representability]\label{swo:cb:thm:automorphism}
\textit{Extension proved in source~15.}\ In $\GBC$, there is a class order automorphism of $\Pbd(b)$ taking a
cut represented by an injective $\Ord$-word to a cut represented by
no such word, and therefore by no raw class well-order.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Take a nonexhaustive word $F$. Neither side of $(L_F,R_F)$ has a set
cofinality toward the cut: a set of first-disagreement coordinates can
be bounded, and a perturbation agreeing with $F$ beyond that bound
improves every proposed bound. Each side consequently fills all its
own set cuts. For a cut with constraints on both sides, use the core
interpolation theorem between bounding points in that side. For an
empty bounding side, use the absence of a set cofinal or coinitial
family toward the removed boundary, together with the unboundedness
away from it. Thus each side is a copy of $\No$.

The class order $\No+\No$ also fills every set cut. If constraints
straddle the summands, choose a point in the first summand above the
set of lower constraints; cases with both bounds in one summand reduce
to that summand. The cases of constraints extending into the second
summand are handled there. Class uniqueness gives $\No+\No\cong\No$.
Hence there is a numerical partition $\No=A+B$ with both sides
isomorphic to $\No$.

Let $L'=\{d:E_d(0)\in A\}$ and $R'=\{d:E_d(0)\in B\}$.
This cut has no crossing cylinder at length one, so it is unrepresented.
Neither side has a set cofinality toward the cut, as is seen already
in its first labels. The preceding interpolation argument shows that
$L'$ and $R'$ are also copies of $\No$. Choose class isomorphisms
$L_F\to L'$ and $R_F\to R'$ and take their union. It is the required
automorphism. All these maps have sets as inputs and outputs.
\end{proof}

Thus even knowing the abstract class order $\Pbd(b)\cong\No$ is insufficient
to identify the enumeration cuts. One must retain predicates for the
cylinders, the evaluation map, or equivalent structure. This supplies
a negative answer to a natural reconstruction question raised in the
prior report. The theorem does not claim that every automorphism of the
core extends to the higher collection of all global enumerations.

\merge\ Source~15 states \cref{swo:cb:thm:automorphism} without naming its
foundation; its proof chooses class isomorphisms of the sides of two cuts
with $\No$, so it is a theorem of $\GBC$, and the words ``In $\GBC$'' are
added at the merge. Its Proposition~4.2 (\cref{swo:cb:prop:fibres}) needs $\GBC$
for the same reason.
Its closing sentence, a ``negative answer to a natural reconstruction
question raised in the prior report'', answers \cref{swo:n16.4} in part
only (\cref{swo:viii:sec:status}).

\subsection{Source 13: the pure order does not recover the prefix cylinders}\label{swo:fs:sec:automorphisms}

The earlier report asks whether prefix structure can be recovered from
the pure order (\cref{swo:n16.4}). We give a negative answer for the
family of all set-prefix cylinders, using only a finite change in how
information is grouped.

\begin{lemma}[Finite tuples as a surreal class order]\label{swo:fs:lem:tuples}
For each positive integer $n$, the class $P_n$ of injective $n$-tuples
of surreals, ordered lexicographically, is isomorphic to $\No$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
First, finite lexicographic powers $\No^n$ fill every set cut. At the
first coordinate, the lower and upper projected values satisfy all
cross weak inequalities. If no cross value is shared, choose a strict
separator for that coordinate and fill the remaining coordinates
arbitrarily. If a value is shared, it is the unique common one; keep
that coordinate and use the active rows in the remaining coordinates.
Continuing this way cannot reach two identical opposing tuples,
because the original cut was strict. This proves the set-cut property.
\Cref{swo:fs:lem:backforth} gives $\No^n\cong\No$.

There is a uniform order isomorphism $\No^n\to P_n$: at coordinate
$i$, map the input value increasingly into the complement of the
previously output finite set, using $h_S$. Recover the input by the
inverse complement map coordinate by coordinate. First disagreements
are preserved. Compose the two isomorphisms.
\end{proof}

Fix an order isomorphism $k:\No\to P_2$. Write
$k(x)=(u_x,v_x)$, where $u_x\ne v_x$. There is a uniform increasing
bijection
\[
 g_x:\No\setminus\{x\}\longrightarrow\No\setminus\{u_x,v_x\},
 \qquad
 g_x=h_{\{u_x,v_x\}}\circ h_{\{x\}}^{-1}.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Cylinder non-rigidity]\label{swo:fs:thm:nonrigidity}
In $\GBC$ there is a uniform order automorphism of $\Hsl$ that maps
some prefix cylinder to a class of enumerations that is not any prefix
cylinder. Thus the family of all prefix cylinders is not invariant
under automorphisms of the pure linear order.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Define $H(E)$ by replacing the first label $x=E(0)$ with the pair
$(u_x,v_x)$, and translating the remaining labels by $g_x$:
\[
 H(E)(0)=u_x,\quad H(E)(1)=v_x,\quad
 H(E)(2+\alpha)=g_x(E(1+\alpha)).
\]
This is a class bijection onto $\No$. The first two output labels
determine $x$ by $k^{-1}$; the inverse of $g_x$ recovers the tail.
Therefore $H$ is a bijection on the virtual domain. Different first
input labels are compared by the order isomorphism $k$, and equal
first labels leave an increasing tail transformation. Hence $H$ is
an order automorphism, with
\[
                              H(C_{(x)})=C_{k(x)}.
\]

Fix a label $u$. Then
\[
 H^{-1}(C_{(u)})=
       \bigcup_{x\in A_u} C_{(x)},\qquad
 A_u=\{x:\text{the first coordinate of }k(x)\text{ is }u\}.
\]
The class $A_u$ contains more than one label, because $P_2$ contains
$(u,v)$ for every $v\ne u$. It is nonempty and proper, since pairs
with another first coordinate also exist. The displayed inverse image
therefore contains enumerations with different first labels, but is
not the whole domain. It cannot be a nonempty-prefix cylinder, all of
whose members have the same first label, and it cannot be the
empty-prefix cylinder, which is the whole domain. Apply the
automorphism $H^{-1}$ to $C_{(u)}$.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{What the counterexample does not say}

The theorem rules out a parameter-free order-theoretic characterization
whose members are exactly the prefix cylinders. It also rules out
recovering their original tree canonically from the pure linear order.
It does not say that no useful interval structure is recoverable, that
every order automorphism arises by block recoding, or that the chosen
core $\Psupp(b)$ is preserved by $H$.

In particular, the expanded structure containing the core, its
set-support filtration, birthday data, or an explicit prefix predicate
may have a much smaller automorphism group. The cut criterion of
\Cref{swo:fs:thm:reconstruction} is correctly a criterion in such
an expanded prefix presentation. Its non-invariance under forgetting
that presentation is a substantive feature, not a foundational flaw.

\subsubsection{Finite block depth is not intrinsic either}

Using $P_n$ instead of $P_2$ replaces one first label by any fixed
positive finite number of distinct labels, with a complement
isomorphism applied to the tail. The same construction gives an order
automorphism that sends first-level cylinders to selected $n$th-level
cylinders. Thus even finite prefix depth has no absolute meaning in
the pure order, despite being indispensable to a particular
lexicographic presentation.

\merge\ Source~13's opening sentence refers to \cref{swo:n16.4}, which its
theorem answers in part. \Cref{swo:fs:lem:tuples} uses the family $h_S$ of
\cref{swo:fs:lem:backforth}.

\section{Class extensions (source 14; source 17)}\label{swo:viii:sec:extensions}

\merge\ Sources~14 and~17 prove the same theorem: for two class realizations
with the same sets and a common baseline, an old core cut is the cut of a
global enumeration in the larger realization exactly when it already is in
the smaller one, and the enumeration is then old. The proof is the
elementarity of the recognition criterion. Source~17 adds that every proper
class extension adds a new global enumeration and a new represented cut
(\cref{swo:gs:thm:class-extension}). Source~14's text, from the second half
of its Section~7, is printed first.

% ---- source 14 (batch-81 manuscript 02), lines 918-960
\begin{theorem}[No new realization of an old trace cut]\label{swo:tc:thm:absolute}
Suppose $(M,\mathcal C)$ and $(M,\mathcal D)$ are models of $\GBC$
with the same set structure, $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal D$, and a
common baseline enumeration $b\in\mathcal C$. If a proper normalized
core cut $D$ belongs to $\mathcal C$, then
\[
 (M,\mathcal C)\models \exists E\in \Hsl\ (D=D_E)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 (M,\mathcal D)\models \exists E\in \Hsl\ (D=D_E).
\]
Moreover, when it exists, the realizing enumeration in the larger model
is already a class of the smaller model.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The canonical support codes, the cylinders, and their membership
relations are defined from the same sets and $b$. Every formula in
(C), (X), and the reconstruction formula has set quantifiers and the
old class parameters $D,b$ only. Its truth is therefore the same in the
two structures. If the larger model contains a realizing enumeration,
the recognition theorem gives (C) and (X) there and hence in the
smaller model. Elementary comprehension in the smaller model constructs
the displayed graph from $D,b$. It is the same graph as the larger
model's enumeration by uniqueness. The converse is immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{swo:tc:n7.3}
An enumeration newly available after such a class extension has a
trace cut not belonging to the old class collection. An old
nonexhaustive branch cut, cylinder edge, or numerical-gap cut is not
turned into the trace of a global enumeration by enlarging only the
class part.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}[Scope of absoluteness]\label{swo:tc:n7.4}
The theorem holds because realizability of this particular kind of cut
has an elementary, uniquely reconstructing criterion. It is not an
assertion that all class-existence questions are absolute, that the
virtual enumeration order is unchanged, or that arbitrary internal
well-foundedness is externally absolute. The set structure and the
baseline must remain fixed. New classes can, and in suitable
realizations do, supply new enumerations and new cuts simultaneously.
\end{remark}

% ---- source 17 (batch-81 manuscript 05), lines 1450-1509
\subsection{Source 17: what changes when the available classes change?}
\label{swo:gs:sec:class-extensions}

Let $(M,\mathcal X)\subseteq(M,\mathcal Y)$ be two transitive two-sorted
models of $\GBC$ with the same sets and $\mathcal X\subseteq\mathcal Y$.
Assume the baseline $b$ belongs to $\mathcal X$. The assertions below can
also be stated internally as preservation statements for a specified
same-set extension; the transitive formulation avoids irrelevant
ambiguities about external well-foundedness.

\begin{theorem}[New enumerations are exactly new represented core cuts]
\label{swo:gs:thm:class-extension}
The set-code carrier $\Psupp(b)$, its order relation, and its labelled
set-prefix cylinders are unchanged between the two models. For any
$E\in \Hsl^{\mathcal Y}$,
\[
 E\in\mathcal X\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L_E\in\mathcal X.
\]
Consequently every genuinely larger class realization
$\mathcal X\subsetneq\mathcal Y$ adds a global enumeration and a
represented cut of the unchanged core.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Support codes and prefixes are sets, and the two models have exactly the
same sets. Their evaluations use the same baseline class. All relations
in the definition of a cylinder are therefore the same.

If $E\in\mathcal X$, elementary comprehension in the smaller model gives
$L_E\in\mathcal X$. Conversely, suppose $L_E\in\mathcal X$. At every
ordinal length, the assertion that a set prefix straddles this cut has
the same truth value in the two models: its witnesses are set codes and
its quantifiers range over their common sets. Thus the smaller model
can reconstruct the unique branch by the elementary formula in
\Cref{swo:gs:thm:recognition}. Its graph must be $E$, so $E\in\mathcal X$.
Coverage is also an elementary assertion with the same set domain.

For the final assertion, choose $A\in\mathcal Y\setminus\mathcal X$.
A global well-order already in $\mathcal X$ gives a class bijection
$g:\Ord^M\to M$. The pullback $D=g^{-1}[A]$ is a subclass of
$\Ord^M$ in $\mathcal Y$ and not in $\mathcal X$, since $A$ is recovered
from it by the same old $g$. Encode $D$ by listing each sorted baseline
pair in increasing or decreasing order according as its index is absent
from or present in $D$. This yields $E_D\in \Hsl^{\mathcal Y}$. Pair
orientation recovers $D$, so $E_D$ is not in $\mathcal X$. Its core cut
is new by the first part of the theorem.
\end{proof}

For pre-existing global enumerations, their comparisons and their
surjectivity are unchanged. A bijection from the common ordinal class
still induces a well-order: any nonempty subclass of its index class has
a least ordinal, witnessed below any one of its members. Thus the old
set-like comparison sits inside the new one with its order intact, even
though the represented-cut collection strictly expands.

This result answers a precise part of the source's class-realization
question. It does not reconstruct the entire class collection from the
\emph{unlabelled external order type} of its admitted enumerations. The
proof uses the baseline and its fixed decoder. That stronger reconstruction
problem remains open here.

\section{Support-restricted suborders and the exact reserve (source 14; source 17)}\label{swo:viii:sec:support}

\merge\ Source~14 measures how much support an interpolant needs; source~17
measures how much support beyond the forced positions a completion of a
partial injection needs. Source~14's Section~9 is printed first, then
source~17's Section~7.

% ---- source 14 (batch-81 manuscript 02), lines 1063-1247
\subsection{Source 14: a sharp hierarchy of support-restricted orders}
\label{swo:tc:sec:support}
Fix an infinite set cardinal $\kappa$ and define
\[
 \mathcal P_{<\kappa}(b)=\{\sigma\in \Psupp(b):|\supp(\sigma)|<\kappa\}.
\]
For an infinite regular cardinal $\theta$, an $\eta_\theta$-order is a
linear order in which every separated pair $A<B$ with
$|A\cup B|<\theta$ has a strict separator, including when one side is
empty. This convention makes $\eta_\omega$ mean dense without endpoints.
The class-sized orders here need not have cardinality $\theta$.

The predecessor distinguishes finite support from arbitrary set support
(\cref{swo:sk:prop:finitesupport}; Section~19 of this report at the pin). We now give an
exact intermediate hierarchy, including singular thresholds. The key
is to compress the support of a separator without preserving its
irrelevant later coordinates.

\begin{lemma}[Small-support extension of a partial injection]
\label{swo:tc:lem:partialextension}
Let $f:D\to\Ord$ be a set injection. It extends to a class permutation
of $\Ord$ with finite support if $D$ is finite, and with support of
cardinality at most $|D|$ if $D$ is infinite. One may require that any
specified set of already prescribed fixed positions, disjoint from
$D\cup f[D]$, stay fixed.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $T_0=D\cup f[D]$. For finite $D$, the complements $T_0\setminus D$
and $T_0\setminus f[D]$ have the same finite cardinality. Choose a
bijection between them and combine it with $f$; fix everything outside
$T_0$. For infinite $D$ of cardinality $\nu$, adjoin a fresh set $B$
of $\nu$ ordinals disjoint from $T_0$ and from the specified fixed
positions. With $T=T_0\cup B$, both $T\setminus D$ and
$T\setminus f[D]$ have cardinality $\nu$. A bijection between them
extends $f$ to a permutation of $T$, again extended by the identity.
The resulting support has cardinality at most $\nu$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Support compression]\label{swo:tc:lem:compression}
Let $A,B$ be separated sets of core codes and let
\[
 S=\bigcup\{\supp(\sigma):\sigma\in A\cup B\}.
\]
There is a strict separator whose support is finite if $S$ is finite,
and has cardinality at most $|S|$ if $S$ is infinite.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
By \Cref{swo:tc:cor:coreeta}, choose a separator $Q\in \Psupp(b)$.
If its support is contained in $S$, nothing remains to prove.
Otherwise let
\[
 \gamma=\min(\supp(Q)\setminus S).
\]
Every input permutation fixes $\gamma$, while $\widehat Q$ moves it.
Thus the first disagreement between $E_Q$ and every input enumeration
occurs no later than $\gamma$. Any permutation agreeing with
$\widehat Q$ through $\gamma$ will preserve all those comparisons.

Let $D=\{\alpha\le\gamma:\widehat Q(\alpha)\ne\alpha\}$.
By minimality of $\gamma$, $D\subseteq S\cup\{\gamma\}$. Keep the
partial injection $\widehat Q\res D$. None of its images is a
prescribed fixed position $\beta\le\gamma$ outside $D$: otherwise
$\widehat Q(\beta)=\beta=\widehat Q(\alpha)$ for a distinct
$\alpha\in D$, contradicting injectivity. Apply
\Cref{swo:tc:lem:partialextension} while retaining those fixed positions.
For infinite $D$ its buffer can explicitly be chosen above $\gamma$.
The resulting permutation agrees with $\widehat Q$ through $\gamma$,
hence is still a strict separator. Its support is finite when $S$ is
finite, and is at most $|S|$ when $S$ is infinite, since
$|D|\le|S\cup\{\gamma\}|$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact support saturation and an attained obstruction]
\label{swo:tc:thm:support}
For every infinite set cardinal $\kappa$, put $r=\cf\kappa$.
Then $\mathcal P_{<\kappa}(b)$ is an $\eta_r$-order but not an
$\eta_{r^+}$-order. More precisely, there are increasing
$(l_i)_{i<r}$ and decreasing $(u_i)_{i<r}$ in $\mathcal P_{<\kappa}(b)$ such that
$l_i<u_j$ for all $i,j$, and every core separator moves at least
$\kappa$ coordinates. A separator of support cardinality exactly
$\kappa$ exists in $\Psupp(b)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For the positive assertion take $A,B\subseteq \mathcal P_{<\kappa}(b)$ with
$|A\cup B|<r$. Fewer than $\cf\kappa$ sets, each of cardinality
$<\kappa$, have union of cardinality $<\kappa$. Their union of
supports therefore satisfies $|S|<\kappa$. Support compression gives
an interpolant with support $<\kappa$. For $\kappa=\omega$ both the
family and all its supports are finite, so the finite clause applies.

For sharpness choose strictly increasing ordinals
$(\lambda_i)_{i<r}$ cofinal in $\kappa$. Consider the injective
prefix
\[
 p:\kappa\to\No,\qquad p(\alpha)=b(\alpha+1).
\]
Every infinite initial cardinal is a limit ordinal, so this formula
uses coordinates below $\kappa$. It moves every coordinate of its
domain relative to $b$.
For each $i$, choose fresh labels
\[
 a_i<p(\lambda_i)<c_i,
 \qquad a_i,c_i\notin\ran(p\res\lambda_i),
\]
and extend the two prefixes
\[
 (p\res\lambda_i)\cat(a_i),\qquad
 (p\res\lambda_i)\cat(c_i)
\]
to enumerations with codes $l_i,u_i$. Their partial ordinal maps have
domains of cardinality $|\lambda_i+1|<\kappa$; by
\Cref{swo:tc:lem:partialextension} they can be completed with support
$<\kappa$, even when a chosen label has a very large baseline index.
Set choice suffices to make the $r$ choices simultaneously.

For $i<j$, comparison at $\lambda_i$ gives $l_i<l_j$ and $u_j<u_i$.
The same first-coordinate argument gives $l_i<u_j$ for every $i,j$.
Suppose any global enumeration $E$ separated the two families and
first differed from $p$ at some $\alpha<\kappa$. Choose $i$ with
$\lambda_i>\alpha$. Both $E_{l_i}$ and $E_{u_i}$ agree with $p$
through $\alpha$. According to its differing value there, $E$ would
lie below both or above both, a contradiction. Hence any separator
satisfies $E\res\kappa=p$. Relative to $b$ it must move all
$\kappa$ coordinates of that prefix. In particular no member of
$\mathcal P_{<\kappa}(b)$ separates the families.

Finally extend $p$ itself by \Cref{swo:tc:lem:partialextension}.
Its domain has cardinality $\kappa$, so the extension has support at
most $\kappa$; the forced moves show the support is exactly
$\kappa$. It separates the two families by comparison at
$\lambda_i$. The obstruction has combined cardinality $r$, hence
violates $\eta_{r^+}$, and its minimum support cost is attained.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Consequences and examples}
For a regular $\kappa$ the answer is exactly $\eta_\kappa$ but not
$\eta_{\kappa^+}$. In particular finite support is dense without
endpoints but can fail a countable cut; countable support fills every
countable strict cut but can fail a cut of size $\omega_1$.
For $\kappa=\aleph_\omega$, the cofinality is $\omega$, so support
of every cardinality below $\aleph_\omega$ still does not guarantee
countable-cut filling. The same construction takes supports cofinal
in the threshold and forces their full union at the limit.

This sharpness statement is stronger than merely exhibiting some gap:
it quantifies how much extra support any solution must use. It also
explains why replacing a singular support bound by its cardinal size
in a saturation argument is invalid. The closure property used in the
positive direction is closure under unions of fewer than
$\cf\kappa$ supports, not fewer than $\kappa$ supports.

\begin{proposition}[Universality without high saturation]
\label{swo:tc:prop:supportuniversal}
Every $\mathcal P_{<\kappa}(b)$ contains an order-isomorphic copy of $\No$, already among
the permutations with support at most two. Thus, in $\GBC$, it contains
every ordinary class linear order up to embedding. Nevertheless no fixed
$\mathcal P_{<\kappa}(b)$ is isomorphic to $\No$, and it is not dense in $\Hsl$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For $x\in\No$, transpose the baseline positions $0$ and $b^{-1}(x)$,
using the identity if these coincide. Call the code $t_x$. Then
$E_{t_x}(0)=x$, so $x<y$ implies $t_x<t_y$. The familiar class
universality of $\No$ follows by inserting points of any ordinary
class linear order, in a fixed set-like global enumeration, between the
images of their earlier lower and upper neighbors; every stage has
only set many constraints. Composing gives the asserted embeddings.

\Cref{swo:tc:thm:support} supplies a set cut not filled by $\mathcal P_{<\kappa}(b)$,
whereas $\No$ fills all set cuts, so the two orders are not isomorphic.
For ambient nondensity, use the prefix $p$ of length $\kappa$ in that
theorem. Choose two distinct fresh next labels and complete both
prefixes to core enumerations. Every enumeration between them shares
$p$ and hence moves at least $\kappa$ baseline coordinates. The
nonempty open interval they determine misses $\mathcal P_{<\kappa}(b)$ entirely.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Cardinality versus location of support]\label{swo:tc:n9.5}
The theorem restricts $|\supp\sigma|$, not the ordinal height of the
support. A transposition with an arbitrarily late baseline coordinate
still has support two. Replacing the cardinality condition by
$\supp\sigma\subseteq\gamma$ for one fixed ordinal $\gamma$ gives
a set-sized permutation space with quite different universality. These
two filtrations should never share an undifferentiated ``bounded'' label.
\end{remark}

\begin{note}[\merge; the finite case is source~08's]\label{swo:viii:note:finitesupport}
At $\kappa=\omega$, \cref{swo:tc:thm:support} is source~08's
\cref{swo:sk:prop:finitesupport} (printed in Part~IV), with the same witness
prefix $p(n)=b(n+1)$ and the same fresh labels; source~14 cites the
finite-support subsection but not the proposition. New in source~14 are the
positive half ($\mathcal P_{<\kappa}(b)$ is $\eta_r$), the threshold at
every infinite $\kappa$, including singular $\kappa$, and the attained
support cost $\kappa$ of a separator. \Cref{swo:tc:prop:supportuniversal}
extends source~08's remark that the finite-support codes contain a copy of
$\No$ (\cref{swo:sk:cor:firstentry}).
\end{note}

% ---- source 17 (batch-81 manuscript 05), lines 899-995
\subsection{Source 17: the optimal extra support needed to extend a partial injection}
\label{swo:gs:sec:support}

The source extends a prescribed prefix inside a sufficiently large
cardinal block. That argument is safe but leaves a more elementary
optimization question: how many \emph{additional moved positions} are
actually necessary? The following answer applies to arbitrary set-sized
partial injections, not just prefixes.

\begin{theorem}[Exact reserve cardinal]\label{swo:gs:thm:reserve}
Let $A\subseteq\Ord$ be a set and let $h:A\to\Ord$ be injective. Define
\[
 D=\{\xi\in A:h(\xi)\ne\xi\},\qquad R=h[D],\qquad S=D\cup R,
 \qquad u=|R\setminus D|,\quad v=|D\setminus R|.
\]
Among class permutations $\pi:\Ord\to\Ord$ with set support which extend
$h$, the minimum possible value of $|\supp(\pi)\setminus S|$ is
\[\tag{S17.6}\label{swo:gs:eq:reserve}
 \boxed{\tau(h)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&u=v,\\
 \max(\aleph_0,u,v),&u\ne v.
 \end{cases}}
\]
Moreover every point of $S$ must move. An extension attaining the bound
can be constructed by a bijection between two explicitly specified sets.
The theorem uses only set choice and elementary operations with the class
of ordinals; with a fixed global choice parameter the construction can be
made uniform.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The fixed points $A\setminus D$ are disjoint from $R$, by injectivity of
$h$. Every $d\in D$ must move. If $r\in R\setminus D$, it already has a
preimage $d\ne r$ under the prescribed map, so an extending permutation
cannot fix $r$. Thus every point of $S$ must move.

Suppose $\pi$ is an extension and put $T=\supp(\pi)\setminus S$. No point
of $T$ is in $A\setminus D$, whose values are prescribed to be fixed.
The support of a permutation is invariant under the permutation and its
inverse. After the prescribed bijection $h:D\to R$ has been removed,
$\pi$ must therefore give a bijection
\[\tag{S17.7}\label{swo:gs:eq:reserve-bijection}
 (R\setminus D)\cup T\ \longrightarrow\ (D\setminus R)\cup T.
\]
In particular $u+|T|=v+|T|$. If $u\ne v$ are finite, finite cancellation
rules out finite $T$, and $\aleph_0$ suffices. If at least one of $u,v$
is infinite, unequal cardinals can be equalized by addition of $|T|$
only when $|T|\ge\max(u,v)$. This follows from the formula for addition
of infinite cardinals as their maximum. These observations prove the
lower bound in \eqref{swo:gs:eq:reserve}.

Conversely, choose a fresh set of ordinals $T$ of cardinality $\tau(h)$,
disjoint from $A\cup R$, and choose a bijection in
\eqref{swo:gs:eq:reserve-bijection}. Combine it with $h:D\to R$, and take the
identity outside $S\cup T$. The result is a permutation extending $h$,
with support contained in $S\cup T$. All points of $S$ move, as proved
above. If $\tau(h)>0$, the lower bound forces exactly $\tau(h)$ further
points to move; if $\tau(h)=0$, no reserve was used. This proves
attainment, including cases where the chosen bijection happens to fix
some points of $T$.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Why a finite reserve can never repair a one-sided shift]\label{swo:gs:n7.2}
Prescribe $h(n)=n+1$ for every $n<\omega$. Then $D=\omega$,
$R=\omega\setminus\{0\}$, and $(u,v)=(0,1)$. No permutation on
$\omega$ extends $h$. More strongly, no extension can use only finitely
many additional moved positions outside $\omega$. Exactly countably many
are necessary and sufficient. One concrete completion chooses fresh
$t_0,t_1,\ldots$, sends $t_0$ to $0$, and sends $t_{n+1}$ to $t_n$;
all other ordinals are fixed.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Finite partial injections require no reserve]\label{swo:gs:n7.3}
When $D$ is finite, $|D|=|R|$ implies $|R\setminus D|=|D\setminus R|$.
Hence every finite partial injection extends to a permutation supported
exactly on $D\cup R$. The distinction between this fact and the preceding
infinite example is precisely the failure of finite cancellation for
infinite sets; finite testing alone cannot find the infinite obstruction.
\end{example}

\begin{corollary}[Application to prescribed surreal prefixes]
\label{swo:gs:cor:optimal-prefix}
Fix a class bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$. If $p:\alpha\to\No$ is an
injective set prefix, apply \Cref{swo:gs:thm:reserve} to
$h=b^{-1}\circ p$. The resulting $b\circ\pi$ extends $p$ and agrees
with $b$ outside a set. Formula~\eqref{swo:gs:eq:reserve} gives the exact minimum
number of moved coordinates beyond the necessarily moved set
$D\cup h[D]$.
\end{corollary}

This is a cardinal optimum relative to a given partial injection and
baseline. It does not assert a minimum \emph{ordinal} support bound, a
minimum birthday of a code, or a canonical extension independent of
choice. Those are different optimization problems. The source's
larger-cardinal completion remains a useful simple implementation; the
reserve formula says exactly when its extra room is genuinely necessary.

\begin{note}[\merge; the reserve theorem in this report]\label{swo:viii:note:reserve}
\Cref{swo:gs:thm:reserve} sharpens source~09's \cref{swo:ec:n8.2}: the
example $n\mapsto n+1$ there is source~17's \cref{swo:gs:n7.2}, and the
theorem says exactly when the larger cardinal of \cref{swo:gl:completion}
is needed and how many extra positions suffice. The two support theorems
are consistent: \cref{swo:tc:lem:partialextension} bounds the support of an
extension of a set injection $f:D\to\Ord$ by $\card D$ when $D$ is infinite
and keeps it finite when $D$ is finite, while \cref{swo:gs:thm:reserve}
computes the least number of moved positions outside the forced set: $0$ for
finite partial injections (\cref{swo:gs:n7.3}), and otherwise $0$ or
$\max(\aleph_0,u,v)\le\card D$. Source~17's
question table maps the reserve theorem to source~11's \cref{swo:n16.6};
that question asks for birthday bounds, and the theorem bears instead on
source~09's direction ``Sharp birthday and support bounds'' and source~08's
question~13 (\cref{swo:viii:sec:status}).
\end{note}

\section{What this Part answers}\label{swo:viii:sec:status}

\merge\ Dated notes, 3 October 2026, in the form of \cref{swo:vi:sec:status};
where the question index of \cref{swo:sec:questions} (dated 2 October 2026)
says otherwise, these notes supersede it.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item \emph{Source~11's \cref{swo:n16.1} and source~09's direction ``Which
cuts of the core represent exhaustive branches?''}
(\cref{swo:ec:sec:research}): \textbf{answered}, in the labelled-tree form
the question asks for. A normalized class cut of the core is the cut of an
injective class word exactly when a crossing prefix exists at every set
length; the word is unique and elementary in the cut; it is exhaustive
exactly when the crossing prefixes cover $\No$
(\cref{swo:tc:thm:recognition}; six proofs, \cref{swo:viii:note:sixfold}).
Every other proper cut is a cylinder edge or a numerical gap after a set
prefix, with unique data (\cref{swo:tc:thm:trichotomy}); the missing labels,
the forbidden repeated labels and the cuts escaping every coherent branch
that \cref{swo:n16.1}'s commentary asks to separate are exactly the coverage
failure, source~15's repeated-label case and the edge and gap cuts. A
recognition from the bare order is impossible (item~(c)).
\item \emph{Source~08's question~8, higher-size cuts and completion}
(\cref{swo:sk:sec:research}): answered for the class cuts of the core
relative to its prefix presentation: the trichotomy and characters
(\cref{swo:tc:thm:trichotomy,swo:tc:thm:characters}), the image of the raw
orders (\cref{swo:ds:cor:rawcutimage}), and source~15's remark that adjoining
the raw orders is neither a Dedekind completion of the core nor a
realization of every core cut (\cref{swo:cb:sec:cuts}). Cuts given by higher
collections of classes stay open.
\item \emph{Source~11's \cref{swo:n16.4}, source~09's direction ``Automorphisms
beyond set-sized partial maps'' and source~08's question~6}: answered in
part, negatively. The automorphism orbits of class cuts of the core are
exactly the four character classes (\cref{swo:tc:thm:orbits}); neither
represented nor exhaustive cuts are invariant under automorphisms of the
bare core (\cref{swo:tc:cor:nonintrinsic,swo:gs:thm:nonextension,swo:cb:thm:automorphism});
the prefix cylinders of $\Hsl$ are not invariant under automorphisms of
$\Hsl$, nor is finite prefix depth (\cref{swo:fs:thm:nonrigidity}). An
automorphism of the core extends to $\Hsl$ exactly when it preserves
represented cuts (\cref{swo:gs:thm:extension-criterion}). Open: the
stabilizer of the exhaustive cuts, and which extra predicates make the
reconstruction unique (source~14's and source~17's own questions).
\item \emph{Source~11's \cref{swo:n16.5}, baselines}: its suggested restricted
first case is settled: a baseline change by an increasing class bijection of
$\No$ is an automorphism of $\Hsl$ and of $\Hall$ carrying one core onto the
other (\cref{swo:gs:prop:relabelling}, source~08's remark in its question~6).
The general case is open.
\item \emph{Source~11's \cref{swo:n16.8}, source~12's \cref{swo:st:n14.8} and
source~08's question~12, class realizations}: answered in part. Over a fixed
set structure and baseline, the represented-cut status of an old core cut is
absolute, its enumeration is old, and every proper extension of the class
part adds a global enumeration and a represented cut
(\cref{swo:tc:thm:absolute,swo:gs:thm:class-extension}). What the unlabelled
external order type remembers is open here (Part~IX prints source~18's
countable models, \cref{swo:sh:sec:countable-factorial-shuffle}, and
\cref{swo:ix:sec:status}~(e) records what they answer).
\item \emph{Source~09's direction ``Sharp birthday and support bounds'' and
source~08's question~13}: answered in part for support. The least support
cardinal of an interpolant in $\mathcal P_{<\kappa}(b)$ is governed by
$\cf\kappa$ (\cref{swo:tc:thm:support}), and the least reserve of a
completion of a partial injection is $0$ or $\max(\aleph_0,u,v)$
(\cref{swo:gs:thm:reserve}). Ordinal support bounds, birthday bounds and the
forced-prefix length remain open, as source~17 says.
\item \emph{Source~11's \cref{swo:n16.6}} is not affected by the reserve
theorem (\cref{swo:viii:note:reserve}).
\end{enumerate}

\merge\ (3 October 2026.) The fourth and last Part of the batch-81 addition
(\cref{swo:sub:batch81}; notation in \cref{swo:sub:notation81}). Part~III
(\cref{swo:part:classes}) compared arbitrary class well-orders of $\No$
directly, extracted the canonical initial set-like part of each, and asked
how far that extraction can be iterated (\cref{swo:n16.3}); Part~V
(\cref{swo:part:models}) compared the two global orders in larger universes.
This Part prints what sources~13--18 prove beyond those Parts, and every
remaining section of theirs on foundations, universes and formalization:
\begin{itemize}
\item their restatements of the order facts and of the direct comparison of
class well-orders (\cref{swo:ix:sec:reproved}), all re-proofs of Parts~I
and~III;
\item the canonical decomposition of a class well-order into proper blocks of

well-order is a block-index order (\cref{swo:ix:sec:blocks}), proved by

about recursion strength (\cref{swo:ix:sec:histories}, source~15);

bound for uniform nonembedding (\cref{swo:ds:sec:coding}, sources~16 and~14);

\Cref{swo:ix:sec:status} records which questions the Part answers. The

\emph{Notation in this Part} (in addition to \cref{swo:sub:notation81}). The

\subsection{Source 15: sign sequences, properness, and cut filling}

We realize a surreal as a sign sequence $s:\alpha\to\{-,+\}$ of ordinal
length $\alpha$. At a first difference the comparison is
$-<\text{undefined}<+$; the birthday is the length. The all-plus sequences
give an increasing copy of $\Ord$, so $\No$ is a proper class. Every set of
surreals has a set bound on its birthdays, by replacement.

The numerical surreal order fills every set cut: if $L,R$ are sets and
$L<R$, some $x$ satisfies $L<x<R$, with either side allowed to be empty.
This is the familiar Conway construction. It implies density and no
endpoints, but it does not assert filling for arbitrary class cuts.
The numerical order and the simplicity relation are distinct: extending a
sign string makes it more complicated in simplicity, but may increase or
decrease its numerical value \cite{Conway,Gonshor,BagayokoHoeven}.

\begin{lemma}[Fresh separators]\label{swo:cb:lem:fresh}
If $L<R$ are sets of surreals and $S$ is a set, there is
$x\notin S$ with $L<x<R$. In particular, deleting a set from $\No$ leaves
a dense order without endpoints.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If every separator belonged to $S$, the class $I=\{x:L<x<R\}$ would be
a set, by separation from $S$. It is nonempty. Apply set-cut filling to
$L\cup I<R$: every member of $I$ is less than every member of $R$.
A resulting separator belongs to $I$ and exceeds all of $I$, a contradiction.
Thus the interval has a point outside $S$. The same proof allows empty
bounding sides.
\end{proof}

In $\GBC$, a forth construction embeds every ordinary class linear order
in $\No$: enumerate its underlying class by $\Ord$, and at each stage
separate the sets of earlier lower and upper images. A back-and-forth
construction shows uniqueness, up to class order isomorphism, of a proper
class order with this set-cut property. Each stage has a set of earlier
values; these are ordinary set-valued ordinal recursions. This is the
classical universality and absolute-linear-continuum phenomenon
\cite{Ehrlich2012,HamkinsUniversal}. It does not apply to a collection whose
elements are themselves class functions.

% ---- source 16 (batch-81 manuscript 04), lines 277-381
\subsection{Source 16: foundations and surreal order facts}\label{swo:ds:sec:foundations}

\subsubsection{Conventions about sets, classes, and choice}

Here $\GB$ has ZF as its set theory and no choice principle built into its
notation. We write $\GBC=\GB+\GC$; global choice implies ordinary set choice.
The set-sized theorems are proved in ZFC. A \emph{class well-order} is a
strict class linear order for which every available nonempty subclass has
a least element. A relation is \emph{set-like} if each predecessor class is
a set. A proper set-like class well-order is uniquely isomorphic to
$\Ord$: send each point to the ordinal type of its predecessor set.

An individual class function $F:\Ord\to\No$ is legitimate. The notation
``$F\in \Hsl$'' below abbreviates that this class function is a bijection; it
does not make $F$ an element of a GB class. Likewise, a uniform family
$(F_i)_{i\in I}$ means one class of triples $(i,\alpha,x)$ whose rows are
the graphs in question. Its index $I$ may be a set or a class of sets. One
cannot silently choose a class for each set index and assume that the rows
assemble into an available uniform family.

\subsubsection{Sign sequences, small cuts, and bounded stages}

We use the sign presentation
\[
 \No=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Ord}\{-,+\}^\alpha,
\]
with numerical comparison at the first different or missing sign, using
$-<\text{missing}<+$. The birthday $\bd(x)$ is the length of the sign
sequence. Every set of surreals has bounded birthdays, whereas all birthdays
occur. Thus $\No$ is proper. The basic separation property is:
\[
 A,B\text{ sets},\quad A<B
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \exists x\in\No\ (A<x<B),
\tag{S16.1}\label{swo:ds:eq:setcut}
\]
with either side allowed to be empty. These are standard facts about the
surreal order \cite{Conway,Gonshor,BagayokoHoeven}; the corresponding
smallness-sensitive primitives in ProveIt are audited in
\Cref{swo:ds:sec:lean}.

\begin{lemma}[Fresh separators]\label{swo:ds:lem:fresh}
If $A<B$ are sets of surreals and $S$ is any set, some
$x\notin S$ satisfies $A<x<B$. Every nonempty numerical interval is a
proper class. Deleting a set from $\No$ preserves the set-cut property.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
First choose $u,v$ with $A<u<v<B$ by two applications of
\eqref{swo:ds:eq:setcut}. The interval $(u,v)$ cannot be a set: if it were, choose
an element above all of $(u,v)$ but below $v$, a contradiction. Hence the
set $S$ cannot exhaust this interval. Any remaining point works. The same
argument gives the assertions about intervals and deletion.
\end{proof}

For infinite cardinal $\kappa$, put
\[
 \No_{<\kappa}=\{x:\bd(x)<\kappa\},\qquad \mu=2^{<\kappa}.
\]
Then $\No_{<\kappa}$ is a set of size $\mu$. For regular infinite $\kappa$ it is
an $\eta_\kappa$ order: every separated pair of sets with total cardinality
less than $\kappa$ has an interpolant in the same birthday stage. Bound the
option birthdays below $\kappa$ using regularity, and use the usual
birthday-controlled separator. At singular $\kappa$ this argument fails
because a small set can have birthdays cofinal in $\kappa$.

\subsubsection{Which uses of recursion are elementary?}

A recursion producing a set at each ordinal stage, with a set history
before each stage and fixed class parameters, is available in GB. One
constructs each set-length approximation by ordinary recursion and joins
the compatible approximations by elementary comprehension. This applies to
the forth and back-and-forth constructions used below.

By contrast, a recursion whose stages are classes is an instance of
elementary transfinite recursion when its defining formula has only set
quantifiers. Such a recursion may exceed GBC even along $\omega$; truth
recursion is a standard example. ETR supplies abstract class well-order
comparability by initial-segment isomorphisms, but we neither identify
comparability with ETR nor assert a necessity result for our particular
constructions \cite{HamkinsWoodin,GitmanHamkins}. Size of the stage and
history, rather than the mere appearance of the symbol $\Ord$, is decisive.

\begin{proposition}[Universality and uniqueness]\label{swo:ds:prop:universal}
In GBC every class linear order embeds into $\No$. Any two proper class
linear orders satisfying \eqref{swo:ds:eq:setcut} are isomorphic, provided they
have set-like global enumerations. The construction can be made uniform in
set parameters when the carrier and order predicates are uniform.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Enumerate the source by an ordinal or by $\Ord$ using global choice. At
each stage insert its next point between the images of its earlier lower
and upper points. These are sets. For an isomorphism alternate forth and
back steps through fixed global enumerations of the two orders, inserting
the next unused point on the appropriate side at each step. Each partial
map is a set. Choose the least permissible point under fixed global
well-orders to make every stage unique. Its graph is the union of the
set-length approximations. With an extra set parameter carried throughout,
the same defining formula gives a uniform class relation for the whole
parameterized family. This is the classical mechanism of surreal
universality and homogeneity \cite{Ehrlich2012,HamkinsEmbeds}.
\end{proof}

% ---- source 18 (batch-81 manuscript 06), lines 302-390
\subsection{Source 18: surreals as sign sequences}

Represent a surreal number by a function
$s_x:\bd(x)\to\{-,+\}$, where $\bd(x)$ is an ordinal. Numerical order
is comparison at the first unequal sign, counting an absent sign as
strictly between $-$ and $+$. Sign extension is the simplicity relation,
which is a tree order, not a total order. This presentation and its
substructures are developed in the standard surreal literature
\cite{Gonshor,BagayokoHoeven}.

We shall repeatedly use the following elementary consequences.

\begin{lemma}[Surreal order tools]
\label{swo:sh:lem:surreal-tools}
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $L,R$ are sets of surreals and $L<R$, some surreal lies strictly
between them. Either set may be empty.
\item The separator can avoid any prescribed set of forbidden values.
\item For infinite initial $\kappa$, every nonempty open interval of
$\No_{<\kappa}$ contains a sign-prefix cone isomorphic to $\No_{<\kappa}$; hence it
has cardinality $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$.
\item $\No_{<\kappa}$ fills every cut with fewer than $r=\cf\kappa$ input
values. Its cofinality, coinitiality, and both characters at every point
are $r$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For (1), choose an ordinal strictly above all birthdays in $L\cup R$.
Comparison in a sufficiently long full binary level supplies a sign
sequence separating the two sets; equivalently use the usual simplest
surreal cut construction. To get (2), the separator interval contains
a proper class of values: an interval is order-isomorphic to $\No$,
or one can extend a sign prefix by arbitrary ordinal lengths. A set of
forbidden values cannot exhaust it.

For (3), first choose a sufficiently long but still $<\kappa$ prefix
whose whole cone lies inside the given interval. Prefix concatenation
preserves numerical order. If $\beta,\gamma<\kappa$, then
$\beta+\gamma<\kappa$, since this sum still has cardinality below the
initial cardinal $\kappa$. This works at singular cardinals too.
Thus concatenating the chosen prefix with every sign word of length
$<\kappa$ gives the required copy. Counting levels gives
$|\No_{<\kappa}|=\sup_{\alpha<\kappa}2^{|\alpha|}=2^{<\kappa}$.

For (4), fewer than $\cf\kappa$ birthdays are bounded below $\kappa$,
so the construction in (1) stays below $\kappa$. Ordinal labels along a
cofinal sequence in $\kappa$ give a cofinal sequence; their negatives give
a coinitial one. No smaller family is cofinal, since its birthdays are
bounded. At a fixed point, append a negative sign and then arbitrarily
long positive tails to approach from below; use the dual construction
above. These give character at most $r$. The small-cut property gives
the reverse inequality.
\end{proof}

Part (2) is also available in the bounded setting when the forbidden
set has size $<\mu$ and a whole interval of separators is available.
This distinction matters: a used prefix in a minimal permutation can
have length much greater than $\kappa$, but it still uses fewer than
$\mu$ labels.

\subsection{Source 18: set and class theories}

Set-sized results are proved in ZFC. In class arguments, GB denotes
G\"odel--Bernays theory over ZF with elementary class comprehension and
Class Replacement. GBC adds Global Choice. A class is a collection of
sets, never an element of another ordinary class. We regard a class
well-order $R$ as a strict class linear order for which every nonempty
available subclass has an $R$-least element. This definition is internal
to the specified two-sorted model.

A class order is \emph{set-like} if every predecessor class is a set.
A proper set-like class well-order is isomorphic to $\Ord$: map a point
to the ordinal type of its predecessors. The range is an initial
subclass of $\Ord$, and if it were a set, Class Replacement would make
the whole carrier a set. Conversely, an $\Ord$ enumeration is set-like.

All uses of class back-and-forth below choose one new set label at each
ordinal stage. The preceding history at a stage is a set, and the next
choice is determined using a fixed global well-order. This is ordinary
set-valued recursion with class parameters. We do not infer that arbitrary
class-valued recursions follow from GBC. Elementary transfinite recursion
has substantially greater strength in general \cite{GHHSW}.

An expression such as $\Hall$ is initially notation for a domain of
class variables, not a class whose members are class relations. A
uniform family $(R_i)_{i\in I}$ means one class relation
$F(i,x,y)$ with set labels $i,x,y$. A set-indexed family of class
relations is not silently replaced by a set of classes.

% ---- source 17 (batch-81 manuscript 05), lines 325-427
\subsection{Source 17: foundations and direct comparison without a class of classes}
\label{swo:gs:sec:foundations}

\subsubsection{Four safe levels}
Our set theorems use $\ZFC$. Our global theorems use $\GBC$, meaning
G\"odel--Bernays set theory with Global Choice; $\GB$ alone includes no
choice principle. This agrees with the conventions in the source and in
Hamkins's account of Global Choice \cite{HamkinsGC}.

A class well-order here is a linear class relation for which every
nonempty admitted subclass has a least element. Set-likeness is an
additional property, not part of that definition. Which subclasses are
admitted is specified by the surrounding class theory or model.

There are four distinct safe ways to interpret a higher-order-looking
statement. One may work with ordinary sets such as $\WO_\mu(X)$; with an
ordinary class of \emph{set codes} such as $\Psupp(b)$; with finitely many class
variables or a uniform class relation coding a family; or externally in a
larger universe in which the objects from the smaller universe are sets.
None permits forming an unrestricted same-level set or class of all
proper classes.

A uniform family indexed by a class $I$ of sets is a single relation
$F\subseteq I\times\Ord\times\No$, with each row $F_i$ an enumeration.
A uniform transformation of enumerations is a formula which defines an
output class from an input class and for which output existence and
uniqueness are proved. It is not a GB function with proper classes as
arguments stored in its graph.

\subsubsection{The direct common-prefix formula}
For a strict class well-order $R$ let
$P_R(x)=\{y:yRx\}$. Given two class well-orders $R,S$ of the same labelled
carrier $X$, define
\[\tag{S17.2}\label{swo:gs:eq:commonprefix}
 C(R,S)=\{x:P_R(x)=P_S(x)\text{ and }
 R\res P_R(x)=S\res P_S(x)\}.
\]
Equality and restriction here expand to quantifiers over elements of $X$;
no class quantifier is hidden in the defining formula.

\begin{proposition}[Direct labelled comparison; background with proof]
\label{swo:gs:thm:rawcomparison}
The class $C(R,S)$ is the largest common labelled initial segment of $R,S$.
If $R\ne S$, its complement is nonempty and the two least residual labels
$a=\min_R(X\setminus C)$ and $b=\min_S(X\setminus C)$ are different.
Declaring $R<_{\lex}S$ exactly when $a<b$ gives a strict linear comparison
of all admitted class well-orders of $X$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If $x\in C$ and $yRx$, the equality of predecessor classes puts $y$ before
$x$ in both orders; agreement below $x$ then gives equal predecessor
classes and equal predecessor orders for $y$. Thus $y\in C$. The same
argument works with $S$, and proves agreement on $C$. Every common labelled
initial segment satisfies the defining condition, so is contained in $C$.
If $C=X$, the relations agree. Otherwise well-foundedness provides the least
residual elements. If $a=b$, both its predecessor classes are $C$ and the
orders there agree, contradicting $a\notin C$.

For transitivity compare $C(R,S)$ and $C(S,T)$ as initial segments of $S$.
Initial segments of a linear order are comparable by inclusion. If one is
properly shorter, its first disagreement is the first disagreement relevant
to comparing $R,T$, and has the same orientation. If the two prefixes are
equal, the three next labels $a<b<c$ give $a<c$. Trichotomy and asymmetry
are immediate. This is an elementary proof; it does not compare arbitrary
abstract class order types by a recursive isomorphism construction.
\end{proof}

This result is already in the merged report (\cref{swo:cf:lex,swo:st:thm:fulllex}).
Its inclusion is important: it eliminates a false dilemma between restricting
to $\Ord$-enumerations and introducing a stronger class recursion theory
merely to define the comparison.

\subsubsection{Choice, recursion, and external semantics}
Global Choice supplies a baseline bijection $b:\Ord\to\No$. The source
also proves the converse strength statement: existence of any class
well-order of the sign-sequence surreals implies Global Choice over
choiceless $\GB$ (\cref{swo:cf:choice}). That converse is not needed in
our proofs; we explicitly assume $\GBC$ for the global results.

Recursion whose value at each ordinal stage is a set is available with
class parameters in $\GBC$: set recursion constructs compatible histories
on each set ordinal, and elementary comprehension collects them. This is
not the assertion that arbitrary class-valued recursions have solutions.
The latter territory is governed by principles such as $\ETR$, whose
strength is substantially more than elementary comprehension
\cite{GitmanHamkins}. We will reconstruct branches by a uniqueness formula,
so that even the appearance of such a class-valued recursion is avoided.

In a transitive two-sorted model $(M,\mathcal X)$, ``all classes'' means
$\mathcal X$. An external observer may have more subclasses of $M$. With a
strongly inaccessible cardinal $\lambda$ in an ambient universe,
$(V_\lambda,\mathcal P(V_\lambda))$ provides a useful full-class
interpretation. Externally, its set-like surreal enumerations are the
$\lambda$-length permutations of $\No_{<\lambda}$, while its unrestricted
well-orders allow all external ordinal types of cardinality $\lambda$
(\cref{swo:st:thm:model}). This is a conditional model construction,
not an assertion that $\ZFC$ proves an inaccessible cardinal exists.

Finally, neither passing to $\KM$ nor enumerating formula strings gives an
internal universal class decoder. The latter would need a uniform truth
predicate, not merely syntax. \Cref{swo:gs:sec:core} gives an independent
diagonal explanation for the failure of exhaustive same-level coding.

% ---- source 13 (batch-81 manuscript 01), lines 534-623
\subsection{Source 13: direct comparison of unrestricted class well-orders}\label{swo:fs:sec:raw}

The class $\No$ itself is fixed throughout this section. A class
well-order $R$ is a strict linear order for which every nonempty
subclass has an $R$-least member. A set-like class order additionally
has a set of predecessors at every point. The totality $\Hall$ is
notation for the domain of such class parameters, not an ordinary
class whose members are relations.

\subsubsection{The largest common labeled prefix}

The following construction is from the earlier report
(\cref{swo:cf:lex}; Section~14 at the pin); its explicit formula is useful because
it does not demand an enumeration of a non-set-like order by $\Ord$.

\begin{proposition}[Elementary labeled comparison]\label{swo:fs:prop:rawlex}
Two distinct class well-orders $R,S$ of $\No$ have a largest common
labeled initial part $G$. There are distinct labels $r,s$ that are the
respective first points after $G$. Defining
\[
                         R<_{\lex}S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r<s
\]
gives a strict linear comparison on $\Hall$ by an elementary formula
with $R,S$ as class parameters. No class-well-order comparability
principle is required.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Define $G$ to consist of those $x$ such that
$\pred_R(x)=\pred_S(x)$ and the two relations agree on that common
predecessor class. Equality and agreement here abbreviate formulas
quantifying over set elements. They do not form the predecessor
classes as elements of a larger collection.

If $x\in G$, all its predecessors belong to $G$. The restrictions of
$R$ and $S$ to $G$ agree, and any common labeled initial part is contained
in $G$. If $G$ were the whole carrier, the relations would agree.
Otherwise take the least points $r,s$ of the complements in the two
orders. Their predecessor classes are both $G$. They cannot coincide,
since their common value would then be a member of $G$.

Trichotomy follows from numerical trichotomy of $r,s$. For transitivity,
consider $R<S<T$. The common prefixes of $(R,S)$ and $(S,T)$ are both
initial parts of $S$, hence one contains the other. If one is properly
shorter, its first disagreement also decides the comparison of $R,T$.
If they are equal, the three next labels satisfy $r<s<t$, which gives
$R<T$. This proves transitivity without assigning an ordinal length
to a proper-class prefix.
\end{proof}

This is not comparison of abstract class order types by initial-segment
isomorphisms. For that different problem, elementary transfinite
recursion is a known sufficient principle \cite[Theorem 6]{HamkinsWoodin}.
Our formula compares identical labels on one carrier, rather than
constructing an isomorphism between unrelated carriers.

\subsubsection{The ordinal head and the residual fiber}

\begin{proposition}[Canonical head; prior structural lemma]\label{swo:fs:prop:head}
For $R\in\Hall$, the points with a set of $R$-predecessors form a
proper-class initial part $H_R$, uniquely enumerated by a class injection
\[
                             F_R:\Ord\longrightarrow\No.
\]
Conversely, for every injective class word $F:\Ord\to\No$, appending
any class well-order of $Y=\No\setminus\ran(F)$ produces a raw order
whose head is $F$. All raw orders with this head form a convex fiber,
with their internal comparison equal to the labeled lexicographic
comparison of well-orders of $Y$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$H_R$ is initial. Were it a set, the least point outside it would have
exactly $H_R$ as its predecessor class and would belong to it, a
contradiction. Ranking each point by the ordinal type of its set of
predecessors gives the unique enumeration: its ranks form a proper
initial subclass of $\Ord$ only if they are a set, so they are all of
$\Ord$.

After an $\Ord$-head is listed, every residual point has a proper class
of predecessors, whereas each head point has a set of predecessors.
This proves the converse. Distinct heads disagree at a set ordinal,
and that disagreement places one entire fiber below the other. Equal
heads leave only the tail comparison, proving convexity. A well-order
on $Y$ is available from global choice, also when $Y$ is proper.
\end{proof}

This is the earlier report's decomposition (\cref{swo:cf:core,swo:cf:fibers};
Section~15 at the pin).
We shall identify exactly which cuts of a fixed dense core these fibers
represent, thereby supplying an additional characterization not contained
in the decomposition alone.

% ---- source 15 (batch-81 manuscript 03), lines 366-489
\subsection{Source 15: native lexicography on class well-orders}\label{swo:cb:sec:classlex}

\subsubsection{Existence, set-likeness, and the first proper block}

A class relation $R$ on $\No$ is \emph{set-like} when
$\pred_R(x)=\{y:yRx\}$ is a set for every $x$. An already-given
set-like class well-order of a proper class has a unique order isomorphism
with $\Ord$: assign to each point the ordinal type of its predecessor
set. The image is initial in $\Ord$ and cannot be a set, since the
inverse map would make the whole carrier a set. This collapse needs GB,
not a separate global choice assumption \cite{HamkinsGC}.

Existence is different. Over GB, the existence of any class well-order of
$\No$, even a non-set-like one, is equivalent to global choice
(\cref{swo:cf:choice}; Theorem~13.1 at the pin). One direction restricts a set-like global
well-order of the universe. For the other, a well-order of $\No$ orders
the sign codes for every $\mathcal P(\alpha)$. Starting with an ordinal
enumeration of a rank stage, transport this order to its power set;
at limits combine the already constructed orders by rank. This set-valued
ordinal recursion produces well-orders of all rank stages and hence a
global well-order. This explains why merely assuming a convenient global
baseline already carries substantive choice information.

An arbitrary class well-order can have type $\Ord+1$, $\Ord+\Ord$, or
much more complicated class types. The final element of an $\Ord+1$
order has a proper class of predecessors. It is still an ordinary
surreal label; the new size occurs in its position in the chosen order.

\subsubsection{A first disagreement after a proper class of agreement}

If $R,S$ are class well-orders of the same labelled carrier $X$, put
$\pred_R(x)=\{y\in X:yRx\}$. A common labelled prefix is initial in
both orders and carries the same restricted relation. The comparison
below is the prior report's elementary construction
(\cref{swo:cf:lex}; Section~14 at the pin); we include its proof because it makes the
foundational advantage precise.

\begin{theorem}[First unequal labels without class ordinals]\label{swo:cb:thm:rawlex}
If $R\ne S$, there are unique distinct $a,b$ such that
\[
 \pred_R(a)=\pred_S(b)=C,
 \qquad R\res C=S\res C.
\]
The class $C$ is their maximal common labelled prefix. If the labels
carry a fixed linear order $<$, declaring $R<_{\lex}S$ when $a<b$
defines a strict linear comparison on the class-well-order predicate.
Its formula has only set quantifiers with $R,S$ as class parameters.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $a$ be the $R$-least point whose predecessor classes in $R$ and $S$
differ, and put $C=\pred_R(a)$. For $y\in C$, these predecessor
classes agree. Such $y$ must also precede $a$ in $S$: otherwise $aSy$
would imply $aRy$. If $zSy$ for $y\in C$, agreement of predecessor
classes gives $zRy$, so $C$ is also $S$-initial. The restricted orders
agree, and $C\subsetneq\pred_S(a)$. Let $b$ be the $S$-least point
outside $C$. Then $bSa$, $b\ne a$, and $\pred_S(b)=C$.
Any other first-disagreement pair must have its first member equal to
the $R$-least point with changed predecessors, proving uniqueness.

For transitivity, suppose $R<S<T$. Their two common prefixes with the
middle order $S$ are initial segments of that same order, hence comparable.
If one is shorter, its first difference also decides $R$ versus $T$;
if they are equal, the next labels satisfy $a<b<c$, which decides the
comparison. Totality and asymmetry follow from unique first disagreement.
Finally the formula can be written directly as
\[
 \exists a,b\ \bigl[a<b\ \land\ \forall z(zRa\leftrightarrow zSb)
 \ \land\ \forall u,v((uRa\land vRa)\Rightarrow(uRv\leftrightarrow uSv))\bigr].
\]
No quantification over a collection of prefix classes is required.
\end{proof}

For example, enumerate $\No\setminus\{a,b\}$ in type $\Ord$, where
$a<b$, and append either $a,b$ or $b,a$. Their first unequal labels occur
after every ordinal stage of the common enumeration. The displayed formula
still compares them. It is not necessary to invent a set ordinal
``beyond $\Ord$'' to name their first difference.

For one given class index order $J$, bijections $J\to\No$ may instead
be compared at the $J$-least unequal coordinate. This agrees with the raw
comparison, but restricts the allowed order type. Two different index
orders should be compared through the induced labelled relations unless
an explicit alignment has been supplied.

\begin{proposition}[Prefix convexity and initial-word fibres]\label{swo:cb:prop:fibres}
In $\GBC$, orders extending a common labelled prefix form a convex family. For an
arbitrary class well-order $R$ of $\No$, let
\[
 I_R=\{x:\pred_R(x)\text{ is a set}\},
 \qquad F_R:\Ord\longrightarrow I_R
\]
be its unique increasing enumeration. Then $I_R$ is a proper class.
Every injective class word $F:\Ord\to\No$ occurs as $F_R$, and its
fibre is a convex copy of the well-order space of
$Y_F=\No\setminus\ran(F)$. Distinct fibres compare at the first
unequal coordinate of their words.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A comparison that first diverges inside a common prefix puts the competing
order on the same side of every extension, proving convexity. The class
$I_R$ is initial and set-like. If it were a set, the least point outside
it would have precisely $I_R$ as its predecessors, a contradiction.
Its enumeration is therefore by all ordinals.

Given $F$, order its range by its ordinal indices and append any fixed
well-order of $Y_F$. Every point of the range has set predecessors, and
every residual point has the proper range of $F$ among its predecessors.
Thus the resulting initial word is exactly $F$. Restriction to $Y_F$ and
concatenation with $F$ give inverse order-preserving maps on the fibre.
For unequal words, first ordinal difference precedes both residual tails.
\end{proof}

If $F$ omits $m$ labels, its fibre has $m!$ elements. An exhaustive word
and a word omitting just one label both have singleton fibres; only the
first is set-like. The unrestricted space has adjacent finite residual
permutation blocks, whereas the set-like space is dense and has no
endpoints. These distinctions are already established in the prior report.

% ---- source 16 (batch-81 manuscript 04), lines 1064-1173
\subsection{Source 16: global choice and direct comparison of arbitrary class well-orders}\label{swo:ds:sec:raw}

Write $\Hsl$ for the predicate of class bijections $\Ord\to\No$, and
$\Hall$ for that of all class well-order relations on $\No$. These are
notations for assertions about class variables. We will also use $\Jinj$
for class injections $\Ord\to\No$, allowing nonexhaustive ranges.

\begin{proposition}[Existence has a precise choice strength]\label{swo:ds:prop:gc}
Over GB, the following are equivalent: global choice; a class bijection
$\Ord\to\No$; a set-like class well-order of $\No$; and an arbitrary
class well-order of $\No$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Global choice gives a set-like global well-order of the universe. Its
restriction to the proper class $\No$ has order type $\Ord$, yielding
the bijection. A bijection induces a set-like well-order, which is an
arbitrary class well-order as well.

For the reverse implication suppose $R$ well-orders $\No$. Every
$\mathcal P(\delta)$ injects into $\No$ by sign sequences of length
$\delta$, so $R$ gives it a well-order. One can now well-order the
hierarchy $V_\beta$ uniformly by set-valued recursion, starting with
$w_0=\varnothing$. At a successor, use the existing well-order
$w_\beta$ of $V_\beta$ to identify it with an ordinal
$\delta$, transfer subsets to $\mathcal P(\delta)$, and use the
restriction of $R$ on their sign codes. At a nonzero limit $\lambda$,
order the disjoint rank layers by their ranks, using
$w_{\gamma+1}\res(V_{\gamma+1}\setminus V_\gamma)$ on layer $\gamma$,
where $\gamma+1<\lambda$. Each history is a set; no choice of an unspecified family
of well-orders is used. Finally order all sets first by rank and then
by the resulting well-order on that rank layer. This is a set-like
global well-order of the universe and supplies global choice. This
expands the choice-equivalence argument recorded in the prior report
(\cref{swo:cf:choice}).
\end{proof}

For distinct $F,G\in \Jinj$, their first unequal ordinal coordinate exists:
minimize the disagreement class below any one witness. Compare
$F(\delta)$ and $G(\delta)$ numerically. This is a total, transitive
lexicographic comparison. For general $R,S\in \Hall$, however, a first
disagreement may occur after a proper class of common labels.

\begin{lemma}[A common labelled prefix without class ordinals]
\label{swo:ds:lem:rawprefix}
