\section{Coding, diagonalization, and a sharper comprehension bound (source 16; source 14)}
\label{swo:ds:sec:coding}

\subsection{Binary class words and representable suborders}

Let $\BB_{\Ord}$ denote binary class functions on $\Ord$, with
first-disagreement comparison. In the sense of uniform transformations,
\[
 \Hsl\equi \Jinj\equi\BB_{\Ord}.
\tag{S16.15}\label{swo:ds:eq:binaryclass}
\]
For one direction, partition the baseline values into ordinal-indexed
pairs and list each pair increasingly or decreasingly according to the
input bit. Here the coordinate pairs are
$\{2\cdot\xi,2\cdot\xi+1\}$, with ordinal multiplication. This
embeds all binary classes into exhaustive enumerations.
For the other, globally enumerate the set codes of $\Pbd(b)$ as
$(q_\xi)_{\xi\in\Ord}$ and send $F\in \Jinj$ to
\[
 D_F=\{\xi:E_{q_\xi}<F\}.
\]
If $F<G$, density gives a core point strictly between them. Thus
$D_F\subsetneq D_G$, whose characteristic words have the same first
difference direction. Inclusion $\Hsl\subseteq \Jinj$ finishes
\eqref{swo:ds:eq:binaryclass}. This extends the earlier report's coding
argument to the injective comparison as well.

Equimorphism is not isomorphism. Binary class words have least and
greatest words and adjacent pairs, while $\Hsl$ and $\Jinj$ are dense and
have no endpoints. Likewise, any one injectively and uniformly indexed
class family in $\Hsl$ is an ordinary class linear order on its indices,
and hence embeds into $\No$ in GBC. This does not supply an embedding
of the entire virtual collection of global enumerations into $\No$.
There is no exhaustive uniform family at the same level.

\begin{theorem}[No exhaustive uniform class of set codes]\label{swo:ds:thm:diagonal}
In GBC, no class of set indices with one uniform evaluation relation
contains every class well-order of $\No$ among its rows. In fact a
set-like well-order is missing from every such family.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use global choice to reindex the rows by $\Ord$, repeating a default
row if the original family was a nonempty set. For each ordinal
$\xi$, sort the two labels $b(2\cdot\xi),b(2\cdot\xi+1)$ as
$a_\xi<c_\xi$. Define a new enumeration by keeping the pair blocks
in ordinal order. Within pair $\xi$, place $c_\xi$ before $a_\xi$ if
$(a_\xi,c_\xi)$ belongs to relation row $\xi$, and otherwise place
$a_\xi$ before $c_\xi$. This local rule is elementary even for empty
or malformed rows. The new enumeration is exhaustive and set-like;
it differs from every well-order row $\xi$ on that pair. The empty-family
case is immediate.
\end{proof}

Formula strings do not evade this theorem. Each fixed formula defines
its own class when comprehension applies, but uniformly evaluating all
formulas over the entire universe would require a suitable truth
predicate. Neither a metatheoretic list of formulas nor a proper class
of their finite syntactic codes supplies such an evaluator.

\subsection{A sufficient bound below full Kelley--Morse}

The prior report proves in KM plus global choice that no fixed
definable total transformation from $\Hall$ to $\Hsl$ is an order
embedding, allowing arbitrary formulas defining the transformation.
For elementary formulas the following sharper sufficient bound holds.

\begin{theorem}[Elementary transformations and $\Sigma^1_1$ comprehension]
\label{swo:ds:thm:sigma}
Work in $\GBC+\Sigma^1_1\text{-}\mathsf{CA}$. Let
$\vartheta(R,E)$ be a fixed formula with only set quantifiers, with
fixed set and class parameters allowed. Suppose it specifies a unique
class output $E\in \Hsl$ for every $R\in \Hall$. The specified
transformation is not an order embedding.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Assume an embedding is specified. Fix numerical labels $a<c$. For
each class bijection $F:\Ord\to\No\setminus\{a,c\}$ form
\[
 R_F=F+(a,c),\qquad S_F=F+(c,a).
\]
These are adjacent raw orders, and different $F$ give disjoint,
ordered pairs. Their alleged images $E_0<E_1$ have a bounded-support
code between them. Let $q_F$ be the least such code in a fixed global
well-order of $\Pbd(b)$. The image intervals are disjoint, so
$q_F=q_G$ implies $F=G$.

The required inverse-evaluation predicate has precisely the form
\[
\begin{split}
 \operatorname{Eval}(q,\xi,x)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
 \exists F\,\exists E_0\,\exists E_1\,[\,
 &\operatorname{Bij}(F)\land\vartheta(R_F,E_0)\land\vartheta(S_F,E_1)\\
 &\land\operatorname{LeastBetween}(q,E_0,E_1)
       \land F(\xi)=x\,].
\end{split}
\tag{S16.16}\label{swo:ds:eq:inverseeval}
\]
The three displayed existential variables range over classes; the
matrix has only set quantifiers. The constructed raw orders can be
substituted directly into the elementary formula $\vartheta$, and
``least code between'' quantifies only over set codes. Thus
$\Sigma^1_1$ class comprehension forms this evaluator.

Its rows are empty or unique bijection graphs, and every such $F$
occurs as a row. Compose each nonempty row with a fixed bijection
$\No\setminus\{a,c\}\to\No$, and fill empty rows with a default.
This is an exhaustive uniformly class-indexed family of global
enumerations. Replace each bijection row by its induced well-order
relation, an elementary conversion, and apply
\Cref{swo:ds:thm:diagonal} to obtain the contradiction.
\end{proof}

This proves a sufficient comprehension bound, not a reversal. It does
not show that $\Sigma^1_1$ comprehension is necessary, nor that the
same proof works for arbitrary $\vartheta$ with unrestricted class
quantifier alternations. The syntax of the claimed transformation is
part of the theorem. The distinction between elementary and impredicative
class definitions is consistent with the known hierarchy around ETR and
KM \cite{HamkinsWoodin,GitmanHamkins,GHHSW}.

% ---- source 14 (batch-81 manuscript 02), lines 1465-1515
\subsection{Source 14: binary class words and global permutations}
A characteristic function $d:\Ord\to\{0,1\}$ can be turned into a
global enumeration by pair orientations. Partition the ordinals into
pairs $2\cdot\alpha,2\cdot\alpha+1$; ordinal multiplication has $2$
on the left. Sort the corresponding baseline labels as $u_\alpha<v_\alpha$.
Put the pair in order $(u_\alpha,v_\alpha)$ when $d(\alpha)=0$ and
$(v_\alpha,u_\alpha)$ when $d(\alpha)=1$. Every baseline label is
used exactly once. The first differing bit produces the first differing
pair in the correct lexical direction.

Conversely, enumerate the core codes by a fixed class bijection
$\Ord\to \Psupp(b)$. The characteristic function of $D_E$ in this
schedule is an order embedding of $\Hsl$ into binary class words:
if $E<F$, then $D_E\subsetneq D_F$ by core density, and the first
changed bit is $0$ versus $1$. Thus the known equimorphism
\[
 \Hsl\equim(\{0,1\}^{\Ord},<_{\rm lex})
\]
is entirely uniform. It is not an isomorphism. The binary class-word
order has endpoints and adjacent pairs of the form
$p\cat(0)\cat(1,1,\ldots)$ and
$p\cat(1)\cat(0,0,\ldots)$; $\Hsl$ is dense without endpoints.
These are class-word constructions, not sets of every binary class.

\begin{theorem}[No exhaustive uniform class of codes, inherited]
\label{swo:tc:thm:nocoding}
There is no uniformly $\Ord$-indexed family containing every member of
$\Hsl$. More generally no ordinary class of set codes, with one uniform
evaluation relation, exhausts all global enumerations.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose $(E_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Ord}$ were such a family. In the
pair at $2\cdot\alpha,2\cdot\alpha+1$, choose the orientation whose
first entry differs from $E_\alpha(2\cdot\alpha)$. At least one of
the two orientations works, since the pair labels are distinct.
The resulting class function is a bijection, as it only reorders
disjoint baseline pairs, and it differs from every row $E_\alpha$ at
the designated coordinate. This is an elementary diagonal construction.

An ordinary proper class of set codes admits a set-like global
enumeration in $\GBC$; a set of codes can be padded to an
$\Ord$-indexed family. Either kind of exhaustive uniform evaluation
would therefore contradict the first assertion. This is the
predecessor's diagonal obstruction in an explicit pair form.
\end{proof}

A skeleton is therefore a dense \emph{test family}, not a list of all
objects. The new cut recognition theorem explains what extra information
a class cut of that test family can encode; it does not defeat the
diagonal theorem by relabelling cuts as sets.

\begin{note}[\merge; repetitions, and the new comprehension bound]\label{swo:ix:note:coding}
The binary-class equimorphism \eqref{swo:ds:eq:binaryclass} and source~14's
display are source~11's \cref{swo:gl:binary} (with source~08's
\cref{swo:sk:thm:binaryclass} and source~12's \cref{swo:st:thm:binaryclass});
source~16 adds the injective words $\Jinj$ between the two ends, by the same
core-density argument. The diagonal theorems \cref{swo:ds:thm:diagonal},
\cref{swo:tc:thm:nocoding} and source~15's \cref{swo:cb:thm:diagonal} (printed
with source~15's foundations in \cref{swo:ix:sec:universes}) are source~11's
\cref{swo:gl:diagonal} and source~12's \cref{swo:st:thm:diagonal}, as are
source~13's \cref{swo:fs:thm:diagonal}, source~17's \cref{swo:gs:thm:diagonal}
and source~18's \cref{swo:sh:thm:noncoding} printed in Part~VIII; all credit
this report. New is source~16's \cref{swo:ds:thm:sigma}: for transformations
defined by a formula with only set quantifiers, $\GBC$ with $\Sigma^1_1$ class
comprehension suffices to refute an order embedding of $\Hall$ into $\Hsl$,
where source~11's \cref{swo:thm:km-nonembedding} used $\KM+\GC$ and arbitrary
formulas. It is a sufficiency result; source~16 asks for the reversal
(\cref{swo:ds:n16.6}). Its proof uses the adjacent raw pairs only through the
disjointness of their image intervals; with the pairs $(E,0)<(E,1)$ of

formed, which bears on source~13's \cref{swo:fs:n15.5}. (This adaptation is an
observation of the merge, not a theorem of either source.)

\subsection{Source 16: an explicit larger-universe interpretation}\label{swo:ds:sec:models}

To treat the entire collections as actual sets, choose an ambient
ZFC universe and assume that $\kappa$ is strongly inaccessible. Consider
the two-sorted structure
\[
 \mathcal M=(V_\kappa,\mathcal P(V_\kappa)).
\]
Its sets are the elements of $V_\kappa$, and its available classes are
\emph{all} external subsets of $V_\kappa$. It satisfies KM plus global
choice. Inaccessibility controls replacement: the image of an internal
set under any available class function has size less than $\kappa$ and
bounded rank. Full class comprehension is immediate from the external
power set. Such full models are a standard way to make the next logical
level explicit \cite{AntosFriedman}.

\begin{theorem}[Exact external identification]\label{swo:ds:thm:fullmodel}
In this full model the internal surreal class is externally
$X=\No_{<\kappa}$, of cardinality $\kappa$. Internally set-like
well-orders are exactly the externally well-ordered relations of type
$\kappa$ on $X$. All internal class well-orders correspond exactly to
the full external set $\WO(X)$. Thus the two comparisons become
\[
 {\Hsl}^{\mathcal M}=\WO_\kappa(X),\qquad
 {\Hall}^{\mathcal M}=\WO(X).
\tag{S16.17}\label{swo:ds:eq:external}
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
All sign sequences of length below $\kappa$ belong to $V_\kappa$,
and these are exactly the internal sign sequences. Strong
inaccessibility gives $|X|=2^{<\kappa}=\kappa$. Every external binary
relation on $X$ is an available internal class. Well-foundedness agrees
in this full interpretation; in particular any external descending
$\omega$-sequence has bounded rank below $\kappa$ and is an internal
set witnessing failure.

A subset of $X$ is an internal set exactly when it has external size
less than $\kappa$. One direction follows from the strong-limit
property of $V_\kappa$; the other follows from regularity bounding the
ranks of fewer than $\kappa$ elements. Consequently an external
well-order of cardinality $\kappa$ is internally set-like exactly
when all its proper initial segments have cardinality less than
$\kappa$, which is exactly external order type $\kappa$.
All other external well-orders are still admitted classes, yielding
the unrestricted identification.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Strict embedding separation in the full model]
\label{swo:ds:thm:externalnonembedding}
In the preceding external interpretation,
\[
 {\Hsl}^{\mathcal M}\emb {\Hall}^{\mathcal M},\qquad
 {\Hall}^{\mathcal M}\not\emb {\Hsl}^{\mathcal M}.
\]
Indeed even $\WO_{\kappa+2}(X)$ does not embed into
$\WO_\kappa(X)$, although both have density and cellularity $\kappa$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Inclusion gives the forward embedding. The target
$\WO_\kappa(X)$ is dense and has a dense subset of size $\kappa$.
For fixed $a<c$ there are $2^\kappa$ prefixes
$F:\kappa\to X\setminus\{a,c\}$. Their two completions
$F+(a,c)<F+(c,a)$ are disjoint adjacent pairs in
$\WO_{\kappa+2}(X)$. An order embedding into the dense target would
turn these pairs into $2^\kappa$ disjoint nonempty open intervals.
Each interval must meet the $\kappa$-sized dense subset, contradicting
Cantor's theorem.
\end{proof}

This rederives the earlier report's full-model nonembedding, while
identifying why equal cardinality, ordinal spectra, density, and
cellularity can still fail to imply equimorphism. The adjacent pairs
provide an additional obstruction when the target is dense.

\subsubsection{Henkin models and internal well-foundedness}

For a general model $(M,\mathcal C)$, one has only the admitted
classes $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal P(M)$, not automatically every
external subset. External families of these classes need not be coded
by any one internal family relation. If the model is externally
countable, both virtual collections can be externally countable, and
the external dense set-like order can admit an external copy of the
raw order. Such an embedding need not be internally definable or
uniformly represented, and so does not contradict
\Cref{swo:ds:thm:sigma} or the internal diagonal theorem.

There is also a precise correction to a common ambiguity. Over GBC,
for a fixed class relation, well-foundedness on nonempty sets,
well-foundedness on all available nonempty subclasses, and absence of
a set-coded descending $\omega$-sequence are equivalent. Therefore
two class expansions with the same sets agree about internal
well-foundedness of any relation they share. Expanding the class
collection can add relations; it does not change that property of a
shared relation. Nevertheless, even a transitive class model can
contain a relation it regards as well-founded that is externally
ill-founded; one must distinguish a general model from a
$\beta$-model \cite[\S3]{HamkinsWoodin}.

The full inaccessible model removes this ambiguity by its explicit
fullness and rank closure. A singular birthday cutoff is a legitimate
set alphabet for \Cref{swo:ds:sec:setbaseline}; it is not an automatic
replacement for $V_\kappa$ in this model-theoretic construction.

% ---- source 14 (batch-81 manuscript 02), lines 1545-1645
\subsection{Source 14: universe-relative models and paradox avoidance}
\label{swo:tc:sec:models}
\subsubsection{A full-class model with externally set-sized objects}
For a concrete interpretation, assume in an external set universe a
strongly inaccessible cardinal $\Omega$ and consider
\[
 (V_\Omega,\mathcal P(V_\Omega)).
\]
Internally the ordinal and surreal collections are proper classes;
externally they are the sets $\Omega$ and $X=\No_{<\Omega}$.
Strong inaccessibility gives $|X|=\Omega$. A baseline is externally a
bijection $b:\Omega\to X$. The core consists of permutations with
support of size $<\Omega$, equivalently bounded support in $\Omega$,
and has external cardinality $\Omega$. The external global-enumeration
order is
\[
 \Bij(\Omega,X),\qquad |\Bij(\Omega,X)|=2^\Omega.
\]
These are the predecessor's full-model calculations
(\cref{swo:thm:universe-nonembedding,swo:st:thm:model,swo:ec:thm:inaccessible};
the universe-model sections at the pin). The lower bound for the
second cardinality is pair orientation; the upper bound counts graphs.
For the core, each bounded stage has fewer than $\Omega$ permutations
by the strong-limit property, while first-entry transpositions supply
$\Omega$ distinct codes.

Internally ``every set cut'' means externally cuts with fewer than
$\Omega$ parameters. Thus the core and $X$ are externally
$\Omega$-sized $\eta_\Omega$-orders. The full enumeration order has
strictly more points while the core remains dense in it. This is an
ordinary set-theoretic example of a dense order and a larger order of
its selected cuts; no paradox occurs.

The new trichotomy becomes an external classification of cuts using
prefixes of length $<\Omega$. A branch extending through all internal
ordinals has external length $\Omega$. It is not an internally set
prefix to which one may apply a small-cut theorem. The coverage
condition is precisely surjectivity onto $X$.

All external well-orders on $X$ also allow order types
$\alpha$ with $\Omega<\alpha<\Omega^+$. They correspond to internal
non-set-like orders, not to additional bijections $\Omega\to X$.
Consequently ``increase the universe so everything is a set'' does not
license replacing one interpretation by another without recording the
allowed ordinal lengths.

\subsubsection{ZFC schemes, GBC, KM, and higher sorts}
In ordinary $\ZFC$, sign sequences and their set-sized fragments can be
handled directly; global statements can be treated as schemes for
specified definable class parameters. A definable baseline must be
supplied where needed. Formula codes alone do not solve the uniformity
problem: evaluating every possible class definition in the whole universe
requires truth resources not furnished by a list of formulas.

In two-sorted $\GBC$, the class parameters and set-coded skeleton are
literal objects of their respective sorts. The classification theorem
has the form ``for every class cut $D$, one of the stated alternatives
holds.'' It is not a third-sort object containing all those cuts.
Stronger comprehension in $\KM$ does not change the rule that proper
classes cannot be members of ordinary classes. A literal collection of
class orders or cuts requires a specified additional sort or an external
universe. Relative consistency assumptions for any such enlargement
must be stated separately.

In a universe-polymorphic type theory, one can form a type of relations
on a fixed small carrier. A larger-universe type can hold all such
relations without identifying it with the original carrier. Lifting a
carrier changes its ambient type level, not its mathematical elements;
constructing surreals with larger allowed ordinal birthdays adds new
elements. These are different operations. A proof assistant should not
hide the distinction under coercions or ambiguous names.

\subsubsection{Which assertions depend on the class realization?}
Changing the available classes while retaining the same sets leaves
each existing support code and each existing prefix unchanged. It can
add new global enumerations, binary class words, and cut classes.
\Cref{swo:tc:thm:absolute} is a more precise invariant than merely
saying that first disagreements are unchanged: it prohibits a new
enumeration from realizing an \emph{old} cut. At the same time the
external cardinality and order type of the entire admitted enumeration
collection can change. The results are compatible, because a new
point brings a new trace parameter.

For unrestricted orders, having an initial branch reconstructible from
an old trace does not similarly force an arbitrary new \emph{tail}
to be old. The trace deliberately forgets that tail. This illustrates why
one must not generalize the absoluteness theorem from set-like
realizations to uniqueness of raw realizations.

\subsubsection{A short paradox audit}
There is no set ordinal containing all ordinals, no surreal whose sign
sequence has domain $\Ord$, and no application here of the surreal
cut constructor to arbitrary proper-class option sets. All recursive
histories used for the main constructions at a set stage are sets.
Class predicates such as ``is a global enumeration'' are never turned
into same-sort membership objects. Equal abstract class types are not
silently represented by a canonical set ordinal. The baseline choice
is explicit. Finally, class-model absoluteness is proved from formulas
with the stated old parameters, not assumed for all higher-order
properties. These restrictions are what allow the positive theorems,
rather than obstacles to developing the subject.

% ---- source 13 (batch-81 manuscript 01), lines 1541-1660
\subsection{Source 13: foundational interpretations without paradoxes}\label{swo:fs:sec:foundations}

\subsubsection{Ordinary set theory: the cutoff-first route}

For any set ordinal $\theta$, the sign sequences of birthday below
$\theta$ form a set. Relations on this set form another set, and the
subset satisfying well-order axioms is available by separation. All
fixed-carrier order theory therefore lives in ordinary $\ZFC$; no
inaccessible cardinal or extra class sort is needed.

When a proof uses a family of all birthday cutoffs, the family is a
class description rather than a set containing the entire surreal
line. A compatible directed system requires explicitly commuting
transition maps. Merely proving existence of an embedding at each
cutoff does not make the union of independently chosen maps a function.

For set-length words, a word is itself a set of ordered pairs. The
class of all such words is a legitimate class of sets. It is not the
same logical object as the totality of class-length words.

\subsubsection{Two-sorted class theory: quantify, do not collect}

In $\GB$ or $\GBC$, class variables can stand for relations on
$\No$. One may assert
\[
 \forall R\,\forall S\,
 [\operatorname{ClassWO}(R)\wedge\operatorname{ClassWO}(S)
   \ \Longrightarrow\ R=S\vee R<_{\lex}S\vee S<_{\lex}R].
\]
There is no need to form an object whose members are $R$ and $S$.
The fraktur notations $\Hsl,\Jinj,\Hall$ used here abbreviate precisely
such restricted class quantification.

A family indexed by an ordinary class $K$ of sets is supplied by one
class relation $T(k,\alpha,x)$. First-disagreement comparison of two
rows is elementary in $T$. If repeated rows occur, a fixed set-like
global well-order selects the least set code in each equal-row class;
row equality itself quantifies only over set coordinates and values.
The distinct-row representatives then form an ordinary class linear
order, which embeds into $\No$.

This explains how every uniformly class-coded portion of $\Hsl$ can
embed into $\No$ while an exhaustive uniform code family is impossible.
The local statement is about a particular class evaluator. It does
not quantify a class of all evaluators or identify all class functions
with their set codes.

\subsubsection{The exact comprehension boundary of the new proofs}

The crossing predicate
\[
 \operatorname{Cross}(L,p)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
 (\exists d\in \Psupp(b)_p\ d\in L)\wedge
 (\exists d\in \Psupp(b)_p\ d\notin L)
\]
quantifies over set codes. ``For every ordinal length a crossing
prefix exists'' is therefore elementary with $L$ as a class parameter.
The uniqueness lemma makes $F(\alpha)=p_{\alpha+1}(\alpha)$ an
elementary class definition. This is the reason cut reconstruction
does not need $\ETR$ or impredicative comprehension.

The uniform complement isomorphisms, support completions, and active
prefixes similarly use set histories. In contrast, the inverse evaluator
in \Cref{swo:fs:thm:kmsplit} asks whether \emph{some class
enumeration} produced a specified code. That is a genuine existential
class quantifier in a class comprehension formula. The proof uses
$\KM$ at exactly this point.

General elementary transfinite recursion allows class-valued stages
along a class well-order. It is distinct from the set-valued recursion
used above. Its relevance to abstract class-well-order comparison is
discussed in \cite{HamkinsWoodin}; none of our direct labeled
comparison arguments relies on the stronger comparison theorem.

\subsubsection{Kelley--Morse does not turn classes into members}

$\KM$ permits class quantifiers in comprehension formulas, but its
classes still have sets as members. Thus even $\KM$ does not justify
an ordinary power class whose elements are all class well-orders of
$\No$. A third sort, a containing universe, or a fixed syntactic
schema is necessary for arbitrary maps, topologies, or families whose
elements are such classes.

Hyperclass forcing is an example of work that explicitly addresses
this higher level, with additional model and coding hypotheses
\cite{AntosFriedman}. Its existence as a theory should not be read as
permission to suppress the level distinction in an argument stated
only over $\GB$ or $\KM$.

\subsubsection{Full universes versus selected class realizations}

The full interpretation $(V_\kappa,\mathcal P(V_\kappa))$ at a
strongly inaccessible $\kappa$ is a convenient sufficient model for
our external cardinal arguments. The available internal surreals are
externally the set $\No_{<\kappa}$, and internal set-like enumerations
have external length $\kappa$. A raw well-order may have any external
ordinal type of cardinality $\kappa$; types beyond $\kappa$ create
proper-class predecessor segments internally.

For a nonfull model $(M,\mathcal C)$, only classes in $\mathcal C$
are available. Changing $\mathcal C$ can change the available
branches, global enumerations, cuts, and external maps without changing
the underlying set universe. The cut theorem remains an internal
statement about the cuts actually present. If an outer class realization
adds a normalized cut satisfying the crossing criterion, its unique
branch becomes available there by elementary comprehension from that
cut. Thus missing classes, not merely missing set elements, are part
of the geometry.

Internal well-foundedness must also be kept separate from external
well-foundedness. Over the relevant global-choice class theories,
class well-foundedness can be tested by the absence of a set-coded
descending $\omega$-sequence; an external descending sequence need not
be so coded in the model \cite[Section 3]{HamkinsWoodin}. This is why
an arbitrary internally well-ordered class is not automatically a
well-order in a surrounding metatheory. Our full inaccessible model
avoids that particular ambiguity, while
\Cref{swo:fs:prop:countable} deliberately studies an external
order of available objects.

\merge\ Source~13's subsection ``Relation-bit lexicography is a different
order'' comes here in its text; it is printed in \cref{swo:cb:sec:alternatives}.

% ---- source 13 (batch-81 manuscript 01), lines 1679-1691
\subsubsection{A concise list of invalid inferences}

The most tempting false steps are logically different. A proper-class
ordinal word is not a surreal; a predicate on surreals is not necessarily
a small set; a set of individual class witnesses is not automatically
a uniform family; a class well-order need not be set-like; an order
embedding need not preserve suprema, cuts, or adjacency; and equal
cardinality, equimorphism, and isomorphism are three distinct claims.
Finally, the isomorphism type of an external available-object order
need not describe the internally definable transformations on that
order. Each of the main theorems above uses at least one of these
distinctions essentially.

% ---- source 15 (batch-81 manuscript 03), lines 2176-2296
\subsection{Source 15: formalization without paradoxes}\label{swo:cb:sec:foundations}

\subsubsection{Four sound frameworks and their different meanings}

\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.20\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.36\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.36\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule Framework & What it directly represents & Important boundary\\\midrule\endhead
ZFC, fixed sets & Relations on a set $X$, all ordinal enumeration types, binary cubes, birthday cutoffs & No set of all surreals; a definable-class claim is a scheme or a formula.\\
Two-sorted GB/GBC & Individual class orders, uniform families, elementary raw comparison and set-interval condensation & Classes contain sets, not other proper classes.\\
KM and recursion extensions & Stronger class comprehension; appropriate class-valued recursions & Stronger comprehension does not add a third sort automatically.\\
Containing universe or stratified types & A lower universe's classes become higher-universe objects & Size and well-foundedness are relative; lifting does not identify all levels.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

\subsubsection{Why Burali--Forti and unrestricted cuts do not arise}

In the sign presentation, each birthday is a set ordinal, while birthdays
are unbounded in the class of ordinals. The order type of an arbitrary
class well-order is not asserted to be a set ordinal. An expression such
as $\Ord+\Ord$ abbreviates a relation on a class of tagged sets. A
collection of all these relations is treated either by class-variable
predicates or in a genuinely larger universe.

Likewise, the cut principle permits sets $L<R$. Substituting all of $\No$
on the left and the empty class on the right would demand a surreal
greater than every surreal and is outside that principle. The represented
cut theorem explicitly admits unfilled class cuts, so it does not smuggle
in such an unrestricted principle.

\begin{theorem}[No exhaustive uniform class of set codes]\label{swo:cb:thm:diagonal}
In GBC no class of set codes with one uniform decoder can list every
class well-order of $\No$. An omitted order can always be chosen set-like.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Reindex any proposed family by $\Ord$, repeating a default row if the
indexing class is a set. Let its rows be $R_\alpha$. Partition a
baseline enumeration of $\No$ into consecutive two-label blocks,
using positions $2\cdot\alpha,2\cdot\alpha+1$. In block $\alpha$,
place its two labels in the order opposite to their relative order in
$R_\alpha$. Listing these blocks constructs a class bijection
$\Ord\to\No$, and its well-order differs from each row on that
row's designated pair. Its definition uses only the one family relation
and the baseline as class parameters.
\end{proof}

This is the prior report's diagonal obstruction, restated to locate the
size boundary (\cref{swo:gl:diagonal,swo:st:thm:diagonal}; Theorems~19.37--19.38
at the pin). An ordinary class
of codes may be dense and realize every set cut without listing every
global enumeration. Formula strings do not evade the theorem: a uniform
semantic evaluation of all formulas of the universe would require an
appropriate truth predicate. Individual formulas, an external collection
of definable classes of a model, and an internal universal evaluator are
different resources.

\subsubsection{Exactly where recursion principles enter}

In GBC, for a class strict linear order, the following internal conditions
are equivalent: every nonempty subclass has a least element; every
nonempty set subset has a least element; and there is no descending
$\omega$-sequence in the model. If a subclass has no least element,
choose below each of its members a witness of least possible set rank,
then use global choice within that rank. Ordinary recursion with this
class parameter constructs a descending $\omega$-sequence, whose range
is a set by class replacement. The other implications are the usual
set well-foundedness arguments. This explains the role of choice in the
equivalence; the article's primary definition remains the subclass
minimum condition \cite[Section 2]{HamkinsWoodin}.

Set-valued recursion along $\Ord$ can be assembled from its unique set
initial solutions using elementary comprehension. This covers the ordinary
surreal forth construction and prefix completions. The raw comparison
formula, simultaneous canonical block quotient, and persistent-cut
reconstruction do not even need a class-valued recursive construction.

A general recursion whose stage value is itself a proper class is a
stronger request. The principle ETR supplies elementary transfinite
recursion along class well-orders. It suffices for comparison of arbitrary
abstract class well-orders by initial-segment isomorphisms
\cite[Theorem 6]{HamkinsWoodin}. That is a different problem from comparing identical
labelled prefixes. The cited work poses converse-strength questions; we
do not turn those questions into a claimed independence theorem or assert
that their historical open status is settled as of the date of this article.
For general class recursion and truth-predicate strength see
\cite{GitmanHamkins,Williams}.

For condensation, a fixed finite number of iterations is available by
substituting elementary formulas. A uniform history on every arbitrary
input is a separate statement; ETR of the appropriate length is sufficient,
but this article proves no necessity. In the polynomial examples the
entire history already has an elementary formula, including at stages
with proper-class many predecessors. A warning about general recursion
must not be used to reject an explicitly defined construction.

\subsubsection{Full-universe and Henkin interpretations}

Let a containing universe have an inaccessible $\kappa$, and consider
$(V_\kappa,\mathcal P(V_\kappa))$. Internally, the surreals are
$\No_{<\kappa}$ and the ordinals are the ambient $\kappa$. Every
external subclass of the set universe is available as a class. Internal
class well-foundedness therefore agrees with external well-foundedness
for these relations.

The internal set-like enumeration space becomes the ambient
$\WO_\kappa(\No_{<\kappa})$, while the full raw space becomes all
ambient well-orders of the carrier. Both have cardinality $2^\kappa$,
and both embed exactly the ordinals below $\kappa^+$, but their finer
structure differs. The set-like space is equimorphic with $\B_\kappa$;
the unrestricted one has unbounded binary coding lengths below
$\kappa^+$ and cannot embed into that one cube. This is a genuine
nonembedding theorem in a specified external model, not a same-level
cardinality argument about a class of classes
(\cref{swo:thm:universe-nonembedding,swo:st:thm:model,swo:ec:thm:inaccessible};
Sections~20--22 at the pin).

For a general two-sorted model $(M,\mathcal C)$, only the classes in
$\mathcal C$ may occur as relations or witnesses. A relation can be
internally well-founded while an external descending sequence is absent
from $\mathcal C$. A countable model may have externally countably many
classes without possessing an internal exhaustive decoder. Adding classes
can add new global enumerations and can destroy the internal well-foundedness
of an old relation by adding a descending witness. The elementary
first-disagreement formula on previously available valid orders remains
the same, but the ambient totality and existence assertions may change.

% ---- source 18 (batch-81 manuscript 06), lines 3368-3509
\subsection{Source 18: containing universes, class realizations, and paradox avoidance}
\label{swo:sh:sec:foundations}

The mathematical distinctions above are also distinctions between
formal objects. A type, a set, a definable class, an available class in
a two-sorted model, and a collection of available classes have different
membership and quantifier rules. A rigorous development should choose
one of the following settings for each theorem.

\subsubsection{Ordinary ZFC and bounded birthday stages}

All results about $\WO_\alpha(\No_{<\kappa})$ are ordinary set theorems.
There is no need for class theory, an inaccessible cardinal, or a
global well-order to construct these spaces. Choice well-orders the
set alphabet, and all enumerations and cuts live in ordinary power
sets. In particular, the exact gap spectrum does not rest on the
existence of an external model or on an unformalized ``class ordinal.''

One may also work in ZFC with definable classes as metanotation.
A particular formula defines a particular global relation, but one
must not silently quantify in the object theory over all formulas and
their semantic truth sets. A uniform truth predicate for the whole
set universe is unavailable. A scheme covering each fixed defining
formula is different from a single theorem about all available classes.

\subsubsection{GBC and named class parameters}

GBC is a natural setting for supplied global orders, uniform families,
the elementary common-prefix comparison, the block decomposition,
and the represented-cut criterion. These constructions use actual
set labels to represent their quotients or prefixes. A block minimum
is a set; the proper block it represents is not an element.

The status of a well-order is relative to the class realization. In a
model $\mathcal M=(M,\mathcal X)$, ``every nonempty subclass'' means
every appropriate member of $\mathcal X$. An external descending
sequence might not be represented in $M$ or $\mathcal X$. Consequently
external countability or external ill-foundedness cannot simply be
substituted for internal set size or internal well-foundedness.
The factorial-shuffle theorem carefully uses external countability
and, for its finite blocks, $\omega$-standardness; it does not assume
that all internal well-orders are externally well-founded.

\subsubsection{A full-class model at an inaccessible cardinal}

For a concrete comparison with the external countable setting, let
$\lambda$ be strongly inaccessible in an ambient ZFC universe and
consider the full class model
\[
 \bigl(V_\lambda,\mathcal P(V_\lambda)\bigr).
\]
Its internal surreal carrier is the ambient set of sign sequences of
length below $\lambda$, of ambient cardinality $\lambda$. Every
ambient subset of the carrier is available as a class. Class
well-foundedness therefore means actual external well-foundedness.
An internal predecessor class is a set precisely when its ambient
cardinality is below $\lambda$: regularity bounds the ranks of a
small set of elements of $V_\lambda$, and inaccessibility gives the
converse cardinal bound.

It follows that, from the ambient viewpoint,
\[
 \Hsl=\WO_\lambda(\No_{<\lambda}),\qquad
 \Hall=\WO(\No_{<\lambda}).
\]
The former has cellularity $\lambda$, since
$\lambda^{<\lambda}=\lambda$. The latter has cellularity $2^\lambda$:
fix a residual set of three labels and vary the $\lambda$-long prefix
on its complement. Each of $2^\lambda$ disjoint cylinders contains
a nonempty open interval. Hence
\[\tag{S18.5}\label{swo:sh:eq:universe-nonembedding}
 \Hall\not\emb \Hsl
 \quad\text{in this full-class interpretation.}
\]
An order embedding would send the endpoints and an interior point of
each such interval to $2^\lambda$ disjoint nonempty intervals in the
target, contradicting its cellularity.

There is no conflict with the external countable-model embedding in
the preceding section. The two class realizations have different
external sizes and admit different external families. There is also
no conflict with surreal universality: $\Hall$ is an external
set of size $2^\lambda$, not an internal class of set labels to which
the internal universality theorem applies.

The canonical block theorem supplies a further consistency check.
An ambient order of the carrier has ordinal type $\gamma$ with
$|\gamma|=\lambda$. Its division
\[
 \gamma=\lambda\cdot\beta+\rho,\qquad \rho<\lambda,
\]
is exactly the external interpretation of the internal decomposition
into $\Ord$ blocks and a final set tail. Thus the class theorem
recovers ordinary ordinal division in this model without treating
$\Ord$ as an internal set.

\subsubsection{KM, stronger recursions, and genuine higher sorts}

KM permits impredicative class comprehension. It remains a two-sorted
theory: classes are not members of classes. To make the whole domain
of global well-orders an object one needs, for example, an explicitly
specified higher sort, an external containing universe, or a carefully
defined unrolling. These are substantive changes of framework, not
notation that erases the diagonal in \Cref{swo:sh:thm:noncoding}.

The use of ETR should be equally explicit. General class-valued
recursions, including iterated truth constructions, exceed GBC
\cite{GHHSW}. ETR is a sufficient framework for suitable
abstract class well-order comparisons and recursive quotient
constructions \cite{Williams}. In contrast, three procedures in this
article have elementary closed definitions or set-valued histories:
comparison of shared labels, simultaneous set-interval decomposition,
and reconstruction of a branch from unique set prefixes. None requires
ETR. We do not infer an exact reverse-mathematical equivalence for an
unspecified iteration of the quotient operator.

\subsubsection{A concise list of invalid identifications}

The following substitutions would change a theorem's meaning or
invalidate its proof.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Replacing $\Ord$ by a set ordinal while still claiming to enumerate
all surreals of the same universe.
\item Treating all class relations as members of a class merely because
each individual relation is available.
\item Replacing an arbitrary class well-order by an $\Ord$ enumeration;
this discards its later proper blocks and set tail.
\item Replacing a proper-class cut by a set cut when applying surreal
interpolation.
\item Using cardinal multiplication where the proof concerns ordinal
lexicographic coding length.
\item Assuming that an order embedding preserves suprema or density
in the ambient order.
\item Treating a set-indexed uniform family of classes as an ordinary
set of class objects.
\item Extending numerical lexicography to isomorphism classes after
discarding the labels on which it depends.
\end{enumerate}
These are mathematical type distinctions, not additional consistency
axioms imposed on the bounded results.

\begin{note}[\merge; internal well-foundedness under class extensions]\label{swo:ix:note:wellfounded}
The last paragraph of source~15's subsection on full-universe and Henkin
interpretations (in \cref{swo:cb:sec:foundations}) says that adding classes ``can destroy the
internal well-foundedness of an old relation by adding a descending witness''.
For class realizations that are models of $\GBC$ with the same sets this is
not so, and source~16's subsection on Henkin models proves the opposite: over
$\GBC$ a class relation is well-founded on all admitted subclasses exactly when
no set-coded descending $\omega$-sequence exists (source~15 proves the same
equivalence in its subsection ``Exactly where recursion principles enter''),
and a descending $\omega$-sequence admitted by a larger realization is a set of
the common set part, by class Replacement, so it was already present. Hence
two $\GBC$ realizations with the same sets agree on the internal
well-foundedness of every relation they share. Source~15's sentence can hold
only for a larger class collection in which that equivalence fails, for
example one that is not a model of global choice; as a statement about $\GBC$
realizations it is withdrawn here. The same correction was made to source~08's
foundations after the Hilbert's-tenth review of batch~80
(\cref{swo:sk:sec:foundations} and the note before it). Source~15's \cref{swo:cb:n13.11} asks
which statements ``require well-foundedness preservation''; by the argument
above, none does among $\GBC$ realizations with the same sets.
\end{note}

\section{An exact external classification in countable models (source 18)}
\label{swo:sh:sec:countable-factorial-shuffle}

The distinction between an internal class and an external collection of
classes leads to a surprisingly uniform external order type. The statement
below concerns the raw labelled comparison of all admitted class well-orders,
including those that are not set-like. It does not concern their abstract
order types. It strengthens the observation that an external countable
collection of admitted orders can embed into the external rational line.

For a linear order $L$, write $x\sim_{\mathrm{fin}}y$ when the closed
interval between $x$ and $y$ is finite. These equivalence classes are the
\emph{finite-condensation blocks}. For a nonempty countable collection
$\mathcal A$ of linear order types, its \emph{shuffle}
$\sigma(\mathcal A)$ is obtained by densely colouring $\mathbb Q$ with one
colour for each member of $\mathcal A$, then replacing a point by the order
type of its colour. A colour-preserving back-and-forth proves that the
resulting order type is independent of the chosen dense colouring. These
are standard order-theoretic constructions; see, for example,
Dimitrov--Harizanov--Morozov--Shafer--Soskova--Vatev,
\emph{On cohesive powers of linear orders}, Definitions 3.3 and 6.2,
\cite{CohesivePowers}. The identification with the
well-order space below is derived here.

\subsection{Terminal tails and finite-condensation blocks}

The next arguments can first be carried out internally in $\GBC$. Let
$X$ be an infinite linearly ordered class, and consider the predicate of
all class well-orders of $X$, with the raw labelled lexicographic comparison.
It is enough that the required well-orders and constructions exist; for
$X=\No$, global choice supplies them.

\begin{lemma}[The maximal finite terminal tail]
\label{swo:sh:lem:finite-tail-existence}
Every class well-order $R$ on an infinite carrier has a unique finite
terminal segment $T_R$ such that $R$ restricted to $X\setminus T_R$ has no
greatest element. Write $n(R)=|T_R|$. Every finite terminal segment of $R$
is contained in $T_R$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $R$ has no greatest element, take $T_R=\varnothing$. Otherwise start at
the greatest element and repeatedly take its immediate predecessor, for
as long as one exists. If this process did not terminate at a finite stage,
ordinary set-valued recursion with parameter $R$ would produce a
descending $\omega$-sequence. Class Replacement makes its range a set,
contradicting well-foundedness. At termination the selected finite chain
is terminal and the remaining prefix has no greatest element. Any finite
terminal segment is obtained by finitely many of the same uniquely
determined predecessor steps, proving maximality and uniqueness.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Adjacency forces a finite residual carrier]
\label{swo:sh:lem:adjacency-finite-residual}
Suppose $R<S$ are adjacent in the lexicographic order of all class
well-orders of $X$. Let $C$ be their common labelled prefix, and let
$a=\min_R(X\setminus C)<\min_S(X\setminus C)=b$ in the ambient label
order. Then $Y=X\setminus C$ is finite.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Keep the prefix $C$, then the next label $a$, fixed. The $R$-tail must
be the greatest available well-order in that prefix cylinder: any greater
tail gives an order strictly between $R$ and $S$. At each subsequent
position, therefore, its label must be the greatest remaining label.
Otherwise choose a larger remaining label and well-order the remaining
carrier to obtain a greater tail. Consequently the reverse ambient
label order on $Y\setminus\{a\}$ is a class well-order.

The symmetric argument, fixing $C$ then $b$, shows that the ambient
label order on $Y\setminus\{b\}$ is a class well-order. On
$Z=Y\setminus\{a,b\}$, both an order and its reverse are therefore
well-orders. This forces $Z$ to be finite. Indeed, if $Z$ were infinite,
repeatedly choosing the least unused point in one of those well-orders
would produce an ascending $\omega$-sequence in that order, hence a
descending $\omega$-sequence in the other. Thus $Y$ is finite.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Factorial blocks]
\label{swo:sh:prop:factorial-blocks}
The finite-condensation block containing $R$ consists exactly of the
orders obtained by keeping $R$ fixed on $X\setminus T_R$ and permuting
the $n(R)$ labels in $T_R$. It is a finite chain of size $n(R)!$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The common-prefix cylinder with residual carrier $T_R$ is convex and
contains exactly its $n(R)!$ permutations. In lexicographic order they
form a finite chain, so they lie in one finite-condensation block.

Conversely, any adjacent order $S$ has a finite residual carrier at the
first disagreement, by the preceding lemma. That residual is a finite
terminal segment in $R$, hence lies in $T_R$. Thus an adjacent step
cannot leave the displayed permutation cylinder. A finite interval is a
finite chain of adjacent steps; no member outside this cylinder can be
at finite distance from $R$. This proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

The cases $n=0$ and $n=1$ both give a singleton block. The maximal
finite-tail length distinguishes these as labelled well-orders, but their
block sizes do not distinguish them in the pure linear order.

\subsection{Every factorial block size occurs densely}

\begin{lemma}[An interval across different blocks contains an infinite
residual cylinder]
\label{swo:sh:lem:infinite-cylinder}
If $R<S$ belong to different finite-condensation blocks, there is a
labelled prefix cylinder lying entirely inside $(R,S)$ whose residual
carrier is infinite. The prefix may be a proper class.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $C$ be the common prefix, $Y=X\setminus C$, and let $a<b$ be the
first unequal labels. The class $Y$ is infinite, since a finite residual
would put the two orders in one finite permutation cylinder.

Consider the following two possible changes. In $R$, at a position
$x\in Y\setminus\{a\}$ outside $T_R$, keep the whole earlier prefix
and replace $x$ by a larger unused label. In $S$, at a position
$x\in Y\setminus\{b\}$ outside $T_S$, keep the whole earlier prefix
and replace $x$ by a smaller unused label. A change of the first kind
gives a prefix cylinder above $R$ and below $S$, because the earlier
first label $a$ remains fixed; a change of the second kind gives the
same conclusion with the first label $b$ fixed. The unused carrier
before such a change is infinite, since the changed position lies
outside the maximal finite terminal tail. Removing one label leaves
the new cylinder with infinite residual carrier.

At least one such change must be possible. Otherwise let
\[
 Z=Y\setminus\bigl(\{a,b\}\cup T_R\cup T_S\bigr).
\]
This class is infinite. In $R$, every $x\in Z$ must be numerically
greater than each of its $R$-successors in $Z$, since any larger unused
successor would permit the first change. Thus $R\restriction Z$ is
the reverse ambient label order. In $S$, every $x\in Z$ must be
numerically smaller than each of its $S$-successors in $Z$, since a
smaller one would permit the second change. Thus $S\restriction Z$
is the ambient order. Both restrictions are class well-orders,
contradicting the infinitude of $Z$ as in the preceding proof.
The orders in this cylinder also lie in blocks different from both endpoint
blocks. For an upward change, its first disagreement with $R$ occurs while
the residual is infinite, and its first disagreement with $S$ occurs at
the original infinite residual $Y$; the downward case is symmetric.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Prescribing the finite tail]
\label{swo:sh:lem:prescribed-tail}
For every $n\in\omega$, every interval joining different
finite-condensation blocks contains an order $W$ with $n(W)=n$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Take the cylinder from \Cref{swo:sh:lem:infinite-cylinder}, with prefix
$P$ and infinite residual carrier $Y$. Choose $n$ distinct labels
$F\subseteq Y$. Well-order $Y\setminus F$ without a greatest element:
if it is a set, use its infinite initial cardinal as order type; if it
is a proper class, use a set-like well-order of type $\Ord$. Both are
available in $\GBC$. Append these labels after $P$, and then append
the $n$ labels of $F$ in any order. The resulting well-order belongs
to the cylinder, and its maximal finite terminal tail is exactly $F$.
\end{proof}

These arguments are parameterwise constructions of individual classes.
They do not assert that the collection of all orders, or its quotient,
is an internal class whose elements are classes.

\subsection{The external classification}

Let $\mathcal M=(M,\mathcal X)$ be an externally countable two-sorted
model of $\GBC$. Write ${\Hsl}^{\mathcal M}$ and
${\Hall}^{\mathcal M}$ for the external sets of its admitted
set-like and arbitrary class well-orders of its internal surreal
carrier. Comparisons are those computed in $\mathcal M$.

\begin{theorem}[Countable-model factorial-shuffle theorem]
\label{swo:sh:thm:countable-factorial-shuffle}
If $\mathcal M$ is $\omega$-standard, then, externally,
\[
 {\Hall}^{\mathcal M}
 \ \cong\ \sigma\bigl(\{1,2,6,24,120,\ldots\}\bigr)
 =\sigma\bigl(\{n!:n\in\omega\}\bigr).
\]
Its finite-condensation quotient is a copy of $\mathbb Q$, and each
factorial block size occurs densely in that quotient. In particular,
the pure external order type is independent of the particular countable
$\omega$-standard model and its admitted collection of classes.

For every externally countable model of $\GBC$, even without
$\omega$-standardness,
\[
 {\Hsl}^{\mathcal M}\cong\mathbb Q.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Internal linearity gives an actual external linear order on each
admitted collection. The collections are countable because the entire
class sort is externally countable. Internal nonemptiness and
variation of the first surreal label make them infinite and give no
endpoints.

In an $\omega$-standard model, the number $n(R)$ of
\Cref{swo:sh:lem:finite-tail-existence} is a standard natural number.
Its $n(R)!$-element permutation cylinder is therefore genuinely
externally finite. \Cref{swo:sh:prop:factorial-blocks} identifies
all external finite-condensation blocks. Its converse is also external:
an external finite interval is a standard finite chain of adjacent
steps, and adjacency has its literal external meaning because the
class sort ranges over precisely the admitted orders.

The quotient is countable, has no endpoints, and is dense by
\Cref{swo:sh:lem:prescribed-tail}. The same lemma makes every block-size
colour dense. The countable colour-preserving back-and-forth identifies
it with the densely coloured rational order used in the definition of
the shuffle. Each finite block is a rigid chain, so this quotient
isomorphism lifts uniquely within each block to the claimed order
isomorphism.

For the set-like orders, their internal lexicographic order is dense:
at the first unequal ordinal position, the common prefix is a set;
choose an unused surreal strictly between the next two labels and
complete the prefix to a global enumeration. The surreal cut-filling
property permits avoidance of the set of used labels. There are no
endpoints by varying the first label. Thus its external order is a
countable dense linear order without endpoints, hence isomorphic to
$\mathbb Q$. This part does not use $\omega$-standardness.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[An explicit computable presentation]\label{swo:sh:n16.7}
For $q\in\mathbb Q$, let $d(q)>0$ be its denominator in lowest terms,
and set $c(q)=(1+v_2(d(q)))!$. Then the lexicographically ordered set
\[
 \bigl\{(q,i):q\in\mathbb Q,\ 0\leq i<c(q)\bigr\}
\]
is an explicit computable copy of the factorial shuffle. For each fixed
$k\geq0$, reduced rationals with denominator of $2$-adic valuation $k$
are dense: choose a sufficiently large odd denominator factor and an
odd numerator inside the desired interval. Cancelling common odd
factors does not change that valuation. This computable presentation
does not supply a computable decoder for the model's class relations.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[The hypothesis cannot simply be dropped]\label{swo:sh:n16.8}
If $\mathcal M$ is $\omega$-nonstandard, choose a nonstandard
$N\in\omega^{\mathcal M}$ and append an internally $N$-element tail
to a global well-order without a last element. The corresponding
internal $N!$-element permutation cylinder is externally an infinite
discrete interval with endpoints. Starting at its first element and
taking the immediate successor any standard finite number of times
produces infinitely many points in one external finite-condensation
block. Consequently the external blocks need not be finite, and the
displayed factorial-shuffle classification fails. The proof requires
standardness of $\omega$, not external well-foundedness of every
admitted class relation; no $\beta$-model assumption is needed.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[External embeddings and intrinsic automorphism orbits]\label{swo:sh:n16.9}
In an externally countable $\omega$-standard model, the unrestricted
order is not externally isomorphic to its set-like suborder: it has
adjacent pairs. Nevertheless it externally embeds into that suborder,
since every countable linear order embeds into $\mathbb Q$.

The automorphism group of the unrestricted external order is the
automorphism group of the rational quotient coloured by factorial
block size. Its point orbits are indexed by a factorial block size
and a position within that block.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Only the automorphism assertion needs comment. Finite-distance blocks
and their sizes are preserved by every order automorphism. Every
colour-preserving quotient automorphism lifts uniquely because finite
chains are rigid. Conversely, the colour-preserving back-and-forth is
transitive on the quotient points of each fixed colour. Hence two
points lie in the same orbit exactly when their block sizes and
within-block positions agree.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Set-likeness is not definable from the external order]
\label{swo:sh:cor:setlike-not-order-definable}
In the countable $\omega$-standard setting, the distinguished subset
${\Hsl}^{\mathcal M}$ is not first-order definable, even with a
finite tuple of parameters, in the pure linear order
${\Hall}^{\mathcal M}$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Set-like orders have no last element and hence lie in singleton blocks.
Orders of type $\Ord+1$ also lie in singleton blocks, since their
maximal finite terminal tail has size one, but they are not set-like.
The preceding automorphism description can exchange any two
singleton-block points.

To allow finitely many parameters, take a surreal label smaller than
the first labels of all the parameter orders. There are both a
set-like order and an order of type $\Ord+1$ starting with that label.
They lie below all the parameters and occupy singleton blocks. A
colour-preserving quotient back-and-forth sends one to the other while
fixing each parameter block, and its lift fixes the parameter points.
No formula with those parameters can distinguish the two points.
\end{proof}

The natural inclusion of ${\Hsl}^{\mathcal M}$ in
${\Hall}^{\mathcal M}$ is not dense. For example, fix a proper
class prefix of type $\Ord$ leaving three labels, and vary the final
three labels. The resulting six-point cylinder has a nonempty open
interval containing no set-like order. More substantially, leaving an
infinite set of labels gives whole intervals between different
finite-condensation blocks that contain no set-like order. Thus the
pure order classification does not classify the expanded pair
$({\Hall}^{\mathcal M},{\Hsl}^{\mathcal M})$, or the external
evaluation relation connecting these orders to their surreal labels.
Those richer structures remain appropriate further research targets.

\begin{note}[\merge; relation to sources~13 and~17 and to Part~V]\label{swo:ix:note:countable}
The second clause of \cref{swo:sh:thm:countable-factorial-shuffle}
($\Hsl\cong\mathbb Q$ externally in every externally countable model) is
source~13's \cref{swo:fs:prop:countable}, with the same proof; source~11
already observed, after \cref{swo:thm:km-nonembedding}, that in such a model
the external set-like order can admit an external copy of the unrestricted
order, which source~18's \cref{swo:sh:n16.9} makes precise.
\Cref{swo:sh:lem:finite-tail-existence,swo:sh:lem:adjacency-finite-residual,swo:sh:prop:factorial-blocks}
are a second proof of source~17's \cref{swo:gs:thm:condensation}. New in this
section are the factorial-shuffle classification of the full order in
countable $\omega$-standard models, its computable presentation, the failure
without $\omega$-standardness, the description of the automorphism orbits,
and the non-definability of set-likeness in the pure order
(\cref{swo:sh:cor:setlike-not-order-definable}).
\end{note}

\subsection{Source 13: a formalization plan tied to the inspected Lean code}\label{swo:fs:sec:lean}

\subsubsection{What already exists at the pinned snapshot}

The inspected source
\code{Surreal/Foundations/SignSequence.lean} defines
\cite{ProveItSigns}:
\begin{lstlisting}
structure SignSequence : Type (u + 1) where
  birthday : Ordinal.{u}
  signAt : Ordinal.{u} -> SignType
  signAt_ne_zero_iff :
    forall i, signAt i != 0 <-> i < birthday
\end{lstlisting}
This display is an ASCII schematic rendering of the actual declaration,
not a new compiled Lean file. The source uses Lean's native logical
notation. Its numerical linear order is lifted from the lexicographic
order of zero-extended sign functions.

\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.43\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.49\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Inspected declaration & Role in this development\\
\midrule\endhead
\code{SignSequence.lt\_iff} & First-disagreement characterization of
numerical comparison.\\[4pt]
\code{ordinalOrderEmbedding} & The all-plus embedding of the ordinal
carrier into the sign carrier.\\[4pt]
\code{birthdays\_bounded} & A strict birthday bound for a family with
an explicit lower-universe smallness instance.\\[4pt]
\code{not\_small} & The whole sign carrier is not small in the
universe indexing its birthdays.\\[4pt]
\code{small\_bounded} & Each fixed birthday-bounded fragment is small
relative to that lower universe.\\[4pt]
\code{exists\_cut\_separator\_of\_birthday\_lt} & A separator of
exactly a prescribed birthday above all option birthdays; the fresh
separator lemma's direct input.\\[4pt]
\code{small\_cut\_fillers} & The constructed carrier realizes every
small strict cut.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

The last two are in \code{SignSequenceCut.lean}
\cite{ProveItCutFill}. They are not merely postulated field axioms: the
inspected source constructs them from fixed-length Boolean
lexicographic words. We inspected the files, not a fresh build of the
project. No theorem in this manuscript is thereby automatically a
kernel-checked theorem.

\subsubsection{Relative smallness must stay visible}

\code{SignSequence.\{u\}} and \code{Ordinal.\{u\}} both live in
\code{Type (u + 1)}, while bounded sign sequences and initial segments
are small relative to \code{u}. A \code{Set SignSequence} is merely
a predicate on the larger carrier. It need not be an admissible small
family of options. The formal counterpart of ``set cut'' therefore
requires an index type with \code{Small.\{u\}}, not just the word
\code{Set} in a declaration.

The same applies to supports and prefix lengths. A support that is a
predicate on a larger type is not automatically a small support.
A code should carry a small graph or an explicit smallness proof.
Otherwise the completion bound, the dense-core distinction, and the
diagonal interpretation can silently change meaning.

A universe-relative approach may take a baseline equivalence
\[
                 b:\code{Ordinal.\{u\}}\simeq
                            \code{SignSequence.\{u\}}
\]
as an explicit parameter. Its existence is not inferred merely because
the types occupy the same universe. A formal project must either
construct the required equivalence, with the intended small-initial-
segment properties, or retain it as a stated assumption.

\subsubsection{Suggested modules and their proof obligations}

The following names are proposals, not claims about existing files.

\paragraph{Exhaustive orders and finite predicates.}
A first module should define exhaustive ordinal enumerations on a
small carrier, prove prefix-freeness, and compare the relation-based
and enumeration-based first-disagreement definitions. These proofs do
not require surreal arithmetic or class theory. The finite checker
included here provides examples, not a substitute for this module.

\paragraph{Prefix codes and completion.}
Represent a moved-point graph canonically and prove evaluation
injective on codes. Prove the complement-cardinality extension lemma
before using any prefix-completion operation. Formulate cylinders by
restriction equality and prove convexity and same-level disjointness.

\paragraph{Small-family interpolation.}
Use an explicit small index type for the two families. Establish a
bound on cross first-disagreement coordinates, then implement the
active-row invariant with a set-sized history. The stopping lemma,
not a generic unbounded recursion tactic, is the critical finite-
length formal obligation at this stage.

\paragraph{Cut traces and failure.}
Define crossing by two existential code witnesses. Same-level
uniqueness and restriction coherence are purely order-theoretic.
Under all-level existence, reconstruct the value at $\alpha$ from the
unique prefix of length $\alpha+1$. Prove trace equality with the
no-greatest-lower normalization stated explicitly. For first failure,
split successor from limit ordinals and prove the boundary formula
rather than assuming that crossing commutes with limit intersection.

\paragraph{Products and recoding.}
First formalize \Cref{swo:fs:lem:split} for ordinary set types and
an order-dense subset. It has no class-theoretic ambiguity and should
be a small, reusable result. The uniform complement-map interface
then supports prefix insertion and finite-block automorphisms. The
$\KM$ inverse evaluator belongs in a model or syntax layer, not in an
unqualified theorem about arbitrary Lean functions on a larger type.

\paragraph{Central words.}
Represent termination by an option type or by a reserved symbol with
an explicit proof that it is not a letter. For injective words,
retain injectivity as an invariant when selecting the shared next
letter. The explicit sign-block embedding can be formalized
independently of the class back-and-forth isomorphism.

\subsubsection{Three complementary formalization routes}

The \emph{cutoff-first route} proves the fixed-set and density-bound
lemmas inside ordinary types. It requires the least foundational
infrastructure and makes cardinal hypotheses explicit.

The \emph{universe-relative route} abstracts a large ordered carrier
with a lower-universe small-cut operation, a set-like enumeration,
and support codes. It can certify the local combinatorics and many
of the new constructions relative to those interfaces. It should not
be described as a proof of every $\GBC$ or $\KM$ metatheorem merely
because it uses two universes.

The \emph{deep model route} formalizes a two-sorted class theory or a
specified model $(M,\mathcal C)$. This is the route for the exact
comprehension schema, the external countable contrast, and the
full-model interpretation. Taking all predicates on an arbitrary
carrier as ``classes'' does not by itself establish the intended
replacement or universe axioms; the model assumptions must be proved
or supplied.

\subsubsection{Verification boundary}

A completed formalization should pin both the repository revision and
its dependency revisions, compile the new modules, and audit theorem
axioms and unfinished proofs. None of those actions is claimed here.
The deliverable is a proof manuscript, a reproducible LaTeX build, and
finite consistency checks. Existing Lean inputs are identified by
actual declarations and source hashes in the audit appendix, so that
a future formalization has concrete starting points.

% ---- source 14 (batch-81 manuscript 02), lines 1646-1765
\subsection{Source 14: a realistic formalization plan}
\label{swo:tc:sec:formal}
The new proofs admit a modular formalization in which most of the work
is ordinary order theory. A full class-theoretic metamodel should not
be the first dependency. The finite checks shipped with this article
are useful regression tests, but do not discharge any infinite or
class-level theorem.

\subsubsection{A generic set-level kernel}
Start with a type $X$ carrying a linear order and a chosen ordinal or
well-ordered index type. An exhaustive presentation is a bijection from
that index type to $X$. For arbitrary well-order types on one fixed
carrier, relations are often easier than a dependent sum over every
ordinal: a relation together with linearity and well-foundedness proofs
is already a set-sized object at the carrier's type level.

Prove the labelled common-prefix comparison before importing surreal
arithmetic. Its main obligations are initiality, agreement of the
restricted relations, existence and inequality of the two next labels,
and transitivity via nested initial segments. For fixed-domain words,
prove the equivalent least-disagreement formulation. Finite relation
matrices and permutation words give independently checkable examples.

A second module handles partial-injection extension. Its specification
must retain \emph{agreement on a prescribed prefix} and the
\emph{support cardinality bound}; bare existence of an extension is not
enough for the compression theorem. The finite case and the infinite
buffer case should be separate lemmas, since equality of infinite
cardinalities of domain and range alone does not imply equality of their
complement cardinalities.

\subsubsection{An abstract saturated alphabet interface}
The core theory needs an ordered alphabet with set-cut filling and fresh
separators, a global baseline in the class version, and set-prefix
completion. Numerical surreal field operations are not required.
A bounded preliminary development may use a regular-cardinal saturated
set order and prefix lengths below that cardinal, with all relevant
smallness hypotheses explicit. It proves the crossing-chain and bounded
versions of the trichotomy without formalizing surreal addition.

For actual sign sequences, the pinned repository already supplies
simplicity lemmas. The inspected declaration
\texttt{existsUnique\_simplest\_separator} requires a proof that a
separator exists. The appropriate architecture imports an independent
small-cut existence theorem and then applies this uniqueness result;
it does not erase the hypothesis to manufacture saturation.
\merge\ The pinned tree already has this architecture: \texttt{small\_cut\_fillers}
in \path{SignSequenceCut.lean} proves that small cuts have fillers, and
\texttt{cut} in \path{SignSequenceCutOperation.lean} is defined from
\texttt{existsUnique\_simplest\_separator} applied to it
(\cref{swo:sec:formal}; the same remark in source~14's audit section,
\cref{swo:tc:sec:foundations}).

\subsubsection{Proposed modules and theorem dependencies}
\begin{longtable}{@{}p{.26\textwidth}p{.64\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Proposed module & Principal obligations\\\midrule\endhead
\texttt{LabelledCommonPrefix} & Initiality, next labels, lexical linearity;
comparison with ordinal enumerations.\\
\texttt{SupportExtension} & Finite extension; infinite buffer; preservation
of fixed positions; cardinal bounds.\\
\texttt{CoreCylinders} & Canonical support codes, prefix completion,
convex cylinders, ordered children.\\
\texttt{CrossingPrefixes} & Elementary crossing predicate; chain and
uniqueness by length; union graph.\\
\texttt{CutTrichotomy} & Unbounded branch; bounded limit edge; terminal
numerical gap; uniqueness.\\
\texttt{ExhaustiveTrace} & Coherence and coverage; graph reconstruction;
trace injectivity.\\
\texttt{SupportSaturation} & Support compression; union bound at
$\cf\kappa$; sharp forced-prefix configuration.\\
\texttt{RawTraceFibers} & Canonical set-like initial branch; tail
concatenation; equality and convexity of trace fibers.\\
\texttt{ClassRealizations} & Same-set structures and elementary
absoluteness with old parameters.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
These are proposed modules, not files claimed to exist or compile.
A dependency path is
\[
 \text{completion}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{cylinders}
 \ \longrightarrow\ \text{crossing chain}
 \ \longrightarrow\ \text{trichotomy}
 \ \longrightarrow\ \text{recognition}.
\]
Support compression can instead import the predecessor's verified-in-writing
core interpolation theorem while that path is being formalized. The
character theorem and support threshold then provide two largely
independent audits of the prefix machinery.

\subsubsection{Class-level interfaces and avoiding a hidden third sort}
A formal metatheory of $\GBC$ can express cuts and enumerations as class
variables and use elementary comprehension explicitly. An alternative
is to formalize the external inaccessible model, where all relevant
collections are sets in a larger type universe. These routes have
different assumptions and should not be conflated.

The central reconstruction specification can be written schematically as
\begin{lstlisting}
Crosses(D, p) :=
  exists a b, InCylinder(a,p) and InCylinder(b,p)
              and D(a) and not D(b)

RecoveredGraph(D, alpha, x) :=
  exists p, Crosses(D,p) and alpha in domain(p) and p(alpha)=x

Coherent(D) := forall alpha, exists p,
  domain(p)=alpha and Crosses(D,p)

Covers(D) := forall x, exists p, Crosses(D,p) and x in range(p)
\end{lstlisting}
This is logical pseudocode, not Lean syntax and not compiled code.
Its purpose is to display the quantifiers: $a,b,p,\alpha,x$ are set
objects. No line chooses a class as an element of a class family.
The proof of functionality precedes any use of the recovered graph as
a function, and the coverage theorem is a separate proof of surjectivity.

\subsubsection{What must be checked before a kernel-verification claim}
A completed formalization must pin its Lean and Mathlib revisions, compile
all files, expose any axioms beyond the chosen foundations, and connect
the generic ordered alphabet to the actual surreal carrier. It must
also verify that internal ordinals, universe lifts, and prefix domains
match the statements. None of those steps has been completed for the new
theorems in this package; the package contains conventional written
proofs and executable finite diagnostics only.

\subsection{Source 15: a concrete Lean architecture}

The inspected ProveIt declaration is
\[
 \texttt{SignSequence.\{u\} : Type (u+1)}.
\]
Its birthday belongs to $\texttt{Ordinal.\{u\}}$. The file provides
\path{ordinalOrderEmbedding}, \path{birthdays_bounded},
\path{small_bounded}, \path{not_small}, and a well-founded
simplicity relation, among other declarations \cite{ProveItSigns}.
The essential statement is relative smallness: the entire sign carrier is
not $u$-small, even though it is a legitimate type one universe higher.
The official Lean universe rules support this distinction
\cite{LeanUniverses}. This article has inspected those declarations but
has not rebuilt the repository or certified any new theorem in Lean.

A practical development should use the following dependencies.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Generic set layer.} Define exhaustive ordinal enumerations
of an arbitrary linearly ordered carrier; prove prefix-freeness,
first-difference comparison, pair orientation, and the successor-cardinal
obstruction. Surreal arithmetic is unnecessary.
\item \textbf{Bounded surreal layer.} Reuse sign order and birthdays.
Formalize the $00/11$ code with terminal $01$, ordinal concatenation,
the max-coordinate scheduler, and the three coding-length cases.
Track ordinal products explicitly instead of replacing them by cardinalities.
\item \textbf{Relative-smallness layer.} For a relation on a higher-universe
carrier, express the assertion that an interval or predecessor type is
$u$-small. Implement the least-representative condensation and its rank
map. This models the chosen set/class boundary without a type of all types.
\item \textbf{Prefix and cut layer.} Define one uniform evaluation relation
on small support codes. State crossing using quantification over small
prefixes and codes, and reconstruct a persistent branch. Quantify over
the cut as a parameter at the permitted universe level.
\item \textbf{Model layer.} To claim a theorem about GB, GBC, or KM itself,
formalize a model or an axiomatic interface for that theory. Universe
polymorphism alone is not a proof that a chosen type-theoretic encoding
satisfies precisely those set-theoretic axioms.
\end{enumerate}

Each layer should record its universe parameters, smallness assumptions,
choice use, and available recursion principle. A relation on the entire
higher-universe sign type with ordinary Lean well-foundedness may encode
external well-foundedness stronger than a Henkin model's internal class
condition. These should be separate definitions, linked only by proved
translation theorems.

\subsection{Source 16: a concrete formalization plan tied to ProveIt}\label{swo:ds:sec:lean}

\subsubsection{Inspected primitives and actual status}

The following declarations were inspected at the pinned repository
revision. They are existing foundations, not formal proofs of the new
results of this article. The earlier well-order report explicitly states
that no theorem with its \code{swo:} labels has a Lean mapping.
