\subsection{Source 17: further research questions and a prioritized program}
\label{swo:gs:sec:questions}

These questions are continuations of this article, not claims that each
is a historically catalogued open problem. The results above narrow their
scope: questions about minimal-slice characters, the displayed gap
spectrum, or mere recognition with the full labelled prefix structure
are no longer left open within this development.

\subsubsection{Set-sized order geometry}
\begin{question}[Nonminimal enumeration types]\label{swo:gs:n15.1}
For $|\alpha|=\mu=2^{<\kappa}$, classify the characters, gap spectrum,
density, and binary coding length of $\WO_\alpha(\No_{<\kappa})$.
Begin with $\alpha=\mu\cdot2$ and $\mu+n$.
\end{question}
A prefix can now use $\mu$ labels before exhausting its coordinate
domain, so residual alphabets can be small, have endpoints, or be finite.
The proof of \Cref{swo:gs:thm:gap-spectrum} suggests replacing the single
residual-alphabet interface by a tree whose nodes carry their actual
residual order types. A theorem expressed only in $|\alpha|$ cannot
capture all such effects.

\begin{question}[Noncardinal birthday cutoffs]\label{swo:gs:n15.2}
Replace the initial cardinal $\kappa$ by an arbitrary infinite ordinal
$\theta$. Which local invariants depend on the ordinal tail of $\theta$,
not merely on $|\theta|$ and $|\No_{<\theta}|$?
\end{question}
Our cone argument uses $\delta+\gamma<\kappa$ for smaller ordinals.
That property fails at many noncardinal cutoffs. A useful first target
is a cutoff of the form $\kappa+\omega$, followed by $\kappa\cdot2$,
with the contributions of each birthday layer kept separate.

\begin{question}[Isomorphism after the invariant calculation]\label{swo:gs:n15.3}
When do two minimal permutation orders with the same values of $r,q$,
$\mu^{<\mu}$ and the same gap spectrum have the same order type?
Which additional invariants distinguish them?
\end{question}
The explicit gap classification provides more information than binary
equimorphism, but still need not determine an order. Candidate invariants
include the arrangement of cylinder-boundary cuts, densities of particular
convex suborders, and the interaction of branch cuts with a chosen prefix
filtration. No general isomorphism conclusion is asserted here.

\begin{question}[Beyond the proved fusion length]\label{swo:gs:n15.4}
Determine the least size of a family of dense open sets whose intersection
fails to be dense. When $q=\omega$, determine complete metrizability and
more precise descriptive topological properties directly from the
permutation presentation.
\end{question}
\Cref{swo:gs:thm:fusion} supplies a lower bound: every family of size at
most $q$ succeeds. For longer constructions, intermediate prefixes can
already have length $\mu$, so the simple small-history argument no longer
applies. This is an obstruction to that proof, not a proof that longer
fusion always fails.

\subsubsection{Global branches, automorphisms, and class realizations}
\begin{question}[The extendible automorphism group]\label{swo:gs:n15.5}
Describe the stabilizer of the represented-cut predicate in
$\operatorname{Aut}(\Psupp(b))$. Can one characterize it by preservation of fewer predicates
than the entire labelled cylinder and coverage structure?
\end{question}
\Cref{swo:gs:thm:extension-criterion} identifies this stabilizer abstractly,
and \Cref{swo:gs:thm:nonextension} shows it is proper. The remaining task
is a useful structural description. Numerical relabellings give a
natural family, but need not exhaust it.

\begin{question}[Changing baselines]\label{swo:gs:n15.6}
For two baselines $b,b'$, when does an automorphism of $\Hsl$ carry
$\Psupp(b)$ onto $\Psupp(b')$? How does the answer depend on their
eventual-agreement classes and on their represented-cut predicates?
\end{question}
Relabelling by an increasing numerical bijection is sufficient when it
carries one baseline to the other. Abstract order-isomorphism of the two
cores is not sufficient by itself; the obstruction proved here explains
why the represented cuts must enter the analysis.

\begin{question}[Recovering a class realization]\label{swo:gs:n15.7}
What information about $\mathcal X$ can be reconstructed from the labelled
core together with its admitted represented cuts? What is lost if the
baseline and cylinder predicates are forgotten?
\end{question}
\Cref{swo:gs:thm:class-extension} detects every proper same-set extension
through new represented cuts. Its pair encoding recovers an individual
ordinal subclass from a suitable enumeration. A stronger reconstruction
should specify the decoding language and distinguish existence of
individual codes from a universal truth or satisfaction predicate.

\begin{question}[Iterated proper-class blocks]\label{swo:gs:n15.8}
Determine the precise recursion strength needed to organize successive
canonical $\Ord$-blocks of a raw well-order along a prescribed index
order. Compare finite iteration, set-length iteration, and class-length
iteration.
\end{question}
One extraction is elementary; iterating a procedure whose state is a
class can require more. The distinctions involving $\ETR$ in
\cite{GitmanHamkins} provide the appropriate setting for a reverse-
mathematical analysis. Our direct comparison and branch recognition do
not by themselves solve this recursion problem.

\begin{question}[The condensed unrestricted order]\label{swo:gs:n15.9}
Classify the dense comparison obtained by collapsing the finite components
of \Cref{swo:gs:thm:condensation}. Which residual fibres remain detectable
from its bare order, and what embeds into it?
\end{question}
Finite adjacency is now fully described. The quotient can still contain
nontrivial fibres with infinite or proper-class residual carrier. It
would be incorrect to conclude from density alone that it is the set-like
order or an ordinary surreal-sized class.

\subsubsection{Effective bounds, coherence, and verification}
\begin{question}[Ordinal and birthday optima for supported completion]\label{swo:gs:n15.10}
Refine the cardinal reserve formula to optimal ordinal support bounds and
optimal birthdays of canonical support codes. Which optima are uniform
without an additional global choice parameter?
\end{question}
Two fresh reserves of the same cardinality can occupy very different
ordinal intervals. \Cref{swo:gs:thm:reserve} isolates the unavoidable
cardinality; ordinal placement and coding complexity remain separate.
A constructive version should specify the representation of partial
injections and the operation used to choose a complement bijection.

\begin{question}[Coherent cutoff embeddings]\label{swo:gs:n15.11}
Construct embeddings between the orders at different birthday cutoffs
which compose exactly and preserve a useful prefix filtration. Determine
which can also preserve cut types or finite condensation.
\end{question}
Appending an arbitrary tail preserves some comparisons but can change
the required enumeration type. A coherent reserve mechanism should be
chosen once for the whole system rather than separately at each pair of
cutoffs. The support theorem may help isolate its minimal size costs.

\begin{question}[First checked milestones]\label{swo:gs:n15.12}
Formalize the reserve theorem, elementary common-prefix comparison, and
set-sized cut trichotomy before attempting the class automorphism theorem.
Can the abstract alphabet interface support other saturated or
non-Archimedean ordered alphabets without changes to the proofs?
\end{question}
These milestones have explicit input and output types and no dependency
on a formal universe of all class well-orders. Their value is not merely
in reproducing finite tests, but in certifying the limit and cardinal
arguments that the tests cannot inspect.

\begin{question}[Typed constructions indexed by presentations]\label{swo:gs:n15.13}
Which algebraic or model-theoretic constructions can use the set orders
$\WO_\alpha(X)$ or uniformly coded global subfamilies as index orders,
while keeping every support and evaluation map within a specified
size level?
\end{question}
A promising first investigation should use a bounded index set, verify
that the output is independent of the chosen presentation in the intended
sense, and only then consider a uniform class version. The analogy with
Kanovei--Shelah is a guide to construction, not permission to use an
uncoded higher-order totality as a set.

\subsection{Source 18: revised research questions and priorities}
\label{swo:sh:sec:research}

The following are proposed directions left after the theorems above.
They are not presented as a list of previously catalogued open
problems. Each states the extra information that is still needed.

\subsubsection{Bounded order types and their completions}

\begin{question}[The arrangement of gaps]\label{swo:sh:n19.1}
For fixed $\kappa$, classify $\WO_\mu(\No_{<\kappa})$ up to order
isomorphism, or classify its completion together with the subset of
realized points. Which features go beyond the complete character
spectrum and the multiplicities proved here?
\end{question}
The new spectrum and counting formulas turn this into an arrangement
problem. In particular, a large family of gaps of one character may
have a highly nontrivial induced order. A first target is
$\kappa=\omega$, followed by $\omega_1$ under specified continuum
arithmetic. Equimorphism with a binary cube does not settle this.

\begin{question}[Longer fixed enumeration types]\label{swo:sh:n19.2}
Determine gap spectra and binary coding lengths for
$\WO_\alpha(\No_{<\kappa})$ when $\alpha>\mu+1$, especially
$\alpha=\mu\cdot2$ and $\mu\cdot\gamma+n$.
\end{question}
Density and cellularity are now known for every $\alpha$ of
cardinality $\mu$, and finite-tail point characters are explicit.
Later infinite blocks can use up an entire $\mu$-sized residual
region, so the minimal-type proof cannot simply be repeated.

\begin{question}[Noncardinal birthday bounds]\label{swo:sh:n19.3}
For a noninitial ordinal $\theta$, determine the spectrum of
$\WO_{|\No_{<\theta}|}(\No_{<\theta})$. Which ordinal features of
$\theta$ survive in interval sizes and cut characters?
\end{question}
The present proof uses the closure $\beta+\gamma<\kappa$ for
$\beta,\gamma<\kappa$, which may fail for $\theta$. The appropriate
replacement is a stratified description of sign cones, not a
substitution of $|\theta|$ for $\theta$.

\begin{question}[Coherent enlargement of cutoffs]\label{swo:sh:n19.4}
Construct embeddings between order spaces for increasing birthday
cutoffs that compose exactly, and specify whether they preserve
minimal enumeration length, prefix cylinders, finite condensation,
or selected cut characters.
\end{question}
Appending a fixed tail gives an embedding of full well-order spaces,
but need not preserve minimum-length strata or compose with a second
independently chosen tail. A global rank-layer schedule gives a
candidate for coherent full spaces; the sharper minimal-stratum
requirements remain separate.

\subsubsection{Class cuts, blocks, and automorphisms}

\begin{question}[Iterating the quotient rather than removing blocks]\label{swo:sh:n19.5}
Choose a precise limit rule and determine the strength of iterating
$R\mapsto B_R$ along specified class well-orders. Which fixed points,
periodic behaviors, or invariants occur?
\end{question}
The single decomposition and ordinary ordinal-indexed block removal
are elementary. The finite-support example is already a fixed point
up to isomorphism. Any claim that repeated condensation automatically
reduces complexity must confront that example. The axiomatic strength
of the genuinely iterated operation is not determined here.

\begin{question}[Order structure on represented class cuts]\label{swo:sh:n19.6}
Study the class cuts satisfying the straddling-prefix criterion,
with predicates marking exhaustive branches and residual tail types.
Which natural automorphisms of the bounded-support core preserve
that distinguished collection of cuts?
\end{question}
The criterion gives a recognition theorem. It does not classify the
automorphism action on all class cuts, or show that every automorphism
of the core extends to the global order. Baseline changes differing
on a proper class of positions are a concrete first case.

\begin{question}[The expanded countable model]\label{swo:sh:n19.7}
Classify
$({\Hall}^{\mathcal M},{\Hsl}^{\mathcal M})$, and then add
the evaluation relation to the surreal labels. Which features depend
on the countable class realization once the pure order has become
the same factorial shuffle?
\end{question}
The pure order cannot define set-likeness even with finite parameters.
An added predicate can therefore retain information that the shuffle
classification necessarily discards.

\begin{question}[$\omega$-nonstandard class models]\label{swo:sh:n19.8}
Describe the external finite-condensation blocks and the elementary
theory of $\Hall$ for countable $\omega$-nonstandard GBC models.
Do these orders share the first-order theory of the standard
factorial shuffle, while realizing additional types?
\end{question}
Internally finite permutation cylinders become externally infinite
discrete intervals. Standard finite adjacency chains inside them
already invalidate the standard classification. Determining the
possible global assembly of these intervals is a concrete
model-theoretic problem; no positive answer to the question is
claimed here.

\subsubsection{Words, encoding, and formalization}

\begin{question}[Sharp word-code bounds]\label{swo:sh:n19.9}
Optimize the birthday of explicit order embeddings of injective and
increasing words, recording separately preservation of numerical
order, prefix extension, and simplicity. Can the centered encodings
be made comparably efficient at singular stages?
\end{question}
The duplicated-sign delimiters provide transparent proofs, rather
than optimal codes. Uniform tree isomorphisms obtained by
back-and-forth supply little direct birthday control.

\begin{question}[The centered increasing order itself]\label{swo:sh:n19.10}
Classify the entire centered increasing-word order up to isomorphism
and determine the intrinsic definability of its all-negative cones
and its positive-limit points.
\end{question}
Its local characters, its complete set-cut obstruction, and the two
types of rooted cones are known here. The contrast between that
intrinsic information and the displayed entry signs makes the
automorphism problem meaningful.

\begin{question}[Weak choice and uniform constructions]\label{swo:sh:n19.11}
Which word-tree isomorphisms and class-core identifications can be
proved without Global Choice? For a specified operation, distinguish
existence, a uniform definable implementation, and an effective
implementation on concrete codes.
\end{question}
The explicit sign embeddings and many cut arguments need no Global
Choice. Our class isomorphisms use deterministic global
back-and-forth. These are different strength claims; a uniform
family of class maps should not be selected without proof.

\begin{question}[A first machine-checked milestone]\label{swo:sh:n19.12}
Formalize the elementary common-prefix relation and the
set-interval decomposition for a supplied class-model relation,
alongside the set-level ordinal spectrum and minimal permutation
cut trichotomy. Can one order-theoretic interface serve all four?
\end{question}
This is a realistic modular target because it avoids almost all
surreal arithmetic. The initial deliverables should expose their
size assumptions in the theorem signatures and make the
conventional proof-to-formal-statement correspondence reviewable.

\section{The sources' conclusions}\label{swo:sec:conclusions}

\merge\ Source~11 has no conclusion section; its summary is
\cref{swo:sec:status}. The conclusions of sources~12, 09 and~08 are printed
whole.

% ---- source 12, lines 1551-1577
\subsection{Source 12's conclusion}

There is a rigorous full lexicographic order of all global surreal
well-orders, provided it is understood as a relation on class objects,
not as an ordinary class containing those objects. Its comparison needs
no universal enumeration of abstract class order types: the largest
common \emph{labelled} prefix is elementary and sufficient.

The set-like suborder has a particularly uniform geometry. It fills
set-indexed cuts, contains every class linear order even locally, and is
equimorphic with binary classes on $\Ord$. The unrestricted order adds
new proper-class prefix phenomena, including finite adjacent blocks.
The diagonal theorem prevents either construction from being exhausted
by a same-level class of set codes.

At set-sized birthday bounds the theory becomes quantitative. The full
well-order space of a carrier of cardinality $\mu$ has exact ordinal
spectrum below $\mu^+$ and binary rank $\mu^+$. The minimal surreal slice
has rank $\mu$, except at singular strong-limit cutoffs, where it has
rank $\kappa\cdot\kappa$. This is an order-theoretic effect of cofinal
blocks of code lengths, invisible to cardinal counting alone.

The inaccessible-rank interpretation shows exactly how these facts can
coexist: internal classes and the external collection of all such
classes occupy different levels. Respecting those levels removes the
apparent paradox without weakening the embedding and universality
questions into trivialities.

% ---- source 09, lines 1524-1546
\subsection{Source 09's conclusions}
The lexicographic well-ordering problem has three different answers,
depending on its carrier. On a fixed set of surreals of size $\kappa$,
the exact ordinal spectrum stops at $\kappa^+$. Allowing arbitrary
set-length words gives a class-universal dictionary order, but prefix
limits give it local order properties different from those of $\No$.
For set-like global well-orders, first disagreement again defines a
linear comparison. Existence of a global enumeration is equivalent to
global choice over $\GB$ with set choice, and all global enumerations
cannot be collected into an ordinary class of set codes.

The eventual-agreement core resolves the constructive side of the
global problem: it is a genuine class, it is isomorphic to the surreal
line, it realizes every uniformly set-sized cut of global enumerations,
and it is dense in every global interval. Bounded reflection explains
why set-indexed configurations can always be studied in a suitable
bounded permutation stage. The explicit missing branch and binary
diagonal identify two independent boundaries: arbitrary class-sized
cuts need not have solutions, and no single uniform class-indexed
coding covers all global enumerations.

These boundaries are not paradoxes. They are the information needed to
state theorems at the correct logical level.

% ---- source 08, lines 1818-1843
\subsection{Source 08's conclusion}

The global enumeration problem has a particularly clean answer once
the types of objects are separated. Set-like well-orders of $\No$ are
represented by class bijections from $\Ord$, and numerical
first-disagreement gives a rigorous virtual linear order. That order
is large enough to encode every class binary word, yet its set-cut
geometry is already witnessed by a single class of set-supported
perturbations. This code class is another copy of the surreal line.

At a fixed set carrier, the structure is different: its exact ordinal
spectrum stops at the successor of the carrier cardinal, and finite
permutation tails account for every jump. At varying set carriers,
termination introduces new local cofinalities. For non-set-like
well-orders, a further index convention or relation code is necessary.
None of these distinctions is optional bookkeeping: each changes a
mathematical conclusion.

The principal proofs are elementary in their stated foundations.
Their formalization should begin with bounded objects and the
repository's existing sign-sequence cut theorem, and only then pass to
the uniform class formulation. The dense-skeleton theorem provides a
concrete target: it combines first-disagreement combinatorics,
controlled set support, small-cut filling, and universe-aware
back-and-forth without requiring a paradoxical collection of all
classes.

\subsection{Source 13: conclusions and result ledger}\label{swo:fs:sec:conclusion}

The strongest organizing principle is not that a single enormous
well-order has been discovered. It is that different notions of
``all'' and different representations produce distinct linear orders,
while a small collection of explicit tools connects them safely.

The fixed-set layer has its own cardinal and ordinal spectra. The
ordinary class of set words depends decisively on termination. The
full set-like enumeration domain has a surreal-sized dense core but
no exhaustive uniform class of set codes. The raw order domain expands
individual branch fibers, not the entire cut space of that core. A
higher-level product can exceed the dense core's capacity even though
ordinary class-indexed sums are absorbed. Finally, pure order
isomorphisms can change the prefix presentation itself.

The follow-up therefore gives explicit answers to several concrete
questions raised by the repository while leaving stronger
classification and minimal-axiom problems clearly identified. The
proofs and their stated size hypotheses are the basis on which these
conclusions should be evaluated.

% ---- source 14 (batch-81 manuscript 02), lines 1927-1955
\subsection{Source 14: conclusion}
The strongest organizing distinction is not between large and small
cardinalities alone. It is between set-coded presentations, class-valued
branches, and raw class relations with further tails. Prefix cylinders
make that distinction mathematically visible.

Every normalized class cut of the set-supported core either stops at
a cylinder edge, stops at a genuine numerical gap, or follows an
injective branch through all ordinals. Exhaustive well-orders are exactly
the branches that cover the alphabet. Because this criterion reconstructs
a graph using only set quantifiers and old parameters, it yields a
no-new-realization theorem for old cuts. Raw well-orders have the same
trace precisely when their canonical initial branches agree, leaving
an explicit residual well-ordering problem in each fiber.

Support restrictions provide a different axis of complexity. Allowing
support of cardinality $<\kappa$ gives exactly the cut-filling threshold
$\cf\kappa$, and the failure beyond it has an attained support cost.
All these layers still contain a copy of the full surreal order. Thus
class universality, density in an ambient comparison order, and
saturation are genuinely different properties.

The resulting theory remains paradox-free because each ``all'' has a
specified sort, each prefix has a specified size, and each use of
surreal cut filling has set option families. The automorphism-orbit theorem sharpens this distinction: bare-order
symmetries can exchange exhaustive traces with nonbranch boundaries.
The principal open targets are now the exhaustive-trace stabilizer, finer support invariants, and the
interaction between raw tail structure and higher class realizations.

% ---- source 17 (batch-81 manuscript 05), lines 1894-1919
\subsection{Source 17: conclusion}
The lexicographic ordering problem separates into several mathematically
substantial structures. On the minimal birthday-cutoff slice, the
relevant parameters are the cardinality $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$ and two different
cofinalities $r=\cf\kappa$, $q=\cf\mu$. Point characters are $(q,q)$,
cylinder cofinalities are $r$, and three distinct cut mechanisms give the
exact gap spectrum. Exhaustiveness is also the key issue in fusion:
a coherent full-length injection need not be a permutation.

The same distinction persists at class scale. A single lower class cut of
a supported core determines an injective global word exactly when its
labelled cylinders straddle at every ordinal length. A separate coverage
condition distinguishes exhaustive words. Reconstruction is elementary,
but exhaustion is invisible to the bare core order: a core automorphism
can carry an exhaustive branch gap to a nonexhaustive one. The represented-
cut predicate is therefore genuine additional structure, and same-set
class extensions change it while leaving the code carrier unchanged.

For unrestricted class well-orders, a proper-class prefix can leave a
finite residual alphabet. The resulting maximal adjacency components are
exactly the factorial blocks of a finite final segment; their condensation
is dense without becoming an ordinary class of all class orders. Across
all these conclusions, typing the objects and bounding the recursion
histories are part of the mathematics, not merely notational cautions.

The proof dependencies are short. Set cuts yield fresh
coefficients after deleting a set. Fresh coefficients and
bounded-support completion yield strong interpolation.
Strong interpolation yields density, local cofinality
statements, the \(\No\)-isomorphism, and cut coding.
Independently, the predecessor comparison yields convex
cones, the canonical initial-part decomposition, and the
finite-residual jump theorem. Pair swaps supply both
positive binary embeddings and the diagonal obstruction.

The bundled Python script checks finite instances of
the two comparison rules and of the sign encoding. It
checks 465 coefficient-code comparisons, 79,800
word-code comparisons, and 266,272 pairs of finite
permutations, with the predecessor rule checked in both
directions and the adjacency criterion compared with the
finite lexicographic order. These checks help detect a
reversed delimiter or an incorrect finite comparison.
They do not verify an ordinal induction, a class
comprehension argument, or a cardinal nonembedding
theorem.

The article contains full mathematical proofs for the
claims it promotes to theorems. It does not claim that
the new results have been checked in Lean, that the
whole repository has been audited, or that every
research question listed here is a previously published
open problem.

\subsubsection{What was checked}

The source audit read the merged surreal well-order article and README,
the reals report README, the project agent instructions, and the
specific sign-sequence and size-obstruction declarations listed above,
at revision \code{491ed8411cccf7bd57916eb7666bbba762e92f96}. The
audit was targeted, rather than a proof that no overlapping statement
occurs anywhere else in the repository. The new arguments were developed
and checked independently within this preparation, including the
set-theoretic scopes of the cut, block, topology, and termination proofs.
This is mathematical review, not a kernel proof or external peer review.

The accompanying Python script checks finite relation-prefix comparison,
the centered and prefix-first sign encodings, and the distinction between
relation-table and enumeration comparison. It evaluates finite surreal
sign strings as exact dyadic rationals, so the numerical side of the
encoding check is independent of the encoded lexicographic comparator.
Its successful finite tests do not establish class comprehension,
transfinite well-foundedness, cardinal arithmetic, or saturation.

The PDF was compiled from the included standalone LaTeX source and
checked for missing references, compilation errors, and layout defects.
The archive includes the source, PDF, finite diagnostic script and its
results, a short build guide, and a source/status note. A standard
TeX installation with the packages named in the preamble is sufficient:
\begin{verbatim}
latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode surreal_well_orders_further.tex
python3 finite_checks.py
\end{verbatim}
No network access is needed to compile the article or run the finite
checks. The bibliography gives pinned repository locations and primary
literature links for independent investigation.

\subsection{Source 09: verification and reproducibility}
\label{swo:ec:app:verification}
The accompanying \texttt{code/finite\_checks.py} uses only Python's
standard library. It checks finite versions of the pair-switch
lexicographic embedding, partial-prefix permutation completion, the
forced-prefix separator algorithm, support extension preserving first
disagreements, and the diagonal switch construction. Exact rational
arithmetic is used for the separator tests. A deterministic random seed
makes the sampled checks reproducible; other suites exhaust their
specified finite ranges.

\textbf{These checks do not verify any transfinite theorem.} Their role
is to detect indexing, orientation, and extension mistakes in the
finite combinatorial mechanisms. Proofs of the infinite statements
are the written arguments in the article. The recorded run passed 164,560 assertions, including 1,101 separator-family
cases. The test report is \texttt{data/finite\_checks.json}. The archive also contains a build
script and a theorem-status ledger.

To compile the article, run \texttt{bash build.sh} in the archive's root
directory. It makes three passes with \texttt{pdflatex}, resolves the
internal bibliography and cross-references, and writes build products
into \texttt{build/} before copying the finished PDF to the root.

\subsection{Source 08: finite regression checks}\label{swo:sk:app:tests}

The package includes \texttt{verify\_finite.py}, requiring Python 3.10
or later and only its standard library. Running it writes
\texttt{verification\_results.json}. The supplied run passed:
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}Y r@{}}
\toprule
Check & Instances \\
\midrule
Consecutive permutation pairs, sizes $1$ through $7$ & 5,906 \\
All increasing pairs of distinct permutations, sizes through $5$ & 7,432 \\
Pair-code order comparisons, bit lengths $0$ through $7$ & 21,845 \\
Sign words of lengths $0$ through $6$ & 127 \\
All sign-code order and prefix-free comparisons & 16,129 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

The permutation test checks both directions of the adjacency rule on
all manageable pairs, not just a few positive examples. The sign test
compares the numerical convention $-<0<+$ with the binary blocks
$00<01<11$, including pairs in which one sign word is a proper prefix.
The pair-code test checks that every output is a permutation of the
correct finite alphabet and that comparisons agree with the input
binary order.

These tests can detect a reversed pair orientation, a wrong terminal
block, or a mistaken finite-tail rule. They cannot prove regularity
arguments, transfinite stabilization, set/class separation, or the
existence of a global isomorphism. Those depend on the mathematical
proofs in the text.

\subsubsection{Specific dependency choices}

The fresh-value lemma uses an already constructed small-cut interface.
The dense-core interpolation argument is written out rather than
attributed only to a theorem name. The global product obstruction
explicitly reuses the earlier report's density and inverse-evaluator
method. The cut and automorphism theorems do not require its
singular-cardinal classification, and the central-word theorem does
not require surreal arithmetic. Thus a later correction in a
nonessential prior theorem would not automatically affect the main
new proofs.

\subsection{Source 13: reproducibility and finite checks}\label{swo:fs:app:checks}

The archive contains the standalone \code{article.tex}, its compiled
PDF, a build script, a standard-library Python checker, its recorded
JSON output, and a status note. No external image or private font file
is required. The bibliography is internal to the TeX source.

The finite checks cover the following distinct mechanisms. First,
they build well-order relations on finite alphabets and compare the
common-predecessor formula with direct permutation lexicography.
Second, they test convexity of every finite prefix cylinder and the
uniqueness and coherence of crossing prefixes at all finite cut
positions. Third, they test finite prefix completion. Fourth, they
compare the central-word sign code with independent rational values
of finite surreal sign sequences.

The test alphabets for the last group are
$-2,-1,-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,1,2$, with all words of length at most three,
including repeated-letter words. Finite signs are evaluated as dyadic
rationals, not merely re-compared by a second copy of the same
lexicographic function. The reserved-marker condition is also checked
by exhibiting the collision that would result from admitting a
trailing zero as a letter.

These tests do not establish class comprehension, ordinal-limit
coherence, global choice, the back-and-forth theorem, or a
transfinite birthday bound. They are reproducible checks of finite
instances and independent representations, with the logical trust
boundary stated explicitly.

\begin{lstlisting}
# Run from the extracted archive directory.
python3 code/finite_checks.py --output data/finite_results.json
bash build.sh
\end{lstlisting}

The build script runs three LaTeX passes to settle cross-references
and the table of contents. A PDF inspection record and checksums are
included in the delivery's status files.

\subsection{Source 14: finite diagnostics and reproducibility}
\label{swo:tc:app:tests}
The accompanying \texttt{verification.py} uses only Python's standard
library. It checks finite instances of the following kernels:
relation-based common prefixes versus enumeration prefixes; convexity
of prefix cylinders; the chain property of crossing prefixes at every
finite cut; extension of partial injections on a finite support;
preservation of all comparisons under support compression; finite
self-delimiting sign and word codes; and pair-orientation coding.
The exact tested ranges, case counts, and pass/fail results are written
to \texttt{verification\_results.json} by the delivered execution.
The delivered run passed every diagnostic. Its principal counts are:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lr@{}}
\toprule
Kernel & Tested cases or comparisons\\\midrule
Labelled common-prefix comparison & 15,018\\
Prefix cylinders / proper finite cuts & 2,371 / 867\\
Finite partial injections & 15,126\\
Compressed candidates / retained comparisons & 3,868 / 66,873\\
Numerical sign-code pairs & 16,129\\
Outer word-code pairs, two termination conventions & 320,000\\
Pair-orientation comparisons & 21,844\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Finite alphabets have endpoints and adjacent labels, unlike the residual
surreal alphabet. Therefore the finite crossing-prefix test checks the
chain lemma, not the full boundary trichotomy. The buffer argument for
infinite partial injections, cofinality at singular cardinals, Global
Choice, and class-model absoluteness are not experimentally verified.
Those assertions stand on their written proofs and remain appropriate
subjects for independent mathematical and formal review.

To reproduce the package locally:
\begin{lstlisting}
python3 verification.py
bash build.sh
\end{lstlisting}
The build script compiles the standalone source twice with
\texttt{pdflatex}; the bibliography is internal, so no external database
or network access is needed for compilation. Standard TeX packages named
in the preamble must be installed. \texttt{SHA256SUMS.txt} records the
delivered source, PDF, scripts, status files, and diagnostic output.
The archive does not include fonts, repository clones, or LaTeX auxiliary
files. The repository itself has not been modified.

\subsection{Source 14: source audit and bibliographic scope}
The primary repository inputs were read through the GitHub connector at
the pinned revision below. The targeted mathematical ranges were the

sections, the universe and formalization discussion, and the continuation
questions. The actual Lean simplicity file was separately inspected.
The metadata in the README distinguishes four source manuscripts from
their merged report. We did not treat their statements as kernel-verified
results or as established published literature.

External sources were used to check the Kanovei--Shelah indexing
construction, the distinction between elementary comparison and
class-valued recursion, and standard surreal background. The consulted
version of the class-recursion paper is explicitly dated in the
bibliography. No unresolved question quoted from it is asserted here
to remain open as of the present date. The new arguments in this article
are self-contained relative to the stated surreal set-cut theorem,
$\GBC$, and explicitly marked inherited set-spectrum results.

audit.

The primary literature was checked for the precise Kanovei--Shelah index,
surreal order versus simplicity, global choice, class well-foundedness and
ETR, and the standard interval-condensation mechanism. In particular the
countable condensation studied by Brown and Su\'arez is related methodology,
not the same as the model-relative set-interval condensation used here
\cite{BrownSuarez}. The final journal and arXiv versions of a source may
have different pagination; theorem references specify the version where
needed.

The accompanying \texttt{examples.py} regenerates the three-label table,
checks the explicit restriction reversal and the Boolean restriction bound,
and checks the finite predecessor-comparison formula. These calculations
are reproducibility aids for finite examples only. They do not validate
cardinal arithmetic, class comprehension, transfinite recursion, or the
new proper-class theorems.

The source is a standalone \LaTeX{} document with an internal bibliography
and no external figures. Build it with

latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error\\
surreal\_lexicographic\_orders.tex
\end{quote}

formulas, and page-layout defects. Mathematical review and layout review
are separate from formal proof checking.

\subsection{Source 17: finite checks and reproducibility}
\label{swo:gs:app:checks}

The package contains \path{finite_checks.py}, which requires only the
Python standard library. Its deterministic recorded run is in
\path{finite_checks.json}. The run passed all of the following checks:
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}Yr@{}}\toprule
Finite mechanism checked & Instances\\\midrule
Predecessor-signature comparison against tuple lexicography & 533,418\\
Exact adjacency condition against consecutive finite permutations & 266,272\\
Convexity of prefix cylinders, carriers of size at most 7 & 16,072\\
Uniqueness and coherence of straddlers at finite cut levels & 852\\
Finite partial-injection extension on its necessary support & 15,126\\
Prefix-free coefficient-code comparison & 961\\
Variable-length word-code comparison (400 words, repetitions allowed) & 160,000\\\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
The empty carrier and empty word are included where appropriate. The
coefficient tests use all sign sequences of length at most four. Word
tests use an alphabet of seven sign sequences of length at most two,
and words of length at most three. Finite partial injections are tested
on carriers of size at most six, including partial maps with fixed points.

These tests do not verify singular cardinals, limits of prefix chains,
class comprehension, large-gap homogeneity, or the necessity of an
infinite reserve. They are consistency checks on the finite mechanisms
used by the proofs, not experimental evidence for an unproved theorem.

To reproduce the checks and build the PDF from a TeX Live installation,

\subsection*{Source 12}
\paragraph{Title-page summary.}

% ---- source 12, lines 86-111
\textbf{Main distinction.} An arbitrary class well-order of $\No$ need not
have order type $\Ord$. Nevertheless, two such well-orders have an
\emph{elementarily definable largest common labelled initial segment},
possibly a proper class. This supplies a lexicographic comparison in GBC
without invoking general class well-order comparability or ETR.

\medskip
\textbf{Principal quantitative result.} Put
$\No_{<\kappa}=\{s:\alpha\to\{-,+\}:\alpha<\kappa\}$ and
$\mu=|\No_{<\kappa}|=2^{<\kappa}$, for an infinite initial cardinal $\kappa$.
The minimal-length permutation order satisfies
\[
\WO_\mu(\No_{<\kappa})\equim
\begin{cases}
\BB_{\kappa\cdot\kappa},&\mu=\kappa\text{ and }\cf\kappa<\kappa,\\
\BB_\mu,&\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\]
where $\BB_\gamma=(2^\gamma,<_{\lex})$ and $\equim$ means mutual
order-embeddability, not isomorphism.

\medskip
\textbf{Status.} This is an AI-assisted, unrefereed research manuscript.
Proofs are supplied for the stated results; historical priority is not
claimed. The accompanying exact finite tests do not verify the transfinite
arguments. No new Lean formalization is claimed.

% ---- hand chunk abs12_mid

\paragraph{Abstract.}

% ---- source 12, lines 117-143
We study the lexicographic order of well-orderings of the surreal numbers,
carefully distinguishing bounded sets of surreals, set-like global
well-orders, and arbitrary global class well-orders. For the full class
problem, ordinal-indexed enumerations are insufficient. We construct the
largest common labelled initial segment of two well-orders directly from
their relations, prove that comparison of their next elements defines a
linear order, and show that this construction needs only elementary class
comprehension once the well-orders exist. Over GB with set choice, the
existence of any class well-order of the surreals is equivalent to global
choice. The collection of all these well-orders is not itself an ordinary
class of GBC or Kelley--Morse theory; a diagonal theorem rules out any
uniform exhaustive coding by a class of sets.

For set-like global well-orders we prove density, interpolation for
set-indexed cuts, local universality for class linear orders, and mutual
embeddability with the lexicographic comparison of binary classes on
$\Ord$. For unrestricted global well-orders we classify adjacent pairs:
they arise precisely from finite residual permutations after a common,
necessarily proper-class, prefix. At a birthday cutoff $\kappa$, we obtain
an exact regular/singular dichotomy for the binary coding rank of
minimal-length enumerations. We also establish the exact ordinal and
binary-cube embedding spectra for the full set-sized order. Finally, a
full-class model based on an inaccessible rank explains exactly how the
bounded and global theories fit together, and provides a rigorous example
in which the full order and the set-like order have the same cardinality
and ordinal spectrum but different coding ranks. Explicit proof-assistant
interfaces and further research questions are included.

% ---- hand chunk abs09_head

\subsection*{Source 09}
\paragraph{Abstract.}

% ---- source 09, lines 98-124
The phrase ``the lexicographic order of all well-orders of the surreal
numbers'' has several mathematically different interpretations. We develop
three: exhaustive enumerations of a fixed set of surreals; all set-length
injective surreal words; and class bijections from the ordinals onto the
surreal numbers, representing set-like global well-orders. For an infinite
set $X$ of cardinality $\kappa$, we give a self-contained proof that its
lexicographic well-ordering space has cardinality $2^\kappa$, contains every
linear order of size at most $\kappa$, and contains an ordinal precisely when
that ordinal is below $\kappa^+$.

For the global problem, we work in G\"odel--Bernays set theory with global
choice and do not pretend that a collection of proper classes is itself an
ordinary class. Fix a global enumeration $b$. Its eventually-equal
perturbations admit canonical set codes. We prove that their lexicographic
order is isomorphic to the surreal line, meets every set-prefix cylinder,
and interpolates every uniformly set-indexed separated pair of families
of arbitrary global enumerations. Thus every class linear order embeds
into this genuine class core. We also prove bounded reflection for
set-indexed families, construct an explicit unfilled
$(\Ord,\Ord)$-configuration, and diagonalize against every uniform
class-indexed list of all global enumerations.

A strongly inaccessible truncation gives a fully set-sized model of the
size distinction: the core has cardinality $\kappa$, whereas all length
$\kappa$ enumerations have cardinality $2^\kappa$. The article includes
foundational and Lean formalization plans, a repository audit, finite
verification code, and a focused research agenda.

\subsection*{Source 08}
\paragraph{Abstract.}

% ---- source 08, lines 90-113
There is no single unqualified object called ``the lexicographic order of
all well-orders of the surreal numbers.'' We distinguish well-orderings of
a fixed set of surreals, well-orderings of varying set-sized subsets,
set-like well-orderings of the whole surreal class, and arbitrary class
well-orderings. For an infinite ordered set $X$ of cardinality $\kappa$, the
exhaustive-enumeration order $\W(X)$ has size $2^\kappa$, contains every
linear order of size at most $\kappa$, and contains an ordinal $\beta$
exactly when $\beta<\kappa^+$. Its adjacent pairs arise precisely from
finite permutation tails.

For the whole surreal class, work in G\"odel--Bernays set theory with
Global Choice. The numerical first-disagreement comparison of class
bijections $\Ord\to\No$ is meaningful without treating classes as elements
of classes. Fix one such bijection $b$. We prove that every set-sized
separated family of global enumerations has a strict separator obtained
from $b$ by a permutation of set support. The class of canonical codes for
these perturbations is therefore order-isomorphic to $\No$. It is a dense,
set-cut-realizing skeleton inside the much larger virtual enumeration
order, and every class linear order embeds into it. The full virtual order
is equimorphic with the lexicographic order of class binary sequences, but
admits no class-uniform exhaustive parametrization. We supply proofs,
cutoff versions, counterexamples to tempting identifications, a
universe-sensitive Lean implementation plan tied to inspected ProveIt
sources, and a research agenda.

\subsection*{Source 13}
\paragraph{Title page.} ``Further research report''. \emph{Lexicographic Orders of Surreal Well-Orderings: Cut reconstruction, asymmetric products, prefix non-rigidity, and size-safe foundations} (PDF metadata: ``Further Structure''). Research manuscript prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov, 3~October 2026.

\paragraph{Abstract.}
We further investigate the lexicographic comparison of well-orderings of
the surreal numbers, separating set-sized alphabets, set-length words,
set-like global enumerations, unrestricted class well-orders, and
code-dependent alternatives. The central new result is an exact
prefix-cylinder criterion for a normalized class cut of a surreal-sized
dense core to be represented by an injective ordinal-class word. Exhaustive
words are characterized by an additional label-coverage condition. Cuts
that fail the criterion have a first failure of one of two precisely
described kinds: a next-label cut or a limit-prefix boundary.

We prove an asymmetric product phenomenon. The global enumeration order
absorbs a surreal left factor, and more generally admits every ordinary
class-indexed lexicographic sum of copies of itself. Its two-point split,
however, does not embed back in the full inaccessible-universe
interpretation, nor by a definable uniform transformation in
Kelley--Morse theory with global choice. Externally countable models give
the opposite answer for unrestricted external maps. A finite-block
recoding automorphism shows that the pure linear order does not recover
its prefix cylinders. Finally, replacing end-first dictionary comparison
by a central termination convention on the nonzero alphabet makes both
arbitrary and injective set-length word orders isomorphic to the surreal line.

The proofs specify their logical size levels. An implementation plan uses
the repository's actual universe-indexed sign-sequence and small-cut
interfaces, without claiming a new Lean formalization.

\paragraph{Title-page status.}
\textbf{Research status.} AI-assisted, unrefereed mathematical manuscript.
The proofs are presented for scrutiny; historical priority and kernel
verification are not claimed. This is a follow-up to the repository's
merged report, not a replacement or a certification of all its results.
The inspected repository snapshot is pinned in \Cref{swo:fs:app:audit}.
Finite checks accompany the article, but do not establish transfinite or
class-theoretic theorems.

\subsection*{Source 14}
\paragraph{Title page.} ``Research continuation''. \emph{Lexicographic Well-Orders of the Surreals II: Cut classification, support thresholds, and class-model absoluteness}. Prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov, 3~October 2026.

\paragraph{Abstract.}
The earlier ProveIt reports identify a set-coded dense skeleton of the
lexicographic order of global surreal enumerations, but leave open which
cuts of that skeleton come from exhaustive enumerations. We answer the
prefix-structured version of that question. Every proper normalized class
cut of the skeleton has exactly one of three forms: an edge of a
set-prefix cylinder, a nonprincipal numerical gap after a set prefix, or
a coherent injective branch of length $\Ord$. The last form is realized
by a global well-order of set-like type exactly when its branch covers
every surreal. Reconstruction is elementary; a separate orbit theorem shows that
bare-order automorphisms can destroy exhaustive representability.

This yields an absoluteness theorem: enlarging the class part of a model
while retaining its sets and a fixed baseline enumeration cannot newly
realize an old skeleton cut by a global enumeration. New enumerations
have genuinely new trace cuts. For unrestricted labelled class
well-orders, the trace map forgets exactly the tail after the canonical
$\Ord$-long initial segment; its fibers are described explicitly.

A separate support analysis gives a sharp hierarchy. If $\kappa$ is an
infinite set cardinal, the permutations of a baseline with support of
cardinality $<\kappa$ form an $\eta_{\cf\kappa}$-order, but not an
$\eta_{(\cf\kappa)^+}$-order. A separated pair of $\cf\kappa$-long
families forces at least $\kappa$ moved coordinates, and this support
cost is attained in the full skeleton. Thus universality for ordinary
class linear orders can coexist with sharply limited saturation.

We distinguish fixed carriers, variable set domains, increasing
subclasses, global set-like orders, unrestricted class relations,
relation-code lexicography, and order-type quotients. The exposition
includes proofs, exact quantifier conventions, a repository audit,
universe-relative and Lean formalization plans, finite regression tests,
and a focused research agenda.

\paragraph{Title-page status.}
\textbf{Research status.} The new results below are proved in this manuscript,
not machine-verified. They are unrefereed and no claim of historical
priority is made. The cut classification is relative to the named prefix
cylinders; it is not a classification in the language of bare linear order
alone. The repository is unchanged.

\subsection*{Source 15}
\paragraph{Title page.} \emph{Lexicographic Orders of Surreal Well-Orders: Interpretations, canonical blocks, represented cuts, and fixed-type spectra}. ``A continuation of the ProveIt research report''. Research article prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov, 3~October 2026.

\paragraph{Abstract.}
There is no single unqualified object called the lexicographic order of all
well-orders of the surreal numbers. The carrier, representation, comparison
alphabet, indexing order, prefix convention, and foundational size level all
affect the answer. We give a systematic account of the principal
interpretations and develop three extensions of the existing ProveIt report.
First, the relation that a closed interval in a class well-order is a set
produces its entire canonical block decomposition by an elementary formula;
every class well-order can occur as the block-index order. Explicit ordinal
polynomials realize arbitrarily long class-indexed condensation histories.
Second, a cut of the bounded-support surreal core is represented by an
injective ordinal-class word exactly when every set-length level has a
cylinder meeting both sides. First failure gives an exhaustive description
of terminal cuts, including repeated-label obstructions and limit-prefix
boundaries. The lower-core-cut map forgets exactly the residual well-order
after the first proper block. Third, for birthday cutoffs we extend the
minimal-slice dichotomy to enumeration types consisting of any admissible set number of
full cardinal blocks followed by a finite tail, with exact binary coding
lengths. Exact local characters and the saturation threshold are computed
for every cardinal birthday cutoff. Complete proofs, counterexamples, foundational assumptions, source
provenance, and a prioritized research program are included.

\paragraph{Title-page status.}
\textbf{Status.} This is an AI-assisted, unrefereed research exposition.
``Extension'' means a deduction beyond the audited repository report, not a
claim of historical priority. Its new theorems have written proofs and
independent mathematical review within this task. They have not been checked
by Lean or another proof assistant. Finite calculations check only the
explicit finite examples.

Repository revision inspected: \texttt{0ecd158fd163bc4aca0ee40ccf6479ca6cf5f2a8}.

\subsection*{Source 16}
\paragraph{Title page.} ``Order theory and foundations''. \emph{Lexicographic Orders of Surreal Well-Orders: Cuts, Canonical Blocks, and the Limits of Set-Sized Coding}. ``A further study of the ProveIt research program''. Research article prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov, 3~October 2026.

\paragraph{Abstract.}
The phrase ``the lexicographic ordering of all well-orders of the surreal
numbers'' describes several substantially different objects. We separate
well-orders on a fixed set, ordinal-length words, numerically increasing
subsets, set-like global well-orders, arbitrary class well-orders, and
relation-table encodings. Building on the ProveIt report, we establish
several extensions. For every infinite alphabet we compute the density and
cellularity of every fixed enumeration stratum, including a transition at
three terminal positions, and prove that every stratum fails conditional
Dedekind completeness. At regular saturated stages we determine the complete
cofinality spectrum of unfilled cuts. For global enumerations we give an
exact prefix-cylinder criterion for the cuts represented by injective
ordinal-class branches, with an additional criterion for exhaustiveness.
Every failure has a first coordinate or limit-prefix obstruction. For an
arbitrary class well-order, the elementary relation ``the interval between
these points is a set'' simultaneously extracts all its canonical
ordinal-class blocks, without elementary transfinite recursion. We also
classify alternative termination conventions, sharpen a comprehension bound
for uniform nonembedding, and give a formalization plan that distinguishes
smallness, Lean universes, and internal class semantics. All new results are
presented with ordinary mathematical proofs; no claim of historical priority
or machine-checked verification is made.

\paragraph{Title-page status.}
\textbf{Repository snapshot.}
\texttt{491ed8411cccf7bd57916eb7666bbba762e92f96}.\\
The source audit is targeted. The article is independent of later changes
to the repository, and its new theorems are not additions to the Lean library.

\subsection*{Source 17}
\paragraph{Title page.} \emph{Lexicographic Well-Orders of the Surreal Numbers, II: Exact cut spectra, branch recognition, optimal support reserves, and automorphism-extension obstructions}. Research manuscript prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov, 3~October 2026.

\paragraph{Abstract.}
We continue the ProveIt report on lexicographic well-orders of surreal
numbers, separating set-sized enumeration spaces, set-length words,
set-like global well-orders, unrestricted class well-orders, and
relation-code orders. For every infinite cardinal $\kappa$, put
$X=\No_{<\kappa}$, $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$, $r=\cf\kappa$, and $q=\cf\mu$.
For the minimal-length enumeration order
$P=\WO_\mu(X)$ we prove that every point has two-sided character $(q,q)$,
that $\cf P=\ci P=r$, and that density, weight, and cellularity are
$\mu^{<\mu}$. Its nonprincipal cut-character spectrum is exactly
\[
 \{(r,r),(q,q)\}\ \cup\
 \{(\theta,r),(r,\theta):\theta\in\Reg,\ \theta<\mu\}.
\]
Here $\Reg$ denotes the infinite regular cardinals.
These statements require neither regularity of $\kappa$ nor
$2^{<\kappa}=\kappa$. We also establish an exact saturation threshold and
a fusion theorem for dense open sets.

In $\GBC$, we give a necessary-and-sufficient cylinder criterion for a
class cut of a bounded-support surreal core to represent an injective
$\Ord$-word; a separate coverage condition characterizes exhaustive
words. The reconstruction is elementary and needs no $\ETR$. This yields
an exact criterion for extending core automorphisms to the full global
enumeration order and an obstruction: some core automorphisms do not
extend. Proper extensions of the available classes necessarily add new
represented cuts while leaving the set-coded core unchanged. A cardinal
deficiency formula gives the optimal number of additional moved positions
needed to extend a set partial injection to a supported permutation.
We also identify maximal finite adjacency components in the unrestricted
order and show that their quotient is dense. All higher-order statements
are formulated without a same-level class of classes.

\paragraph{Title-page status.}
\textbf{Status.} The new assertions have ordinary mathematical proofs in
this manuscript. They are not claimed to be historically first,
peer-reviewed, or Lean-verified. The repository was read at the pinned
revision stated in \Cref{swo:gs:sec:audit}; it was not modified or built.
Finite checks supplied with this article test finite mechanisms, not the
transfinite theorems. The remaining questions are explicitly distinguished
from the results proved here.

\subsection*{Source 18}
\paragraph{Title page.} \emph{Lexicographic Well-Orders of the Surreal Numbers: Cuts, canonical class blocks, and changes of interpretation}. Research article prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov, 3~October 2026.

\paragraph{Abstract.}
The phrase ``the lexicographic ordering of all well-orders of surreal
numbers'' describes several different objects. We give a common framework
for well-orders of fixed sets, fixed enumeration types, set-length words,
numerically increasing words, ordinal-indexed global enumerations, and
arbitrary class well-orders. We retain the repository's elementary
comparison by common labelled prefixes and develop its unresolved
topological and foundational questions.

For $X=\No_{<\kappa}$ and $\mu=2^{<\kappa}$ we compute the density,
cellularity, point characters, saturation threshold, and complete
Dedekind-gap character spectrum, including exact multiplicities, of the
minimal permutation order $\WO_\mu(X)$. A third terminal position causes its density and cellularity
to reach $2^\mu$. For arbitrary class well-orders, an elementary
set-interval equivalence yields a canonical decomposition into
$\Ord$ blocks and a final set ordinal, without ETR. The quotient can be
isomorphic to the original order. An exact prefix criterion recognizes
which class cuts of a dense core are represented by global well-orders;
a repeated-label cut gives an explicit obstruction. We also classify the external full
lexicographic order of every countable $\omega$-standard GBC model as a
dense shuffle of finite chains of factorial sizes, and show that its pure
order does not define the set-like fragment. Finally, termination
conventions distinguish word orders isomorphic to $\No$ from orders with
limit-prefix obstructions and even adjacent pairs.

All new claims are supplied with conventional proofs. Their status is
relative to a pinned repository snapshot, without a claim of literature
priority or machine verification. Explicit size boundaries and a staged
formalization plan accompany a revised research agenda.
